    Important Words
    • avikṛtāḥ — actually undisintegrated
      A- (privative) + vikṛta (transformed, modified). The total material energy never actually disintegrates; the apparent diversity is phenomenal, not ontological. A direct argument against the naive realist who takes the multiplicity of elements as ultimate.
    • virājam — the cosmic manifestation
      From vi-√rāj — 'to shine forth, manifest'. The virāj-puruṣa is the universal form, the gross body of Bhagavān's external energy. Gauḍīya reading: virāj is real (Bhagavān's body) but is not the supreme — the puruṣottama is beyond and within it.
    • guṇaiḥ — by the modes of nature
      Instrumental plural of guṇa. The three modes are the actual operators of material change; Bhagavān remains untouched by them even while in their midst. Sattva, rajas, tamas are His servants, not His conditioners.
    • tat-guṇa-agrahaḥ — untouched by their qualities
      Tat (their) + guṇa (modes) + agraha (non-seizure, non-grasping). Bhagavān is in the modes (san api) yet does not absorb their nature. The classic 'lotus leaf in water' position — present but unwet. Key against the Māyāvāda mistake that liberation means escaping qualities; for the Vaiṣṇava, qualities are escaped while remaining engaged.
    • sarva-ātmanaḥ — the soul of all
      Sarva (all) + ātmā (self). Bhagavān is the ātmā of every ātmā — the Paramātmā within the jīvātmā. NOT 'all is ātmā in monistic non-difference' but: He is the indweller of every individual self. Acintya-bhedābheda: one as ātmā-of-ātmās, distinct as paramātmā from jīvātmā.
    • ātma-vastunaḥ — the substance of every self
      Ātmā (self) + vastu (substance, reality) + genitive. Bhagavān is the very substance underlying every conscious being. The Gauḍīya gloss: the jīva borrows its very being from Him every instant — quintessential bhedābheda.
    The mahat-tattva, the total material energy, is undivided, but because of the material modes of nature, it appears to separate into earth, water, fire, air and ether. Because of the living energy [jīva-bhūta], these separated energies combine to make the cosmic manifestation visible, but in fact, before the creation of the cosmos, the total energy is already present. Therefore, the total material energy never actually enters the creation. Similarly, although You are perceived by our senses because of Your presence, You cannot be perceived by the senses, nor experienced by the mind or words [avāṅ-mānasa-gocara]. With our senses we can perceive some things, but not everything; for example, we can use our eyes to see, but not to taste. Consequently, You are beyond perception by the senses. Although in touch with the modes of material nature, You are unaffected by them. You are the prime factor in everything, the all-pervading, undivided Supersoul. For You, therefore, there is no external or internal. You never entered the womb of Devakī; rather, You existed there already.
    Purport

    This same understanding is explained by the Lord Himself in Bhagavad-gītā (9.4) : mayā tatam idaṁ sarvaṁ jagad-avyakta-mūrtinā mat-sthāni sarva-bhūtāni na cāhaṁ teṣv avasthitaḥ “By Me, in My unmanifested form, this entire universe is pervaded. All beings are in Me, but I am not in them.” The Supreme Personality of Godhead is not perceivable through the gross material senses. It is said that Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s name, fame, pastimes, etc., cannot be understood by material senses. Only to one who is engaged in pure devotional service under proper guidance is He revealed. As stated in Brahma-saṁhitā (5.38) : premāñjana-cchurita-bhakti-vilocanena santaḥ sadaiva hṛdayeṣu vilokayanti One can see the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Govinda, always, within oneself and outside oneself, if one has developed the transcendental loving attitude toward Him. Thus for people in general, He is not visible. In the above-mentioned verse from Bhagavad-gītā, therefore, it is said that although He is all-pervading, everywhere present, He is not conceivable by the material senses. But actually, although we cannot see Him, everything is resting in Him. As discussed in the Seventh Chapter of Bhagavad-gītā, the entire material cosmic manifestation is only a combination of His two different energies, the superior, spiritual energy and the inferior, material energy. Just as the sunshine is spread all over the universe, the energy of the Lord is spread all over the creation, and everything is resting in that energy. Yet one should not conclude that because He is spread all over He has lost His personal existence. To refute such arguments, the Lord says, “I am everywhere, and everything is in Me, but still I am aloof.” For example, a king heads a government which is but the manifestation of the king’s energy; the different governmental departments are nothing but the energies of the king, and each department is resting on the king’s power. But still one cannot expect the king to be present in every department personally. That is a crude example. Similarly, all the manifestations that we see, and everything that exists, both in this material world and in the spiritual world, are resting on the energy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The creation takes place by the diffusion of His different energies, and, as stated in the Bhagavad-gītā, He is everywhere present by His personal representation, the diffusion of His different energies. One may argue that the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who creates the whole cosmic manifestation simply by His glance, cannot come within the womb of Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva. To eradicate this argument, Vasudeva said, “My dear Lord, it is not very wonderful that You appeared within the womb of Devakī, for the creation was also made in that way. You were lying in the Causal Ocean as Mahā-Viṣṇu, and by Your breathing, innumerable universes came into existence. Then You entered into each of the universes as Garbhodakaśāyī Viṣṇu. Then again You expanded Yourself as Kṣīrodakaśāyī Viṣṇu and entered into the heart of all living entities and entered even within the atoms. Therefore Your entrance into the womb of Devakī is understandable in the same way. You appear to have entered, but You are simultaneously all-pervading. We can understand Your entrance and nonentrance from material examples. The total material energy remains intact even after being divided into sixteen elements. The material body is nothing but a combination of the five gross elements — namely earth, water, fire, air and ether. Whenever there is a material body, it appears that such elements are newly created, but actually the elements are always existing outside of the body. Similarly, although You appear as a child in the womb of Devakī, You are also existing outside. You are always in Your abode, but still You can simultaneously expand Yourself into millions of forms. “One has to understand Your appearance with great intelligence because the material energy is also emanating from You. You are the original source of the material energy, just as the sun is the source of the sunshine. The sunshine cannot cover the sun globe, nor can the material energy — being an emanation from You — cover You. You appear to be in the three modes of material energy, but actually the three modes of material energy cannot cover You. This is understood by the highly intellectual philosophers. In other words, although You appear to be within the material energy, You are never covered by it.” We hear from the Vedic version that the Supreme Brahman exhibits His effulgence and therefore everything is illuminated. We can understand from Brahma-saṁhitā that the brahmajyoti, or the Brahman effulgence, emanates from the body of the Supreme Lord. And from the Brahman effulgence, all creation takes place. It is further stated in the Bhagavad-gītā that the Lord is the support of the Brahman effulgence. Originally He is the root cause of everything. But persons who are less intelligent think that when the Supreme Personality of Godhead comes within this material world, He accepts material qualities. Such conclusions are not mature, but are made by the less intelligent.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The mahat-tattva, the total material energy, is undivided, but because of the material modes of nature, it appears to separate into earth, water, fire, air and ether. Because of the living energy [jīva-bhūta], these separated energies combine to make the cosmic manifestation visible, but in fact, before the creation of the cosmos, the total energy is already present. Therefore, the total material energy never actually enters the creation. Similarly, although You are perceived by our senses because of Your presence, You cannot be perceived by the senses, nor experienced by the mind or words [avāṅ-mānasa-gocara]. With our senses we can perceive some things, but not everything; for example, we can use our eyes to see, but not to taste. Consequently, You are beyond perception by the senses. Although in touch with the modes of material nature, You are unaffected by them. You are the prime factor in everything, the all-pervading, undivided Supersoul. For You, therefore, there is no external or internal. You never entered the womb of Devakī; rather, You existed there already.
    Commentary

    This verse gives an example. You enter into Devaki’s womb just like the undifferentiated mahat tattva and other elements (ime) enter the universe but do not enter it, or appear to be created but actually are not. Though you appear to be born, you are not. The maha tattva, possessing within it various distinct elements such as earth, joining with consciousness, creates the material universe. Though the elements appear to have entered into the creation (anugata iva), because they remain present outside as well, one cannot say they have entered. Though they appear to arise within the universe, they actually existed before the universe. The elements are touched by the gunas , but you as the supreme cause are not touched by the gunas, though you enter into the universe. Though you are perceived as full of qualities which can be perceived by the intelligence, you, full of bliss, do not accept the qualities of matter, whose essence is suffering. Why? Because you are not covered by the gunas of matter. Those who are covered by the material gunas take up those qualities. The gunas do not contaminate you internally or externally. The jiva however, contacts the objects of sound and touch externally, and internally experiences lamentation, and illusion. Not only you , pervading everywhere as Paramatma (sarvatmanah), but also all objects related to you in the spiritual world (atma vastunah), such as the devotee, dhama and pastimes, are untouched by matter.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Though you seemed to have entered mahat-tattva and other elements it is impossible. This is explained in two verses. Entering means that a person outside enters within. Since the elements already existed as the cause (with effect inherent in them) and simply manifest as the effect within the universe, they really do not enter. Since you are the supreme cause, you also do not enter or touch the universe. Thus, though you have this nature, when you enter, it is your great mercy. Śrīdhara Svāmī explains this. Guṇaiḥ can mean “with qualities” or “with objects.” You exist with qualities such as being under the control of prema. You have attraction to such qualities. These qualities can be inferred by intelligence but not realized. Na tat-samaś cābhyadhikaś ca dṛśyate: the Lord has no equal or superior. (Śvetāśvatāra Upaniṣad) Why can we not understand you? You are everything (sarvasya). You are the giver of consciousness to all beings or you spread everywhere (savrātmanaḥ). You exist by yourself. You are the highest goal which appears by itself (ātma-vastunaḥ). Therefore you are constantly filled with unlimited qualities since you are always controlled by the prema of your devotees (tad-guṇāgraḥ). Thus you have appeared as our son. This is the greatest result for us.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    You do not enter the elements or, though you do not enter, you enter. An example is given. This is explained in two verses. Because at first mahat-tattva and other elements were the cause, and existed separately as coverings, they do not enter the universe (iha), though they seem to enter. The total material energy is undivided, but because of various potencies it appears as separate elements. Combining together, the elements produce the universe. Or though the energy is undivided, by manifesting your (te) māyā-śakti (tathā), the various elements produce the universe. Or because the elements exist separately, by an inconceivable method (tathā), they do not enter the universe. Or for many births I have known your glories. But today I have become successful. Starting in verse 13, Vasudeva explains. For many lives I have directly known you as most worthy of worship. This he explains in three lines. I have become successful because you have entered Devakī’s womb, though you are beyond prakṛti. His entering Devakī is further described in verses 15-16.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa never 'entered' Devakī's womb — He was already there, all-pervading yet personal, untouched by the guṇas; sense-perception cannot grasp Him, only bhakti can.
    Practical Applications
    • When you catch yourself imagining Kṛṣṇa as a localized object 'out there,' pause and remember: He already pervades this room, this body, this breath — speak to Him as already-present.
    • Refuse to reduce Kṛṣṇa to 'energy,' 'consciousness,' or 'the Self' today — name Him personally in your prayer, even once, as the Supreme Person who is simultaneously inside and outside everything.
    • Apply the senses-have-limits principle concretely: when your mind insists 'if I can't perceive Him, He must not be real,' answer it as Vasudeva did — eyes cannot taste, yet taste exists; reach for Him through hearing and chanting (śravaṇa-kīrtana) instead.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I still treating Kṛṣṇa as one more 'thing' my senses must verify before I trust Him — and what would change today if I accepted that He is already inside and outside the situation I am trying to control?
    • Which area of my life am I quietly running on the assumption that I am the cause and container of what happens there, when in truth the energies were already in place long before I arrived?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Before opening Instagram or checking results (exam scores, crush replies, internship outcomes), pause for ten seconds and remember: Kṛṣṇa is already in this scroll, this notification, this room — He didn't 'arrive' when something good happened. Practice noticing Him in the boring seconds, not just the dopamine hits.
    • When a friend group pressures you to drink, hook up, or mock someone — recall sann api tad-guṇāgrahaḥ. Kṛṣṇa is present in the room, untouched by what is happening. You are not unwitnessed at parties just because no parent is there. Let that change what you do, not as fear, but as the dignity of being constantly accompanied.
    • Pick one course, sport, or skill where you secretly believe 'I have to do this alone, Kṛṣṇa is busy with bigger things.' This verse says He is sarvātmā — fully present in your calculus problem, your audition, your gym set. Bring Him into one specific micro-task today and see if your performance comes from a less anxious place.
    householder
    • When you walk into your house tonight after work, before greeting anyone, stop at the threshold and recall: Kṛṣṇa was in this house all day while I was away. My family was never alone. This shifts how you re-enter — not as the provider arriving with fresh attention, but as one returning to a place He has been holding.
    • Make a financial or career decision this week — a job change, a big purchase, a school for the kids — by first acknowledging He is already inside the outcome, not waiting outside it. Then act with full effort and offer the result. The verse refuses the modern householder's split between 'sacred time' (morning sādhana) and 'real life' (the spreadsheet).
    • With your spouse this week, have one disagreement consciously aware that Kṛṣṇa is the antaryāmī of both of you — the same Supersoul in both hearts. Notice how it changes whether you fight to win versus fight to find truth. Real karuṇā here is serving the soul of your spouse, not just keeping the peace at the cost of avoiding things.
    senior
    • Sit with the line 'You never entered the womb of Devakī; rather, You existed there already' and apply it to your own death. He will not 'come for you' at the end — He is already in the room, already in the body, already the witness of every breath you have ever taken. Practice dying into a presence that was never absent.
    • Identify one attachment — a property, a role in the family, a grudge from decades ago, a reputation — and recognize that whatever spiritual reality it pointed toward was already fully present in Kṛṣṇa. Loosening the grip is not loss; it is recognizing the sunshine was always coming from the sun, not from the object you mistook for the source.
    • Mentor one younger person this month — a grandchild, a junior at the temple, a neighbor's son — not by giving advice, but by helping them see that Kṛṣṇa is already in their college admissions, their marriage anxiety, their career confusion. Your legacy at this stage is not your accomplishments but your capacity to point others toward the One who was always there.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Sliding from 'beyond the senses' into impersonalism — concluding Kṛṣṇa is a formless field rather than the Supreme Person who simply cannot be grabbed by gross perception.
    • Using the verse's 'all-pervading' language as a license to skip sādhana — telling oneself 'He is already everywhere, so I do not need to chant, hear, or serve under guidance' — when the verse and purport explicitly say He is revealed only through pure devotional service under proper guidance.
    • Mistaking the mahat-tattva analogy for pantheism — thinking the material elements ARE Kṛṣṇa, instead of seeing that He is the source untouched by the modes, simultaneously within and aloof.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Vasudeva tells Kṛṣṇa, 'You did not enter Devakī's womb — You were already there.' Share with your partner: where in your own life have you mistakenly thought Kṛṣṇa 'arrived' (a kīrtana, a temple visit, a crisis) when in fact He was already present? Where do the two of you genuinely disagree about whether His presence is constant or episodic?
    • The verse insists Kṛṣṇa is sann api tad-guṇāgrahaḥ — touching the guṇas yet untouched. Take a hard test case together: a corrupt politician who chants, an abusive parent who 'does pūjā,' a celebrity guru caught in scandal. Does this verse let them off the hook? Does it let us off the hook? Push each other — do not settle for a polite middle.
    • Vasudeva uses a rigorous philosophical argument (mahat-tattva, the elements pre-existing the body) to steady himself in a moment of terror — Kaṁsa's prison, an infant about to be killed. Discuss: when has abstract tattva actually helped you in a concrete crisis, and when has it felt like a cope? Where does your group disagree on whether 'philosophy' is a real shelter or a distraction from bhakti?
    Role Play

    Two students. Student A is a college senior who just got rejected from medical school for the second time and has begun saying, 'Maybe Kṛṣṇa was never really with me — if He were, this wouldn't have happened.' Student B is a friend from the same bhakti-vṛkṣa group. Using SB 10.3.15-17 — that Kṛṣṇa is anāvṛta, all-pervading, never absent, with no inside or outside — Student B must console A without (a) flattening the pain into 'it's all māyā,' (b) promising A will get in next year, or (c) drifting into impersonalism ('the Self is always there'). After 5 minutes, swap. Then debrief: where did the verse actually help, and where did it feel like a verse being weaponized to shut down grief?

    Objections & Responses
    • If Kṛṣṇa is everywhere already, why bother with temple worship, deity service, or pilgrimage? This verse seems to make ritual redundant — He's in my room as much as in Vṛndāvana.
      Vasudeva is not arguing that Kṛṣṇa is uniformly accessible — he is arguing Kṛṣṇa is uniformly present. Those are different claims. The sun is everywhere by its rays, but you still need eyes, and you still face the sun to feel its warmest. Prabhupāda quotes Brahma-saṁhitā: premāñjana-cchurita-bhakti-vilocanena santaḥ sadaiva hṛdayeṣu vilokayanti — only the eye anointed with prema-bhakti actually sees Him. Deity worship, the holy dhāma, the verses of Bhāgavatam — these are the collyrium. Without them, omnipresence is a doctrine you assent to; with them, it becomes a Person you meet. The verse refutes the idea that He is absent; it does not refute the means by which we come to perceive Him.
    • This sounds exactly like pantheism or the 'divine spark' spirituality I hear from yoga teachers — God is in everything, everything is God, find the divinity within. Why call this Gauḍīya if it sounds like every other monism?
      Read the verse again — it says the opposite of monism. mat-sthāni sarva-bhūtāni na cāhaṁ teṣv avasthitaḥ: all beings rest in Me, but I am not in them. Kṛṣṇa is sarvātmā, the Supersoul of all, but He remains a distinct, transcendent Person — Devakī's son, Yaśodā's child, the flute-player of Vṛndāvana. The pantheist collapses Kṛṣṇa into the creation; this verse maintains the creation rests on Kṛṣṇa while He stands aloof, anāvṛta, uncovered by any of it. Prabhupāda is explicit: less intelligent persons think when He appears here He becomes material. The 'divine spark' line erases the personhood that the entire Bhāgavata-dharma is built on. We are not seeking the Self; we are seeking Him, and He has a name, a form, parents, and a flute.
    Analogy

    Five colored threads woven into one cloth seem to be five different things, but the cloth was never not-one — the loom held all five together from the start. So with the mahat-tattva and the five gross elements: they look like separate energies pieced together, but the total energy was whole before the weaving. Bhagavān is the loom; nothing was ever truly assembled or truly disassembled.

    Stories
    Kapila's instruction to Devahūti

    In SB 3.25–33, Kapiladeva — Bhagavān as the original teacher of Sāṅkhya — instructs His mother Devahūti precisely on the order of the elements: how mahat-tattva differentiates into ahaṅkāra, then the tan-mātras, then the gross elements. The taxonomy in this verse is Kapila's taxonomy.

    The Gauḍīya line preserves the Sāṅkhya enumeration but corrects its godless interpretation: the elements do not self-organize; the puruṣa-avatāra Viṣṇu glances upon prakṛti, and the cascade begins. Vasudeva's prayer is reciting Kapila's catechism back to its Author.

    Important Words
    • ātmanaḥ — of the self
      Genitive of ātman. Gauḍīya distinction: ātman here means jīvātmā — the individual soul — to be distinguished from Paramātmā and from Brahman. The fool conflates the body with the jīvātmā; the wise see the jīvātmā as distinct from the body AND as eternally subordinate to Paramātmā.
    • dṛśya-guṇeṣu — in the visible (bodily) qualities
      Dṛśya (visible) + guṇa (quality, attribute). The visible attributes of the body — color, age, strength, beauty. The locative says: he is 'situated AMONG' these features and mistakes his being for them. Sharp diagnostic — modern identity-formation lives entirely in dṛśya-guṇa.
    • abudhaḥ — a fool, rascal
      A- (privative) + budha (one who has buddhi, intelligence). Without intelligence. Strong word; Prabhupāda translates 'rascal' to keep the bite. Bhakti-śāstra does not soften the diagnosis: bodily identification is not a mild error but the foundational stupidity from which all suffering flows.
    • vinā anuvādam — without analytical consideration
      Vinā (without) + anuvāda (reflection, repeated discussion). The fault is not just ignorance but unwillingness to think it through. Modern variant: refusing the inquiry 'what am I, really?' because the answer would unsettle the comfortable identification.
    • tyaktam — rejected
      Past participle of tyaj — 'to abandon, give up'. The śāstra-vādins have already rejected the body-as-self conclusion, yet the fool keeps clinging. The word marks the gap between śāstric availability and personal acceptance — a perennial failure.
    • upādadat — accepts (anyway)
      Present participle of upā-√dā — 'to take up, accept, appropriate'. The fool actively reaffirms what has been refuted. Bondage is not passive ignorance; it is active mis-identification, renewed every moment.
    One who considers his visible body, which is a product of the three modes of nature, to be independent of the soul is unaware of the basis of existence, and therefore he is a rascal. Those who are learned have rejected this conclusion because one can understand through full discussion that with no basis in soul, the visible body and senses would be insubstantial. Nonetheless, although his conclusion has been rejected, a foolish person considers it a reality.
    Purport

    Without the basic principle of soul, the body cannot be produced. So-called scientists have tried in many ways to produce a living body in their chemical laboratories, but no one has been able to do it because unless the spirit soul is present, a body cannot be prepared from material elements. Since scientists are now enamored of theories about the chemical composition of the body, we have challenged many scientists to make even a small egg. The chemicals in eggs can be found very easily. There is a white substance and a yellow substance, covered by a shell, and modern scientists should very easily be able to duplicate all this. But even if they were to prepare such an egg and put it in an incubator, this man-made chemical egg would not produce a chicken. The soul must be added because there is no question of a chemical combination for life. Those who think that life can exist without the soul have therefore been described here as abudhaḥ, foolish rascals. Again, there are those who reject the body, regarding it as insubstantial. They are of the same category of fools. One can neither reject the body nor accept it as substantial. The substance is the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and both the body and the soul are energies of the Supreme Godhead, as described by the Lord Himself in Bhagavad-gītā (7.4-5): bhūmir āpo ’nalo vāyuḥ khaṁ mano buddhir eva ca ahaṅkāra itīyaṁ me bhinnā prakṛtir aṣṭadhā apareyam itas tv anyāṁ prakṛtiṁ viddhi me parām jīva-bhūtāṁ mahā-bāho yayedaṁ dhāryate jagat “Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intelligence and false ego — all together these eight comprise My separated material energies. But besides this inferior nature, O mighty-armed Arjuna, there is a superior energy of Mine, which consists of all living entities who are struggling with material nature and are sustaining the universe.” The body, therefore, has a relationship with the Supreme Personality of Godhead, just as the soul does. Since both of them are energies of the Lord, neither of them is false, because they come from the reality. One who does not know this secret of life is described as abudhaḥ. According to the Vedic injunctions, aitadātmyam idaṁ sarvam, sarvaṁ khalv idaṁ brahma: everything is the Supreme Brahman. Therefore, both the body and the soul are Brahman, since matter and spirit emanate from Brahman. Not knowing the conclusions of the Vedas, some people accept the material nature as substance, and others accept the spirit soul as substance, but actually Brahman is the substance. Brahman is the cause of all causes. The ingredients and the immediate cause of this manifested material world are Brahman, and we cannot make the ingredients of this world independent of Brahman. Furthermore, since the ingredients and the immediate cause of this material manifestation are Brahman, both of them are truth, satya; there is no validity to the expression brahma satyaṁ jagan mithyā. The world is not false. Jñānīs reject this world, and foolish persons accept this world as reality, and in this way they are both misguided. Although the body is not as important as the soul, we cannot say that it is false. Yet the body is temporary, and only foolish, materialistic persons, who do not have full knowledge of the soul, regard the temporary body as reality and engage in decorating this body. Both of these pitfalls — rejection of the body as false and acceptance of the body as all in all — can be avoided when one is fully situated in Kṛṣṇa consciousness. If we regard this world as false, we fall into the category of asuras, who say that this world is unreal, with no foundation and no God in control ( asatyam apratiṣṭhaṁ te jagad āhur anīśvaram ). As described in the Sixteenth Chapter of Bhagavad-gītā, this is the conclusion of demons.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    One who considers his visible body, which is a product of the three modes of nature, to be independent of the soul is unaware of the basis of existence, and therefore he is a rascal. Those who are learned have rejected his conclusion because one can understand through full discussion that with no basis in soul, the visible body and senses would be insubstantial. Nonetheless, although his conclusion has been rejected, a foolish person considers it a reality.
    Commentary

    But can the material gunas bestow some sort of happiness? This verse answers. He is unintelligent who thinks that the objects seen such as a woman, garland etc. are enjoyable, because they give misery, lamentation and illusion, since they can only be possessed temporarily. They induce one to repeated birth. The mimasakas conclude that wealth and possessions are the most valuable things and think themselves intelligent. But their arguments are not without rebuttal. They don’t have true wisdom. What the devotee rejects with scorn they accept with eagerness.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “The devatās sometimes appear as a son to some people. Why are you attached to me being your son?” Two verses answer. Other than you, the supreme creator and cause, others cannot be the goal since they are not independent. Or the person who discerns a devatā as supreme, since among them that devatā has attractive qualities directly perceivable (ātmanaḥ dṛṣyaḥ guṇeṣu), without giving regard to you, the root of all forms, (sva-vyatirekataḥ) is a fool since the devatā subject to perception (tad-manīṣitam) is not supreme (samyak), since one cannot discern the truth without mutual discussions (anuvādam), without devotional association. That person accepts what is rejected by the devotee.

    Personal Guidance
    Body and soul are both real energies of Kṛṣṇa — neither reject the body as illusion nor cling to it as the self; honor both in His service.
    Practical Applications
    • Today, when grooming or feeding the body, do it as upkeep of Kṛṣṇa's property — not as servicing 'me,' and not as something to despise.
    • Notice when you slip into 'I am this body' or its mirror 'the body is nothing' — and correct yourself to: both are His energies.
    • Refuse the asura conclusion that the world is unreal or godless; speak and act today as if every atom rests on Kṛṣṇa.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I quietly behaving as if my body is independent of the soul — decorating it, fearing for it, identifying with it — even though I would never say so aloud?
    • Which side of the abudhaḥ ditch do I tend to fall into more often: treating the body as all-in-all, or dismissing it as unreal — and what does that pattern reveal about my unwillingness to see Kṛṣṇa as the substance behind both?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the two camps in your feed this week: the gym/skincare/optimization camp that worships the body, and the 'nothing matters, it's all a simulation, vibes only' camp that dismisses it. Name one friend in each camp — and remember the verse calls both abudhaḥ. Don't pick a side; serve the soul in each.
    • Before your next exam, do not pray 'help me get the marks' (body-as-everything) and do not say 'marks don't matter, I'm a soul' (body-as-illusion). Instead: study with full effort because this body and intelligence are Kṛṣṇa's energy, and offer the result to Him. Watch how that changes your anxiety.
    • On social media you curate a 'self' — angles, filters, captions. Sit for ten minutes tonight and ask: which version of me am I defending when someone unfollows? The decorated body, or the soul? If the answer is the body, you have just met the abudhaḥ this verse describes — and you can choose differently tomorrow morning.
    householder
    • In family decisions this week — schools, medical care, finances — refuse both extremes: the materialist 'only the body and its security matter' and the bypasser 'it's all māyā, why bother planning.' Plan rigorously, provide thoroughly, and offer the whole effort to Kṛṣṇa as His energy serving His energy.
    • When raising your children, teach the body's care (sleep, food, exercise, study) as sādhana, not as ultimate goal. Tell them once this week, in plain words: 'Your body is real and your soul is real — both belong to Kṛṣṇa, and that is why we take care of both.' Watch what they do with that.
    • In your career, name the one decision you have been postponing by telling yourself 'it's all temporary anyway.' That is jñānī-style escapism wearing spiritual clothes. Make the decision this week with full karma-yoga seriousness — the work is Kṛṣṇa's energy; do it well and offer the fruit.
    senior
    • As the body's strength wanes, watch carefully for the tempting drift into 'the body was never real anyway' — the verse warns this is the same foolishness as the young man who thought it was everything. Care for the body as Kṛṣṇa's energy until the last day; do not abandon it philosophically before He withdraws you from it.
    • In mentoring younger family members, do not let your hard-won detachment curdle into dismissiveness about their worldly concerns — their marriages, mortgages, careers. Their world is not false. Counsel them as one who has seen both the body's limits and its sacred function as a vehicle for service.
    • Spend one session this month writing down what you are leaving behind — property, relationships, reputation — and beside each item write: 'energy of Kṛṣṇa, returning to Kṛṣṇa.' Not 'illusion I am escaping' and not 'treasure I am losing.' This is the dhīra's vyatireka, performed in real time as life closes.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking 'the body is not the self' for 'the body is false' — sliding into the māyāvāda position the verse explicitly rejects, and then neglecting bodily duties under a spiritual pretext.
    • Swinging to the opposite extreme: treating the body as substantial in its own right — pouring time, money, and anxiety into its decoration as if it had any standing apart from the soul and Kṛṣṇa.
    • Using 'everything is Brahman' as a flat slogan that erases personal surrender to Kṛṣṇa, instead of seeing that body and soul are both His energies and therefore both call for engagement in His service.
    Discussion Prompts
    • The verse calls a person abudhaḥ (foolish) for treating the body as independent of the soul. In your circle of family and friends, which side does the culture lean toward more aggressively today: 'the body is everything' (materialist decoration) or 'the body is nothing real' (spiritual bypassing)? Share a concrete example of each from the past month.
    • Prabhupāda insists 'the world is not false' and rejects the slogan brahma satyaṁ jagan mithyā. Where in your own sādhana have you been quietly using the world's unreality as a reason to avoid responsibility — work, family, money, the body's care? Push back honestly on each other: where is renunciation real, and where is it cosplay?
    • The verse hinges on the word vyatireka — distinguishing what is dependent on what. Practice it out loud: pick one thing you treasure (a relationship, a skill, this body) and walk your partner through whether it has independent existence or is an energy of Kṛṣṇa. Where does the argument get hard? Where do you catch yourself talking like an impersonalist?
    Role Play

    A teacher splits the class into trios. One student plays a college freshman whose roommate has just discovered a popular wellness influencer who teaches that 'the body is just a vessel, an illusion — only awareness is real,' and is now neglecting sleep, nutrition, and class attendance to 'transcend.' A second student plays the freshman's mother, a Sunday-school materialist who insists 'the body is the only thing that's real — get a job, eat protein, forget this nonsense.' The third student plays a Gauḍīya elder visiting campus, who must — in five minutes, without lecturing — show both that they are abudhaḥ in the same way: one rejecting the body as false, the other accepting it as all in all. The elder must land the point that both body and soul are energies of Kṛṣṇa, and offer one concrete next step to each. Rotate roles so every student plays the elder.

    Objections & Responses
    • Modern biology has explained life entirely through chemistry and DNA. The 'soul' is an unfalsifiable holdover. Prabhupāda's egg-in-the-incubator challenge is just an argument from ignorance — give science another fifty years.
      Notice what the verse actually does: it does not stop at 'the body needs a soul' — it goes further and says rejecting the body as insubstantial is equally foolish. So the Gauḍīya position is not anti-science; it is anti-incompleteness. Chemistry is real, DNA is real — these are Kṛṣṇa's bhinnā prakṛti, His separated material energy, described in BG 7.4. What chemistry cannot account for is the parā prakṛti, the conscious knower who experiences the chemistry. The challenge is not 'wait and see if you can build life'; it is: in your own first-person experience right now, can you reduce the one who is reading these words to the words themselves? If not, you have already met the jīva. Science describes the inferior energy beautifully. It is silent, by method, about the superior one.
    • But many respected Vedāntists — Śaṅkara's followers — teach exactly brahma satyaṁ jagan mithyā. Who is Prabhupāda to call that conclusion foolish? Isn't this just sectarian Vaiṣṇava polemics?
      It is not sectarian; it is textual. The verse itself, spoken before any Gauḍīya commentary, says samyag yatas tyaktam upādadat pumān — the foolish person picks up again what has already been thoroughly rejected by careful analysis. Kṛṣṇa Himself in BG 7.4–5, which Prabhupāda quotes in the purport, calls both matter and the living entities His prakṛti — His energies. An energy of the Real cannot be unreal; it can only be temporary, dependent, and misunderstood. The Gauḍīya line, following Śrī Caitanya, holds acintya-bhedābheda: the world is simultaneously one with and different from Kṛṣṇa, inconceivably. That preserves the personal Lord, the reality of His energies, and the seriousness of our service in this world. To dismiss the jagat as mithyā is, as the purport warns, to slip toward the asura's view in BG 16.8 — asatyam apratiṣṭhaṁ te jagad āhur anīśvaram. The disagreement is not about respect; it is about what the verse will and will not allow us to say.
    Analogy

    A man stands before a mirror and shouts at the reflection for being late to dinner — never noticing that the reflection cannot eat. The materialist who identifies with his body is shouting at the reflection: scolding the image, dressing it, polishing it, mourning when it cracks — and never feeding the one who actually stands there. Vasudeva names this folly with exact charge: abudhaḥ, rascal.

    Stories
    Bharata Mahārāja reborn as a deer

    Bharata Mahārāja, in SB 5.7–9, became so attached to a baby deer that at the moment of death his consciousness was on the deer; he took a deer's body in his next birth. The point of the story is that bodily identification — even at one remove, even with a beloved animal — sets the next body.

    The folly Vasudeva names here is the same: treating dṛśya-guṇeṣu, the visible bodily features, as one's real identity. Bharata's deer-life is the parable of the principle this verse states philosophically.

    Maitreya questioning the four Kumāras

    When the four Kumāras — eternal child-sages — appear in SB 3.15, they are not identified by their bodies (which appear as five-year-olds) but by their fixed consciousness in Bhagavān. The Bhāgavata is contrasting them with the materialists Vasudeva indicts: the Kumāras KNOW the body is not the self, and so their bodies remain forever young.

    Bodily identification ages the body; ātma-jñāna leaves it untouched. The fool grasps what cannot be held; the wise see through what cannot be the self.

    Important Words
    • anīhāt — from the one free of endeavor
      A- (privative) + īhā (effort, striving). Bhagavān does not 'work' to maintain creation. Unlike the impersonal Brahman of some schools (which cannot act), AND unlike a strained demiurge (which must labor), He governs effortlessly — His nature itself is the principle of order.
    • aguṇāt — from the one untouched by guṇas
      A- (privative) + guṇa. Nirguṇa in the proper Vaiṣṇava sense — not 'without qualities' (Bhagavān is overflowing with infinite spiritual qualities) but 'untouched by the material modes'. This is the precise Gauḍīya reading against the Advaitin reading.
    • avikriyāt — from the unchanging one
      A- (privative) + vikriyā (modification, change). His svarūpa never changes even as His līlā unfolds. Eternally Kṛṣṇa, eternally young, eternally in Vraja. The fixed point on which the cosmic dance turns.
    • brahmaṇi — in the Supreme Brahman
      Locative of brahman. In Vasudeva's mouth, brahman = parabrahman = Bhagavān. The Gauḍīya doctrine that Brahman, Paramātmā, and Bhagavān are three aspects of the same tattva — with Bhagavān as the fullest — is implicit. Brahman is not a separate impersonal reality but Bhagavān's effulgence.
    • tvat-āśrayatvāt — because of being sheltered in You
      Tvat (You) + āśraya (shelter, dependence) + tva (abstract suffix) + ablative. Because everything has its existence by sheltering in Bhagavān, the cosmos works automatically. Key sambandha-tattva word: every existing thing is āśraya-dependent on Him.
    O my Lord, learned Vedic scholars conclude that the creation, maintenance and annihilation of the entire cosmic manifestation are performed by You, who are free from endeavor, unaffected by the modes of material nature, and changeless in Your spiritual situation. There are no contradictions in You, who are the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Parabrahman. Because the three modes of material nature — sattva, rajas and tamas — are under Your control, everything takes place automatically.
    Purport

    As stated in the Vedas: na tasya kāryaṁ karaṇaṁ ca vidyate na tat-samaś cābhyadhikaś ca dṛśyate parāsya śaktir vividhaiva śrūyate svābhāvikī jñāna-bala-kriyā ca “The Supreme Lord has nothing to do, and no one is found to be equal to or greater than Him, for everything is done naturally and systematically by His multifarious energies.” ( Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8) Creation, maintenance and annihilation are all conducted personally by the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and this is confirmed in Bhagavad-gītā ( mayādhyakṣeṇa prakṛtiḥ sūyate sa-carācaram ). Yet ultimately the Lord does not need to do anything, and therefore He is nirvikāra, changeless. Because everything is done under His direction, He is called sṛṣṭi-kartā, the master of creation. Similarly, He is the master of annihilation. When a master sits in one place while his servants work in different duties, whatever the servants are doing is ultimately an activity of the master, although he is doing nothing ( na tasya kāryaṁ karaṇaṁ ca vidyate ). The Lord’s potencies are so numerous that everything is nicely done. Therefore, He is naturally still and is not directly the doer of anything in this material world.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O my Lord, learned Vedic scholars conclude that the creation, maintenance and annihilation of the entire cosmic manifestation are performed by You, who are free from endeavor, unaffected by the modes of material nature, and changeless in Your spiritual situation. There are no contradictions in You, who are the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Parabrahman. Because the three modes of material nature-sattva, rajas and tamas—are under Your control, everything takes place automatically.
    Commentary

    From your statements that you are the creator through prakrti it is understood that prakrti is your energy and non different from you. You are the material cause of the universe. But you are without contact with the gunas internally or externally. How is that possible? This verse answers the question. O Lord, the sruti says that creation, maintenance and destruction of the universe arise from you, who are without action, quality and change. But how can the creator be inactive? Though you are Brahma and Siva, the creator and destroyer, at the same time you are without action (aniha), You are the reservoir of opposite qualities. How? Because you are the shelter of the gunas, the action of creation and destruction are ascribed upon you. Though prakrti is the Lord’s energy ,it is his external energy. It is not his svarupa or svabhava. Thus you are not in contact with the gunas internally or externally. This conclusion is established here. Or, how can my son be Brahma and Siva? Actually you are not Brahma or Siva--you are the shelter of both. You says this yourself: brahmano hi pratithaham. Brahma says: adyo’vatarah purusah parasya... Since you are the shelter of Brahma and Siva (tad asrayatvat) you are called the creator and destroyer indirectly. The qualities of a person being sheltered are often ascribed to the shelterer. Just as when the country is fortunate, the king is called fortunate. In this way you are Brahma and Siva. This is also in accordance with the concept of rasa. The form of Krsna is distinct in terms of rasa, though though he is one with other forms of the Lord. Brahma, Siva and Krsna are one form: Rasenotkrsyate krsna rupam esa rasa sthiti. (bhaki rasamrta sindhu)

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Śṛīdhara Svāmī explains this verse. This explanation is based on that. Anīhāt means the Lord is without disturbance or without change since he is devoid of anything except his svarūpa. Though there are transformations by the guṇas, there is no fault in you since you are only its material cause. There may be a doubt that you can also be the indirect cause (nimitta) (since you are also the material cause). You are actually Brahman in nature (brahmaṇi), and only by attribution of guṇas does it seem that you undergo change. Or you are established as the possessor of unlimited qualities, as the faultless cause of everything since you are both the efficient and material cause as proved by your statement (tvattaḥ) prakṛtiś ca pratijṣā-dṛṣtantanurodhena: Brahman is also the material nature (prakṛti) because this view is not contradicted by the statements and examples given in the scriptures. (Brahma-sūtra 1.4.23) The fear of contradiction is refuted starting with words like vibho (O Lord!) The three words aguṇāt, akriyāt and anīhāṭ are explained as follows. Though you have no relationship with the three guṇas (aguṇāt), because you are the material cause, you seem to become the guṇas. But there is no possibility that you can deviate from your svarūpa (anīhāt). Because you are the efficient cause, you have no external or internal actions (akriyāt). Therefore you are called vibhu. Kṛtsna-prasakti-niravayava-śabda-vyāpako vā: the jīva is absorbed in activity with all his parts for it is said that the jīva has no parts. (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.26) Therefore statements about you are untrue, because we see that you are worshipped in different forms, and thus not situated in one place. But this statement does not apply to you, if you are accepted as the efficient cause. Śrutes tu śabda-mūlatvāt: the defects if the jīva do not apply to Brahman because of the declaration of scripture; scripture is the root of knowledge about spirit. (Brhama-sūtra 2.1.27) The wise speak from authority when they say that you are the cause, maintenance and destruction of everything. What doubt can there be if the śruti, the self-manifesting authority, says that you are beyond the four defects, that you are without material guṇas and that you are the cause of the universe? There is no contradiction here. You are the one form of supreme bliss without change (brāhmaṇi) but also the Lord possessing all inconceivable śaktis (īśvare). The cintāmaṇi or load stone remain unchanged though they attract other objects or pieces of iron. acintyāḥ khalu ye bhāvā tāns tarkeṇa yojayet prakṛitbhyaḥ paraṁ yac ca tad acintyasya lakṣaṇam Inconceivable states are not subject to material logic since they are beyond the material situation. That is the quality of the inconceivable. Mahābhārata There is no contradiction in you, who are the supreme cause with various inconceivable śaktis working together, as proved by the Purāṇas. All contradictions on both sides are eliminated by strongly establishing the inconceivable śakti. There is no alternative to this. There can be no opposing arguments because this śakti is supremely suitable to the Lord, being superior to all else, and since it is devoid of dependence on matter and ignorance, being supreme bliss beyond words and mind. “That’s alright. In the spiritual world, the Lord with his śakti is faultless with his six qualities. But as the cause of the material world possessing śaktis of the three guṇas, full of fault, he becomes faulty.” You are the shelter of the material śakti. Because this śakti is only a shadow, you cannot be contaminated by the faults of matter. On the other hand, the guṇas do not function unless they take shelter of you. Though the guṇas act as the cause, this is only a product of your inconceivable power.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “Why should I be worshipped?” The knowers of the Vedas or the Vedas say that the creation of the universe comes from you who are without desire, who depend on nothing else, who are devoid of relationship with material guṇas, and who are devoid of transformations like anger. Or Lord (vibho), endowed with all powers! You are able to carry out creation, maintenance and destruction of the universe, being superior to it, as previously described. The three descriptive terms mentioned indicate the Lord’s independence from prakṛti. But still you create (without desire), maintain (without guṇas) and destroy the world (without anger). “This looks like a contradiction.” Just as for the one person who is the Lord and Brahman there is no contradiction since all the powers belong to Brahman, beyond māyā, so there is no contradiction if the Lord produces the material universe. “There is no contradiction within the absolute truth, but there is contradiction in creating the universe which is māyā.” The creation takes place in you by the guṇas of māyā, since you are the shelter of those guṇas. There is no contradiction whether you have or do not have a relationship with the guṇas, Or you are continually served by the guṇas, since you are their shelter. No one else is. Because of that, there is no contradiction. You are to be worshipped because of your form of power.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa effortlessly directs creation, maintenance, and dissolution through His energies — surrender removes your imagined burden of being the doer.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one moment today when you grasp for control of an outcome, and consciously hand it back to Kṛṣṇa as the true director.
    • Before each task, whisper that Kṛṣṇa is the akartā who acts through His śaktis — then act with full effort but without the weight of proprietorship.
    • Refuse the ahaṅkāra-thought 'I made this happen' tonight when reviewing your day, and instead name three places His energies carried the work.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I straining and 'endeavoring' as if I were the doer, when the verse says even the cosmos itself unfolds under Kṛṣṇa's effortless glance — what would it look like to act today as His instrument rather than as the proprietor of outcomes?
    • Which of the three guṇas — sattva, rajas, or tamas — is currently driving the activity I most identify with as 'mine,' and how does recognizing that this guṇa is itself under Kṛṣṇa's control change the way I approach my next task?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Before your next exam, formally place the result at Kṛṣṇa's feet — study with full intensity, then refuse the 3 a.m. spiral of 'what if I fail.' The fruit is His department; the effort is yours.
    • Notice this week how social media trains you to believe you are the doer — every post a bid for credit. For one full day, do something genuinely good (help a classmate, clean up a space) and tell no one. Feel what it is like to act without claiming.
    • When a friend group dynamic goes sideways and you feel powerless, remember: the guṇas are moving through everyone, including you. Your job is not to control the outcome but to act in sattva — speak truth gently, refuse gossip, take shelter in Kṛṣṇa instead of in your peer group's approval.
    householder
    • In the next family financial decision (a job change, a school choice, a big purchase), do the homework rigorously, then explicitly hand the outcome to Kṛṣṇa before deciding. Watch how much of your stress was about pretending to be the controller.
    • When your child's life is not unfolding the way you planned — grades, friendships, choices — practice tvad-āśrayatvāt: take shelter in Him rather than in your parental ahaṅkāra. Your duty is faithful action (sva-dharma as parent), not engineered outcomes.
    • At work, when a project succeeds, resist the inner claim 'I did this' for thirty seconds before the next thought. When it fails, resist the inner claim 'I caused this collapse' for the same thirty seconds. Both are ahaṅkāra; both block real surrender.
    senior
    • Look at the institutions, businesses, or family roles you built and are now releasing. Practice seeing them as His all along — you were a servant in the master's house. The release is lighter when you were never the owner.
    • When you mentor someone younger, refuse the temptation to take credit for their growth or blame for their stumbles. Plant, water, and step back — the unfolding is under His direction, not yours. This is the dhīra-bhāva applied to legacy.
    • As the body's transitions accelerate — health, energy, independence — meditate on anīhād aguṇād avikriyāt: He is changeless. Each loosening attachment is a chance to rest more fully in tvad-āśrayatvāt, taking shelter in the One who does not change while everything around you does.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking Kṛṣṇa's nirvikāra (changeless, non-endeavoring) nature for the impersonalist's inactive, attribute-less Brahman — and quietly drifting from devotion to a personal Lord into worship of a vague 'stillness' or 'consciousness.'
    • Using 'everything happens automatically under His control' as a license for fatalism or laziness — neglecting one's sva-dharma and sādhana on the pretext that Kṛṣṇa is doing it all anyway.
    • Reading 'free from endeavor' as meaning Kṛṣṇa is distant or uninvolved, and thereby losing the intimacy of the personalist relationship — forgetting that creation, maintenance, and annihilation are conducted personally by Him through His śaktis.
    Discussion Prompts
    • The verse says Kṛṣṇa is anīhā — without endeavor — yet creation, maintenance, and annihilation are personally His. Share with your partner: where in your own life have you confused 'doing nothing visible' with 'doing nothing real'? Where have you mistaken visible exertion for actual potency? Push back if your partner gives a tidy answer.
    • Prabhupāda's purport compares the Lord to a master who sits still while servants run his estate. Discuss honestly: does this metaphor land for you, or does it feel like a justification for absentee authority? If you resist it, name what you resist — and let the others press you on whether the resistance is philosophical or just modern egalitarian conditioning.
    • The verse insists there is 'no contradiction' in the Lord — guṇa-less yet master of guṇas, changeless yet originator of all change. Where in your own sādhana do you demand a non-contradictory God on your terms (only loving, only just, only personal, only impersonal)? What gets exposed when Kṛṣṇa refuses to be flattened?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A is a working professional who has just been passed over for a promotion despite a year of relentless effort; she is convinced the universe is unjust and that 'if there were really a God in charge, this would not have happened.' Student B is her older Vaiṣṇava friend who has been studying SB 10.3.19. Student B must, without quoting the verse academically, help Student A see that (a) the Lord is anīhā — His non-doing is not absence, (b) the guṇas operating 'automatically' under His control include the rajas of her workplace and her own ahaṅkāra of expecting fruits, and (c) tvad-āśrayatvāt — taking shelter in Him — is the only stable footing. After 6 minutes, switch roles with a new scenario: a parent whose child has fallen seriously ill. The teacher then asks each pair: where did you slip into material compassion? Where did you offer real compassion?

    Objections & Responses
    • If Kṛṣṇa is 'free from endeavor' and everything happens automatically through the guṇas, then He is functionally identical to an impersonal law of nature. Why insist on a Person at all? This sounds like dressed-up deism.
      The verse itself anticipates this and refutes it: tvayīśvare brahmaṇi no virudhyate — there is no contradiction in You, the Supreme Person who is also Parabrahman. A law cannot direct; it can only describe. The guṇas do not self-organize into cosmos, sustenance, and dissolution — they are upacaryate, served, by taking shelter in Him (tvad-āśrayatvāt). Prabhupāda's master-and-servants image is exact: the master's stillness is not absence but sovereignty. The impersonalist collapses the master into the activity of the servants and then wonders where the master went. The Gauḍīya line holds both: He acts personally, and yet na tasya kāryaṁ karaṇaṁ ca vidyate — His potencies (śakti) do the work because they are His, not in spite of Him.
    • Saying 'everything takes place automatically because the guṇas are under His control' is a perfect recipe for fatalism — and worse, it lets the powerful off the hook. Famine, injustice, abuse: all just guṇas doing their thing under divine management?
      This is the same confusion Arjuna had on the battlefield, and the Gītā's whole pivot is the answer. The verse does not say you have no role; it says the Lord is the ultimate śṛṣṭi-kartā so that you can act without the crushing burden of imagining you are. That is the opposite of fatalism — it is the foundation of karma-yoga (BG 2.47, in your related verses). You still act; you act as His instrument, with nyāya, with kāruṇya, with pratijñā. Real compassion — serving the soul — requires you to oppose abuse, feed the hungry, speak the truth. What the verse forbids is the ahaṅkāra of thinking you, separately from Him, are the doer or the rescuer. Fatalism says 'nothing I do matters.' This verse says 'everything you do matters, but never as your independent act — always as service under His shelter.'
    Analogy

    Watch a master conductor with a symphony of a hundred musicians. He never plays a note. He stands still, raises his hands, and the music creates, sustains, and resolves itself by his presence and signal. Bhagavān's role in creation, maintenance, and annihilation is exactly this — never moved, never strained, yet all three guṇas perform their parts under His silent eye.

    Stories
    Kṛṣṇa as charioteer at Kurukṣetra

    Kṛṣṇa never lifts a weapon, never aims an arrow — yet at Kurukṣetra He controls the entire field. Holding the reins of Arjuna's chariot, He maneuvers, instructs, and at one point lifts the Sudarśana to test the warriors. The whole war proceeds 'tvat-āśrayatvāt' — by being grounded in Him.

    The verse's image fits exactly: anīhāt (without endeavor), aguṇāt (untouched by guṇas), avikriyāt (unchanging), He governs all events. Arjuna's hand draws the bow; the cosmic order draws breath from Kṛṣṇa's stillness behind it.

    Important Words
    • tri-loka-sthitaye — for the maintenance of the three worlds
      Tri (three) + loka (world) + sthiti (maintenance) + dative. The threefold cosmos — bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ — is held in being by Viṣṇu specifically. The white-Viṣṇu form is the sustaining function. Pure personalist cosmology: maintenance is the work of a Person.
    • sva-māyayā — by His own (internal) energy
      Sva (own) + māyā. Important distinction: this is NOT the māyā that deludes the jīva (which is bahiraṅga-māyā) but Bhagavān's own (svarūpa-śakti / yoga-māyā). The trimūrti forms are projections of His internal energy for cosmic governance — līlā, not delusion.
    • śuklam — the white (form)
      Śukla — white, pure. The color of sattva, of Viṣṇu, of dharma in its purest expression. Iconographically the white form of Viṣṇu maintains; in Gauḍīya theology this whiteness is the satya-yuga manifestation, distinct from but issuing from the original Kṛṣṇa-svarūpa.
    • raktam — the reddish (form)
      Rakta — red, the color of rajas. Brahmā's reddish complexion corresponds to the creative function in the mode of passion. Creation requires activity, drive, multiplication — all rajasic. Bhagavān assumes the color of the function He performs.
    • kṛṣṇam ca — and the dark (form)
      Kṛṣṇa here means 'dark-colored' — Śiva's complexion at the time of annihilation, the color of tamas. The same syllables that name svayaṁ bhagavān also name the destructive function's color, but the Gauḍīya gloss is firm: Kṛṣṇa-the-name belongs primarily to the all-attractive Person; the kṛṣṇa-varṇa of annihilation is a different reference.
    My Lord, Your form is transcendental to the three material modes, yet for the maintenance of the three worlds, You assume the white color of Viṣṇu in goodness; for creation, which is surrounded by the quality of passion, You appear reddish; and at the end, when there is a need for annihilation, which is surrounded by ignorance, You appear blackish.
    Purport

    Vasudeva prayed to the Lord, “You are called śuklam. Śuklam, or ‘whiteness,’ is the symbolic representation of the Absolute Truth because it is unaffected by the material qualities. Lord Brahmā is called rakta, or red, because Brahmā represents the qualities of passion for creation. Darkness is entrusted to Lord Śiva because he annihilates the cosmos. The creation, annihilation and maintenance of this cosmic manifestation are conducted by Your potencies, yet You are always unaffected by those qualities.” As confirmed in the Vedas, harir hi nirguṇaḥ sākṣāt: the Supreme Personality of Godhead is always free from all material qualities. It is also said that the qualities of passion and ignorance are nonexistent in the person of the Supreme Lord. In this verse, the three colors mentioned — śukla, rakta and kṛṣṇa — are not to be understood literally, in terms of what we experience with our senses, but rather as representatives of sattva-guṇa, rajo-guṇa and tamo-guṇa. After all, sometimes we see that a duck is white, although it is in tamo-guṇa, the mode of ignorance. Illustrating the logic called bakāndha-nyāya, the duck is such a fool that it runs after the testicles of a bull, thinking them to be a hanging fish that can be taken when it drops. Thus the duck is always in darkness. Vyāsadeva, however, the compiler of the Vedic literature, is blackish, but this does not mean that he is in tamo-guṇa; rather, he is in the highest position of sattva-guṇa, beyond the material modes of nature. Sometimes these colors ( śukla-raktas tathā pītaḥ ) are used to designate the brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas and śūdras. Lord Kṣīrodakaśāyī Viṣṇu is celebrated as possessing a blackish color, Lord Śiva is whitish, and Lord Brahmā is reddish, but according to Śrīla Sanātana Gosvāmī in the Vaiṣṇava-toṣaṇī-ṭīkā, this exhibition of colors is not what is referred to here. The real understanding of śukla, rakta and kṛṣṇa is as follows. The Lord is always transcendental, but for the sake of creation He assumes the color rakta as Lord Brahmā. Again, sometimes the Lord becomes angry. As He says in Bhagavad-gītā (16.19) : tān ahaṁ dviṣataḥ krūrān saṁsāreṣu narādhamān kṣipāmy ajasram aśubhān āsurīṣv eva yoniṣu “Those who are envious and mischievous, who are the lowest among men, are cast by Me into the ocean of material existence, into various demoniac species of life.” To destroy the demons, the Lord becomes angry, and therefore He assumes the form of Lord Śiva. In summary, the Supreme Personality of Godhead is always beyond the material qualities, and we should not be misled into thinking otherwise simply because of sense perception. One must understand the position of the Lord through the authorities, or mahājanas. As stated in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (1.3.28) , ete cāṁśa-kalāḥ puṁsaḥ kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    My Lord, Your form is transcendental to the three material modes, yet for the maintenance of the three worlds, You assume the white color of Viṣṇu in goodness; for creation, which is surrounded by the quality of passion, You appear reddish; and at the end, when there is a need for annihilation, which is surrounded by ignorance, You appear blackish.
    Commentary

    Concerning this there is a question. It is well known that the creation takes place through Brahma. Then, how are you also the creator? Brahma and others are your forms alone. That is the intention of this verse. You, by your svarupa (svamayaya), manifest yourself as pure (sukla) Visnu. Here sukla cannot mean white, because Visnu is black. At the time of destruction of all people you are black in color and for creation in the mode of passion you are red. But we cannot say that Visnu is nourished or influenced by sattva guna and therefore described as white. Visnu does not have connection with sattva guna as Brahma and Siva have with the other gunas. Visnu is close to sattva but does not touch it. In 10.88.55 it is said: Harir hi nirgunah saksat, sattvadayo na santise and sruti says. saksi cetah kevalo nirgunas ca

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “Why do you say I am the cause and destruction? These actions are done by Brahmā and Śiva.” The verse indicates that he does not speak contrary. Viṣṇu is white. This means he is pure, since he is beyond the guṇas, and merely assists sattva by closeness. With your form (varṇam) as Viṣṇu you appear in the world for maintaining it by your mercy (sva-māyayā). You appear as Brahmā full of rajas for creating, with the color red, indicating passion to nourish the world. You appear as Śiva full of tamas with anger indicated by the color black. Black does not indicate his form. Colors seen by the eye cannot determine the guṇas. Baka and other demons, full of tamas, were white. Vyāsa, Śukadeva and others, full of sattva, were blackish in complexion. The colors are also used to denote the varṇas like brāhmaṇa. Kṣīrodakaśāyi Viṣṇu the guṇa avatāra of sattva is blackish. Śiva is white. Their expansions are of various colors. Thus, though Brahmā is described as red bodied, that is not the meaning here. Viṣṇu is beyond the guṇas. He is not in the guṇas like others. harir hi nirguṇaḥ sākṣāt puruṣaḥ prakṛteḥ paraḥ Viṣṇu is beyond the guṇas, he is completely beyond matter. SB 10.88.3 śivaḥ śakti-yutaḥ śaśvat tri-liṅgo guṇa-saṁvṛtaḥ vaikārikas taijasaś ca tāmasaś cety ahaṁ tridhā Śiva is always united with his personal energy, the material nature. Manifesting himself in three features in response to the entreaties of nature’s three modes, he thus embodies the threefold principle of material ego in goodness, passion and ignorance. SB 10.88.5 Thus Viṣṇu cannot be said to be covered by sattva-guṇa as the other two are covered by rajas and tamas. Viṣṇu appears with the desire to protect. Even though it said that they all are not affected by transformation of the guṇas, since it is explained that the goal is to destroy the tamas in people (if Śiva is in tamas, how could he destroy it?) Viṣṇu has a form of sac-cid-ānanda at all times. Otherwise there would be contradiction to thousands of other of statements concerning Viṣṇu and his devotees.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “Why do you say I am the cause of creation and destruction? These actions are done by Brahmā and Śiva.” You accept sattva. This means that you accept to be the presiding deity of sattva, because the deity and the guṇa are considered non-diffferent. Or since you are without contradiction, or are the cause of creation etc. (saḥ), you are generally have a white form (varṇam) as the manvantara avatāras like Yajṇa. By your mercy (māyayā) though you are by nature the protector, you accept these forms. Since protection is your nature, maintenance is mentioned first. The Lord is distinguished from these forms as the source or avatārī by the word saḥ. You accept a dark blue and reddish form (kṛṣṇam) for destruction of the universe (janātyaye). Creation, maintenance and destruction arise from you.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa stays untouched by the guṇas even while wielding them as creation, maintenance, and destruction — fix your eye on the Person, not the colors.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today which guṇa is coloring your mood — rajas-restlessness, tamas-dullness, sattva-clarity — and refuse to mistake that color for your real self or for Kṛṣṇa.
    • When you meet someone whose surface (caste, complexion, role, temperament) tempts a quick judgment, pause and address the eternal soul behind the varṇa, as Vasudeva addressed the Lord beyond His colors.
    • Before sleep, hand back the day's three movements — what you built, what you sustained, what ended — to Kṛṣṇa, acknowledging He alone is the unchanging doer through the modes.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I mistaking the colors of the guṇas — the moods of sattva, rajas, or tamas passing through me — for my actual identity, and what would change if I held them as Kṛṣṇa's potencies rather than as 'me'?
    • When I encounter someone whose outer 'color' (caste, role, temperament, appearance) seems to mark them as low or high, where am I falling into bakāndha-nyāya — the duck's logic — and judging by surface rather than by their position in relation to Kṛṣṇa?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When an exam result, a breakup, or a friend-group shift hits, name the guṇa at work out loud — 'this is rajas churning,' 'this is tamas closing in' — and remember Kṛṣṇa is the one untouched person behind all three. Don't take the mode personally.
    • Audit your social-media feed for a week with the bakāndha-nyāya test: which accounts have you been chasing for their śukla appearance (clean aesthetic, calm voice) that are actually feeding you tamas? Unfollow three.
    • Before a high-stakes test or interview, pray specifically to Kṛṣṇa as the personal Lord behind the rajas of striving — not to 'the universe,' not to 'my best self.' Notice how the prayer changes when the addressee is a person, not a force.
    householder
    • When a family decision involves creation (a new child, a business launch), maintenance (a marriage, a job kept), or ending (selling a home, leaving a role), explicitly identify which of the three you are in, and offer that specific phase to Kṛṣṇa as His potency working through you.
    • Teach your children the difference between Kṛṣṇa and the demigods using this verse — that Brahmā and Śiva are real and to be respected, but Kṛṣṇa alone is the personal Supreme. A five-minute dinner conversation is enough; do it this week before the culture does the teaching for you.
    • When a financial setback or a child's failure tempts you to read it as cosmic injustice, recall harir hi nirguṇaḥ — the Lord is not staining Himself with your tamas. The setback is His arrangement (nyāya), not His indifference. Act with kṣamā, then act.
    senior
    • Your body is now visibly in the kṛṣṇa-varṇa phase — the verse names it without flinching, and so should you. Each morning, acknowledge that annihilation is a potency of the same Lord who maintained you for sixty years; the manager has not changed.
    • Mentor a younger person specifically on the personalist distinction — that surrender is to Kṛṣṇa, a person, not to 'the light' or 'the source.' Your generation is the last that can transmit this without translation loss; don't postpone it.
    • Loosen one attachment this month that you have been preserving out of rajas-residue (a property, a title, a grudge, a possession). Offer it to the Lord who presides over endings, and notice that vairāgya at this stage is not loss but alignment with the season Kṛṣṇa Himself has set.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading śukla, rakta, and kṛṣṇa literally — as skin tones or aesthetic preferences — instead of as representations of sattva-, rajo-, and tamo-guṇa, and then importing modern racial or aesthetic prejudices into one's understanding of the Lord and His devotees.
    • Concluding that because Kṛṣṇa 'assumes' the modes for creation, maintenance, and annihilation, He is therefore touched or limited by them — collapsing the personal Supreme into an impersonal field of guṇas, when the verse and purport insist harir hi nirguṇaḥ sākṣāt: He remains transcendental throughout.
    • Using 'beyond the modes' as a license to neglect one's varṇāśrama duties or to treat Brahmā and Śiva as interchangeable demigods on Kṛṣṇa's level, rather than recognizing that creation and annihilation are conducted by His potencies while He alone is svayaṁ bhagavān.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Vasudeva insists Kṛṣṇa is nirguṇa even while assuming the white, red, and black colors of maintenance, creation, and annihilation. Share with your partner: when in your own life have you mistaken Kṛṣṇa's working through the guṇas (a hard reversal, a sudden ascent) as His personal disposition toward you? Where did that misreading take you?
    • Prabhupāda warns against bakāndha-nyāya — the duck logic of judging by surface color. Pair up and challenge each other: name one person, teaching, or institution you have written off based on its 'color' (its guṇa-appearance), and one you have over-trusted for the same reason. Disagree honestly if your partner's read seems naïve.
    • If Brahmā (rakta, creation), Viṣṇu (śukla, maintenance), and Śiva (kṛṣṇa, annihilation) are all functions through which the one Lord acts, what does it mean — practically, not poetically — to say surrender is to Kṛṣṇa personally and not to 'the divine functions'? Push your group: where does this distinction actually change a decision you would make this week?
    Role Play

    Two students play roommates. Roommate A has just lost a parent and is sinking; a well-meaning friend (Roommate B) keeps offering 'the universe has a plan,' 'energies are shifting,' 'your loved one is now pure light.' Roommate A finally says, 'Stop. I need something real.' Roommate B must now attempt to share the substance of SB 10.3.20 — that creation, maintenance, and annihilation are Kṛṣṇa's potencies, that He personally remains untouched and untouchable by tamas, and that the loss is not a cosmic accident but His arrangement — without lapsing into impersonalist platitudes or inventing pastimes. After 4 minutes, swap roles. Debrief: where did the language drift toward 'the Self' or 'energy'? Where did it land as Kṛṣṇa, the person?

    Objections & Responses
    • If Kṛṣṇa 'becomes' Brahmā for creation and 'becomes' Śiva for destruction, isn't this just polytheism dressed up — or worse, a theology where God is responsible for every evil because tamas is His own color?
      Vasudeva is precise: sva-māyayā — by His own potency. The Lord does not personally enter rajas or tamas; He deploys these guṇas through empowered functionaries (Brahmā, Śiva) while remaining harir hi nirguṇaḥ sākṣāt, untouched. This is not polytheism: Kṛṣṇa is bhagavān svayam (SB 1.3.28), and Brahmā and Śiva are His aṁśa-kalāḥ — portions, not rivals. As for evil: annihilation is not malice but mercy, the cleansing the cosmos requires. The Lord arranges it without being soiled by it, the way a surgeon cuts without becoming the disease.
    • This whole color scheme sounds like a pre-modern attempt to map deities onto the guṇas — quaint mythology. A modern devotee can drop the color symbolism and keep the ethics.
      Prabhupāda anticipates exactly this move and refuses it. He cites Sanātana Gosvāmī to say the colors are not the literal pigments of Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva, but designations of sattva, rajas, and tamas — the actual operative forces behind every event in your life: the rise of an idea (rajas), the holding of a marriage (sattva), the death of a friend (tamas). Drop the symbolism and you lose the diagnostic. The verse is not decoration; it is how a devotee reads the day. And the personalist core — that one Lord, Kṛṣṇa, presides over all three through His potencies — is what keeps the ethics from collapsing into either fatalism or self-help.
    Analogy

    A master painter dips one brush into three pigments — white for the dawn, red for the noon, black for the dusk — and paints a single landscape in three movements. The brush, the hand, the painter never change colors; only what is painted does. Bhagavān assumes Viṣṇu (white), Brahmā (red), Śiva (black) for creation's three phases; the colors are on the canvas of līlā, not on Him.

    Stories
    Mohinī-mūrti at the churning of the milk ocean

    Bhagavān assumed the Mohinī form (SB 8.8–9) to retrieve the nectar from the asuras and distribute it to the devas. He took a form whose color and gender were quite other than His normal Vaikuṇṭha appearance, yet His svarūpa never altered. The līlā required that mūrti; the inner identity was unchanged.

    This verse's logic is the same: the white, red, and black colors of trimūrti are functional forms taken by Bhagavān's sva-māyā for cosmic work. The Person behind the colors is one — Viṣṇu, who in His original Vraja form is Kṛṣṇa, śyāma-sundara.
