    Important Words
    • rirakṣiṣuḥ — desiring to protect
      Desiderative form of √rakṣ — 'desiring-to-protect'. The motive behind avatāra is named: not philosophical demonstration, not display, but rakṣaṇa of devotees and dharma. BG 4.8: paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ — the same protective intent.
    • avatīrṇaḥ asi — You have descended
      Past participle of ava-√tṛ ('to cross down') + asi. The verb avatīrṇa-bhū gives us 'avatāra'. Bhagavān has crossed down — He does not 'reincarnate' (a karma-bound process) but descends by His own will, retaining full transcendence.
    • akhila-īśvara — Lord of all without exception
      Akhila (without remainder, complete) + īśvara (controller). The verse names what Kaṁsa fails to recognize — that the prisoner's newborn is the unconditional Lord of every being including Kaṁsa himself. Sambandha-jñāna's apex: there is no remainder of reality outside His īśvaratva.
    • rājanya-saṁjña-asura-koṭi-yūtha-paiḥ — by millions of demon-leaders called kings
      An extended compound. Rājanya (royal, kṣatriya-class) + saṁjña (named, so-called) + asura (demon) + koṭi (ten million) + yūtha (host) + pa (leader). The saṁjña — 'named-as' — is the bite of the word: these are asuras NAMED kings. Gauḍīya social diagnosis: titles do not change tattva.
    • nihaniṣyase — You will kill
      Future of ni-√han ('to slay'). Bhagavān's protection includes destruction of asuras — non-pacifist, non-sentimental. Real karuṇā for the saintly requires real daṇḍa for the demonic. Vaiṣṇava ethics does not flinch from this.
    O my Lord, proprietor of all creation, You have now appeared in my house, desiring to protect this world. I am sure that You will kill all the armies that are moving all over the world under the leadership of politicians who are dressed as kṣatriya rulers but who are factually demons. They must be killed by You for the protection of the innocent public.
    Purport

    Kṛṣṇa appears in this world for two purposes, paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśāya ca duṣkṛtām: to protect the innocent, religious devotees of the Lord and to annihilate all the uneducated, uncultured asuras, who unnecessarily bark like dogs and fight among themselves for political power. It is said, kali-kāle nāma-rūpe kṛṣṇa avatāra. The Hare Kṛṣṇa movement is also an incarnation of Kṛṣṇa in the form of the holy name ( nāma-rūpe ). Every one of us who is actually afraid of the asuric rulers and politicians must welcome this incarnation of Kṛṣṇa: Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa, Hare Hare/ Hare Rāma, Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma, Hare Hare. Then we will surely be protected from the harassment of asuric rulers. At the present moment these rulers are so powerful that by hook or by crook they capture the highest posts in government and harass countless numbers of people on the plea of national security or some emergency. Then again, one asura defeats another asura, but the public continues to suffer. Therefore the entire world is in a precarious condition, and the only hope is this Hare Kṛṣṇa movement. Lord Nṛsiṁhadeva appeared when Prahlāda was excessively harassed by his asuric father. Because of such asuric fathers — that is, the ruling politicians — it is very difficult to press forward the Hare Kṛṣṇa movement, but because Kṛṣṇa has now appeared in His holy name through this movement, we can hope that these asuric fathers will be annihilated and the kingdom of God established all over the world. The entire world is now full of many asuras in the guise of politicians, gurus, sādhus, yogīs and incarnations, and they are misleading the general public away from Kṛṣṇa consciousness, which can offer true benefit to human society.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O my Lord, proprietor of all creation, You have now appeared in my house, desiring to protect this world. I am sure that You will kill all the armies that are moving all over the world under the leadership of politicians who are dressed as kṣatriya rulers but who are factually demons. They must be killed by You for the protection of the innocent public.
    Commentary

    O father, in truth you know about me. But if you know, then say why I have appeared in your house? This verse answers. "Taking the name of a king you will kill all the troops directed by the asuras in order to protect the devotees and also the citizens in general."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Now I have attained you as a son though you come to protect the people. This is fortunate for the world and fortunate for me. You desire to protect all people submerged in an ocean of suffering, but especially your devotees, the Yādavas. Genitive case is used instead of accusative case in asya lokasya (you desire to protect the people). O powerful Lord! O Lord of all beings! It is impossible that you have appeared. But yet you have appeared, and in my house, with a relation to me, and even in a prison. Such great mercy! You will repeatedly (ni) kill all the armies moving about constantly (nir) and with purpose (vi), along with a host of demonic kings disguised as kṣatriyas. The word “with” is used to show that by destroying the armies, the kings will also be destroyed. Nirvyūhyamānāh can also mean nirvyūḍhamānāḥ meaning “constantly (ni) arranged in phalanxes.” This however is not accepted by Śrīdhara Svāmī.

    Personal Guidance
    Welcome Kṛṣṇa as the true protector — He descends to crush asuric rulers and shelter the innocent; today, take refuge in His holy name.
    Practical Applications
    • Chant the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahā-mantra audibly today as the very incarnation of Kṛṣṇa who protects you from asuric harassment.
    • Refuse to place ultimate hope in any politician or worldly ruler — name one such attachment and consciously withdraw it, placing that trust in Kṛṣṇa instead.
    • Notice when news or social media is breeding fear of asuric power, and immediately turn to nāma-saṅkīrtana as your concrete act of shelter.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my own life am I tolerating 'asuras dressed as kṣatriyas' — leaders, voices, or influences I follow because they wear the costume of authority, even though they are leading me away from Kṛṣṇa?
    • Devakī recognizes Kṛṣṇa as akhileśvara appearing in her own house — what would change today if I treated my home, body, and daily situation as the very place He has descended to protect, rather than waiting for protection to arrive from elsewhere?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the 'asuras in costume' in your own feed today — influencers, politicians, even gurus packaged as wisdom — and unfollow one whose actual fruits are agitation, envy, or contempt for ordinary people.
    • When a peer-pressure situation has you cornered (a group chat, a party, a campus stance you are being shamed into), chant sixteen names quietly before responding, and let Devakī's prayer — that Kṛṣṇa protects those who take shelter — be your actual backbone instead of social courage.
    • Pick one 'kṣatriya-dressed' authority in your student life (a manipulative senior, a gaslighting coach, an exploitative internship) and stop pretending its costume is real; speak about it honestly to one trustworthy elder this week.
    householder
    • In family financial decisions this month, refuse partnership with anyone whose money smells asuric — the contract that requires a small lie, the client who harasses staff, the scheme dressed as opportunity — even at real cost to income.
    • Teach your children, by name, the difference between a leader and an asura-in-kṣatriya-clothing, using one concrete current example at the dinner table; do not raise them politically naive in the name of being spiritual.
    • Establish a household kīrtana or japa time as your family's actual security policy — not as ornament — trusting Devakī's logic that the home where Kṛṣṇa is invited becomes the protected home.
    senior
    • Use your remaining decades to mentor younger householders in distinguishing real protectors from asuras-in-costume; your pattern-recognition is the inheritance younger people most need and least have.
    • Loosen your grip on the political outcomes you have agonized over for forty years — Devakī hands the army-killing to Kṛṣṇa, and so can you; redirect that energy into chanting the holy name as your final, most potent activism.
    • Make your home, however small, a place where Kṛṣṇa is openly invited — pictures, prasāda, kīrtana — so that grandchildren and visitors experience what Devakī experienced: that the Lord's presence in a house is its real defense against the age.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the verse as a license for political activism or vigilante 'demon-slaying' — treating particular human rulers as the asuras to be killed, rather than recognizing that Kṛṣṇa Himself (and His holy name in this age) does the annihilating, while our work is sincere chanting and shelter.
    • Spiritualizing the verse into a vague 'inner demons' metaphor and thereby losing its concrete claim that real, organized, asuric leadership exists in the world — and that the practical response is not introspection alone but taking shelter of nāma-rūpe Kṛṣṇa avatāra, the Hare Kṛṣṇa movement.
    • Mistaking Devakī's mood for fearful flattery and trying to imitate it as performance, instead of cultivating her actual realization — that Kṛṣṇa is the proprietor of all creation (vibho, akhileśvara) — so one's prayers for protection become hollow petitions rather than confident surrender.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Devakī calls these rulers 'asuras dressed as kṣatriyas.' Where in your own life do you encounter authority that wears a righteous costume but acts demonically — and where, honestly, do you yourself wear that costume?
    • Prabhupāda says the Hare Kṛṣṇa movement itself is Kṛṣṇa's incarnation in this age, our protection from asuric rulers. Does that claim land for you as literal truth, as metaphor, or as something you resist? Be honest with each other about the resistance.
    • Devakī asks Kṛṣṇa to *kill* the demon-armies — not reform them, not educate them. Where in our discourse have we softened this verse into something more palatable, and what is lost when we do?
    Role Play

    Two students are siblings at the bedside of their elderly father, who has been a lifelong devotee. The father is afraid: a corrupt local official has been harassing the family business and a court date is coming. One sibling (Student A) wants to fight politically — hire lawyers, mobilize contacts, expose the official publicly. The other sibling (Student B) wants to lean entirely on chanting and Kṛṣṇa's protection through the holy name, citing this verse and Prabhupāda's purport. They have ten minutes to come to a shared decision before the father wakes up and asks what they will do. Play it out, then debrief: where did Devakī's prayer actually point — passive trust, active protection, or something both of you missed?

    Objections & Responses
    • This is just political grievance dressed up as scripture. Calling rulers you dislike 'demons' and asking God to kill them is exactly the kind of religious framing that fuels real-world violence and authoritarianism.
      The verse is Devakī's prayer, not a license for us to identify and execute demons. The asura-quality Prabhupāda names is precise — rulers who capture power 'by hook or by crook' and harass innocents under invented emergencies. Our weapon, explicitly, is the holy name, not the sword. A Gauḍīya teacher takes this verse as a diagnosis of the age and a refuge in nāma, not as a permission slip. If anything, it disarms our own political rage by handing the killing to Kṛṣṇa and leaving us with the chanting.
    • Why do I need Kṛṣṇa personally to come and protect anyone? If there is a divine intelligence in the universe, surely it works through justice and karma without needing a blue cowherd boy born in a prison.
      That is the impersonalist instinct, and the verse is its direct refutation. Devakī does not address an abstract justice; she addresses *akhileśvara*, the proprietor of all, who has just *appeared in her house*. The personalist line insists that protection is not a mechanism but a Person who responds, who descends, who takes birth where He is loved. Karma alone does not pull a child out of Kaṁsa's prison — Kṛṣṇa does. The blue cowherd boy is not embarrassing scripture we have to apologize for; He is the whole point.
    Analogy

    A king disguises himself as a traveler to enter a region where bandits dressed as nobles oppress the people; the moment he sets foot, the entire militia he has secretly arranged begins to mobilize. Kṛṣṇa's birth in Kaṁsa's prison is the king setting foot; the asuras dressed as kṣatriyas are about to discover what kind of guest has arrived.

    Stories
    Vāmana approaching Bali's sacrifice

    Bhagavān as Vāmana entered Bali's sacrificial arena as a small brāhmaṇa boy. Bali, an asura who happened to be virtuous, did not see the king-in-disguise immediately. The dwarf form was the entry; the cosmic step was the response to demonic over-reach.

    The Bhāgavata's pattern: Bhagavān comes apparently small (a dwarf, an infant in a prison) precisely when the asuras have grown too large. The verse's 'rirakṣiṣuḥ' — 'desiring to protect' — is the recurring motive across every avatāra.

    Rāma's mission to remove Rāvaṇa

    Daśaratha's son was apparently a prince of Ayodhyā. Rāvaṇa, in Laṅkā, was apparently a ten-headed king with infinite military strength. The Rāmāyaṇa reveals the actual proportions: a king-disguised-as-a-prince came down specifically to remove a demon-disguised-as-a-king.

    This verse cites that same logic. The 'rājanya-saṁjña-asura' — those called kings but actually asuras — are the perennial target of Bhagavān's descents. Politics in any age is the asura-stage; the avatāra is the answer.

    Important Words
    • asabhyaḥ — uncivilized
      A- (privative) + sabhya (one who belongs to the sabhā — assembly of cultured persons). The Sanskrit is sharper than 'uncivilized' — Kaṁsa is one who has expelled himself from the company of those who recognize dharma. Prabhupāda's gloss: asura means uncivilized; sura means civilized. The categories are moral, not ethnic.
    • sura-īśvara — Lord of the suras
      Sura (the civilized, the devotee-class) + īśvara (Lord). Kṛṣṇa is the Lord specifically of those who recognize dharma. Bhagavān has a side; impartiality at the cosmic level does not mean equal regard for sura and asura at the practical level.
    • abhisarati — will come immediately
      Abhi (toward) + √sṛ (go, rush). Forceful verb — 'rushes toward'. In Sanskrit poetry abhisara is also the term for a tryst-bound heroine running to her beloved; the irony here is that Kaṁsa 'abhisaras' Kṛṣṇa with raised weapons, not with prema. Even hostile attention to Bhagavān is a kind of intense fixation.
    • udāyudhaḥ — with raised weapons
      Ud (up) + āyudha (weapon). The asura's posture before Bhagavān: armed and lifted-up. Contrast with Vasudeva's posture three verses earlier: nata-aṅgaḥ, body bowed. Bhagavān's appearance reveals the body-language of every heart.
    • agrajān te — Your elder brothers
      Agra-ja (first-born) + accusative plural + te (Your). Devakī's anguish: Kaṁsa already killed six of her sons. The verse carries her mother's grief into the appeal — she has the receipts of asura-violence and asks Kṛṣṇa to not be the seventh.
    O my Lord, Lord of the demigods, after hearing the prophecy that You would take birth in our home and kill him, this uncivilized Kaṁsa killed so many of Your elder brothers. As soon as he hears from his lieutenants that You have appeared, he will immediately come with weapons to kill You.
    Purport

    Kaṁsa has here been described as asabhya, meaning “uncivilized” or “most heinous,” because he killed the many children of his sister. When he heard the prophecy that he would be killed by her eighth son, this uncivilized man, Kaṁsa, was immediately ready to kill his innocent sister on the occasion of her marriage. An uncivilized man can do anything for the satisfaction of his senses. He can kill children, he can kill cows, he can kill brāhmaṇas, he can kill old men; he has no mercy for anyone. According to the Vedic civilization, cows, women, children, old men and brāhmaṇas should be excused if they are at fault. But asuras, uncivilized men, do not care about that. At the present moment, the killing of cows and the killing of children is going on unrestrictedly, and therefore this civilization is not at all human, and those who are conducting this condemned civilization are uncivilized asuras. Such uncivilized men are not in favor of the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement. As public officers, they declare without hesitation that the chanting of the Hare Kṛṣṇa movement is a nuisance, although Bhagavad-gītā clearly says, satataṁ kīrtayanto māṁ yatantaś ca dṛḍha-vratāḥ. According to this verse, it is the duty of the mahātmās to chant the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra and try to spread it all over the world to the best of their ability. Unfortunately, society is in such an uncivilized state that there are so-called mahātmās who are prepared to kill cows and children and stop the Hare Kṛṣṇa movement. Such uncivilized activities were actually demonstrated in opposition to the Hare Kṛṣṇa movement’s Bombay center, Hare Kṛṣṇa Land. As Kaṁsa was not expected to kill the beautiful child of Devakī and Vasudeva, the uncivilized society, although unhappy about the advancement of the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, cannot be expected to stop it. Yet we must face many difficulties in many different ways. Although Kṛṣṇa cannot be killed, Vasudeva, as the father of Kṛṣṇa, was trembling because in affection he thought that Kaṁsa would immediately come and kill his son. Similarly, although the Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement and Kṛṣṇa are not different and no asuras can check it, we are afraid that at any moment the asuras can stop this movement in any part of the world.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O my Lord, Lord of the demigods, after hearing the prophecy that You would take birth in our home and kill him, this uncivilized Kaṁsa killed so many of Your elder brothers. As soon as he hears from his lieutenants that You have appeared, he will immediately come with weapons to kill You.
    Commentary

    "Though I know all your glories, I cannot cross the ocean of unintelligence. So now I will inform you all evil Kamsa." Anticipating that his son will say, "No father, he will not kill me because he will be overcome with the sweetness of my form," Vasudeva answers, "He is uncivilized, without taste for rasa. His servants will inform him of your birth and he will come here. I can see him come now. So hide your form. I am afraid of what will happen when he comes desiring to kill you."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The meaning is according to Śrīdhara Svāmī. Though you will kill the demons, bewildered by parental affection I give you this information. Or because he is the worst of the lot, and because we, your devotees are suffering so much, you should take action now and deal with him first. It is necessary because of his evil actions. Abhyahanat is sometimes seen instead of nyavadhīt. It means “crush on the stone.” Abhisarati though in the present tense, indicates action not yet completed. Uttering “O lord of the devatās” Vasudeva indicates that such activity of Kaṁsa is suitable for the demons who are enemies of the devatās, his devotees.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Those who are not devotees cannot understand your glories, though you directly appeared in this room to benefit the whole world. Previously Kaṁsa killed your elder brothers by throwing them on stone. Now he will come running with weapons in his hands. O lord of the devatās! Vasudeva indicates that such activity of Kaṁsa is suitable for the demons who are enemies of the devatās, his devotees. Therefore be alert.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa cannot be killed and His movement cannot be stopped, yet asuric opposition is real — serve Him with steady courage anyway.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where fear of asuric opposition — ridicule, pushback, social cost — is making you soften your stand for Kṛṣṇa, and refuse to soften it.
    • Speak one clear word in defense of cows, children, brāhmaṇas, or the holy name when the moment arises, instead of staying conveniently silent.
    • Refuse to outsource your protection to your own cleverness — chant the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra deliberately today as Vasudeva trembled yet trusted Kṛṣṇa.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life have I been quietly behaving like Kaṁsa — sacrificing innocents (people, principles, time, integrity) for the sake of my own sense-gratification or self-preservation, and what 'prophecy' am I trying to outrun?
    • Vasudeva trembled in affection even though Kṛṣṇa cannot be killed — where am I confusing protective fear for devotion, and what does it ask of me to act with steady duty rather than anxious affection when the asuric forces seem to close in?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When a group chat or social feed turns into a pile-on against a classmate — even one who 'deserves' it — refuse to add the next message. That moment of crowd-cruelty is the asabhya pattern in miniature; protecting the defenseless starts with the chat you're actually in today.
    • Pick the one person in your year who is routinely talked over — the quiet kid, the foreign student, the unfashionable one — and have one real conversation with them this week. Vedic kṣamā says the weak are excused even when at fault; in your context, that means actively making space for the voiceless before they ask.
    • When you're afraid your faith looks weird on campus (chanting, japa beads, prasāda, no dating, no drinking), notice the trembling — that's Vasudeva's affection, not weakness. Don't hide it and don't perform it; just keep one daily practice visible without apology, and let Kṛṣṇa handle the social fallout.
    householder
    • Audit one recurring household expense or career choice this week through the asabhya/sabhya lens: is this money or time funding cruelty somewhere upstream — factory dairy, exploitative labor, content that degrades children — and what is one substitution you can actually sustain? Authenticity (adambhitva) means the kitchen and the bank statement match the altar.
    • When you feel the Vasudeva-trembling for your children's future — their school, their friends, the culture coming for them — convert anxiety into one concrete protection this month: a family kīrtana evening, a weekly reading, a clear screen-time boundary. Effort is yours; outcomes are Kṛṣṇa's.
    • In a workplace conflict where someone genuinely is behaving asuric, practice nyāya without ahaṅkāra: name the behavior precisely, once, in the right forum — then drop it. No corridor gossip, no moral superiority at home. Righteous judgment is surgical, not a lifestyle.
    senior
    • Identify one 'Kaṁsa' you've been carrying for decades — a person, an institution, a wound — and formally release them in your daily sit this week. At this stage, vairāgya is not theoretical; unfinished resentment is the heaviest thing you'll try to carry across the threshold.
    • Mentor one younger devotee or family member specifically on how to act with udyama while trembling — share an actual story from your life where you served Kṛṣṇa scared. Your lived non-anxiety in the face of obstruction is teaching the next generation can't get from books.
    • Quietly arrange your affairs — will, possessions, unfinished apologies — as Vasudeva arranged the transfer of the child: with care, without drama, trusting the Lord with the part you cannot control. Legacy in the Gauḍīya line is not what you leave behind; it is what you have already handed to Him.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading 'asabhya' as a label for distant historical villains (Kaṁsa, ancient tyrants) rather than recognizing the same asuric pattern in one's own willingness to harm cows, children, elders, or brāhmaṇas — directly or by participating in systems that do — for the sake of personal comfort.
    • Treating Vasudeva's trembling as a failure of faith and concluding that a real devotee should feel no fear — when in fact the verse honors the natural affection of a parent and shows that fearful affection and steady surrender can coexist; the misstep is using 'spiritual bypass' to suppress legitimate concern instead of channeling it into protective action.
    • Spiritualizing the verse into pure allegory and missing its concrete civilizational claim — that protecting cows, women, children, elders and brāhmaṇas is the mark of human civilization — and thereby excusing oneself from any practical, costly stand against the asuric currents of one's own time and place.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Vasudeva trembles for Kṛṣṇa even though Kṛṣṇa cannot be killed — Prabhupāda links this to our own fear that asuras can stop the saṅkīrtana movement. Where in your own seva does affection slide into anxiety, and is that anxiety a form of bhakti or a subtle lack of faith? Push back on each other — don't let the group settle on a tidy answer.
    • Prabhupāda calls a society that kills cows and children 'uncivilized' and names its leaders asuras. In your own circle, naming someone an asura feels harsh, even un-Vaiṣṇava. When is such naming nyāya (righteous judgment) and when is it our own ahaṅkāra dressed up as discrimination? Bring a real example you actually disagree about.
    • Vedic civilization says cows, women, children, elders, and brāhmaṇas should be excused even when at fault. Modern instinct says equal accountability for all. Argue the Vaiṣṇava position to a partner who genuinely doesn't accept it — and notice where you yourself flinch.
    Role Play

    Two students sit across from each other. Student A is a devotee who has just learned that the city council in their town is moving to ban public Hare Kṛṣṇa saṅkīrtana in parks, calling it a 'public nuisance' — exactly the language Prabhupāda flags in the purport. Student B is a thoughtful, secular neighbor and friend who broadly likes the devotees personally but agrees with the council: 'It's loud, it's religious, it doesn't belong in a public space.' Student A must (1) not retreat into platitudes, (2) not demonize Student B, (3) speak from the verse — Kaṁsa-like obstruction is expected, the movement cannot ultimately be checked, yet Vasudeva-like care and effort are still required. After 5 minutes, swap roles. Then debrief: where did Student A drift into either appeasement or aggression, and what would steady udyama in Kṛṣṇa's service have actually looked like?

    Objections & Responses
    • Calling people who disagree with you 'uncivilized asuras' is exactly the kind of religious othering that causes violence. Prabhupāda's purport sounds like the rhetoric of every fundamentalism.
      Notice what Prabhupāda actually marks as asuric: the killing of cows, children, elders, brāhmaṇas — the deliberate harming of those who cannot defend themselves. He is not naming people asura because they hold a different view; he is naming a specific civilizational pattern by its fruits. The Gauḍīya line is rigorously personalist — every jīva is part-and-parcel of Kṛṣṇa, including Kaṁsa, whom Kṛṣṇa Himself liberates. Real karuṇā is serving the soul, not flattering the ahaṅkāra. Refusing to name cruelty as cruelty, in the name of niceness, is the material compassion the Gītā explicitly pivots away from. The check on this is not silence but humility: we name the pattern, not the eternal worth of the person.
    • If Kṛṣṇa cannot be killed and the movement cannot ultimately be stopped, why did Vasudeva tremble — and why should we exert ourselves at all? Isn't the whole purport just contradiction?
      This is the heart of the verse. Vasudeva trembles in vātsalya — paternal affection — not in philosophical doubt. He knows tattva and yet he feels. Prabhupāda is showing us that bhakti is not a flatline of detached certainty; it includes legitimate care for what we love, expressed as effort. Karma-yoga (BG 2.47) gives us the form: the right to action, never to its fruits. We act with full udyama to protect Kṛṣṇa's movement, His devotees, His cows — and we surrender the outcome to Him, knowing He is never actually in danger. Vairāgya is not the absence of effort; it is the absence of proprietorship over results. Trembling Vasudeva who still hides the child is the model — not the cool spectator who does nothing because 'Kṛṣṇa will handle it.'
    Analogy

    A wolf who has already eaten the lambs hears that the shepherd has arrived in the field — his ears prick, his teeth bare, he runs not away but TOWARD the meadow with bared fangs. Kaṁsa is exactly this wolf. The news of Kṛṣṇa's birth will not cause him to repent; it will draw him sword-in-hand to the cradle. Asurā nature does not soften before Bhagavān; it sharpens.

    Stories
    Hiraṇyakaśipu hearing of Prahlāda's devotion

    When Hiraṇyakaśipu heard that his own son Prahlāda was a devotee of Viṣṇu, his response was not curiosity but escalating attempts to kill the boy — poison, fire, the elephants, the cliff. SB 7 chronicles each attempt and each rescue.

    The asura-mind, hearing news of bhakti or of Bhagavān, does not soften — it organizes violence. Devakī's anxiety in this verse is not paranoid; it is realistic. The Bhāgavata-narrative pattern is consistent: asuras hear and arm themselves.

    Rāvaṇa hearing of Rāma's approach

    When word reached Laṅkā that Rāma had crossed the ocean with the vānara army, Rāvaṇa did not consider returning Sītā. His court split; Vibhīṣaṇa urged surrender, was banished, and joined Rāma. Rāvaṇa armed himself, even knowing the auguries against him.

    The pattern repeats: bhakti and avatāra polarize. Some surrender (Vibhīṣaṇa); the rest harden (Rāvaṇa, Kaṁsa). Bhagavān's appearance is never neutral data; it sorts the world.

    Important Words
    • ātmajam — her own son
      Ātma (self) + ja (born). 'Born of one's own self' — the standard Sanskrit term for child. The word matters here because Devakī, even after seeing the four-armed form, still relates to Him as her ātmajam — vātsalya-rasa is preserved; aiśvarya does not erase relationship.
    • mahā-puruṣa-lakṣaṇam — with the marks of the Supreme Person
      Mahā-puruṣa (great Person) + lakṣaṇa (mark, sign). The śāstric criterion-set by which the Supreme Personality of Godhead is identified — Śrīvatsa, Kaustubha, four arms, the divya emblems. Iconography in service of theology.
    • upādhāvat — offered prayers (rushed to)
      Upa (near) + ā-√dhāv ('to run toward'). Literally 'ran toward'. The same root underlies prati-upādhāvat in BG contexts of running for shelter. Devakī, even while terrified of Kaṁsa, RUNS toward Kṛṣṇa with prayer. Bhakti reflexively closes the distance.
    • bhītā — afraid
      Past participle of √bhī. Real, named fear — fear of Kaṁsa. Bhakti is not the absence of fear; it is the redirection of fear into surrender. Devakī's bhīta-citta drives her to upādhāvat — her terror itself becomes the engine of stuti.
    • su-vismitā — thoroughly astonished
      Su (well, fully) + vismitā (astonished). Wonder is not suppressed by fear; both arise together. In rasa-śāstra, vismaya is the foundational bhāva of adbhuta-rasa. Devakī's verse is the perfect site for that rasa — astonishment at the impossible (Bhagavān as my child) is now her lived state.
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī continued: Thereafter, having seen that her child had all the symptoms of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Devakī, who was very much afraid of Kaṁsa and unusually astonished, began to offer prayers to the Lord.
    Purport

    The word suvismitā, meaning “astonished,” is significant in this verse. Devakī and her husband, Vasudeva, were assured that their child was the Supreme Personality of Godhead and could not be killed by Kaṁsa, but because of affection, as they thought of Kaṁsa’s previous atrocities, they were simultaneously afraid that Kṛṣṇa would be killed. This is why the word suvismitā has been used. Similarly, we are also astounded upon thinking of whether this movement will be killed by the asuras or will continue to advance without fear.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī continued: Thereafter, having seen that her child had all the symptoms of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Devakī, who was very much afraid of Kaṁsa and unusually astonished, began to offer prayers to the Lord.
    Commentary

    Seeing her husband’s fear, seeing that her newly born child did not withdraw his form, but was instead smiling, Devaki became astonished. "What shall I do? This child, identifying himself as God, has no fear of Kamsa." She became completely wonder struck. "In front of the supreme Lord, Kamsa is nothing. So why should we be afraid? What nonsense we are."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After Vasudeva praised the Lord (atha), Devakī praised him. She gazed at him, who was long expected, as he manifested his divine form (enam). She gazed at the Lord, who had appeared from her womb. This produced feelings of possessiveness in her. “He has come from my womb.” Though his development in the womb was only an imitation, to hide that fact, her senses were covered by yoga-nidrā or the power of the Lord. Therefore she calls him her son. Out of fear of Kaṁsa, she then saw him as Svayam Bhagavān (mahā-puruṣam) but becoming surprised at that, she began praising him. Her fear shows the preponderance of seeing Kṛṣṇa as her son.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After Vasudeva’s prayers, Devakī, seeing this eighth son born from her womb, spoke. Though he was not born, but just entered her womb already alive, thinking he was born is permissible because the Lord exhibits this semblance of birth out of great affection. Thus she says that he has been born from her womb. Following the ways of material birth, she gave birth, without seeing her son at first. Then she saw him, as described in this verse. Or she could not see her son at first because of fear generated by the Lord’s powers. Later, after Vasudeva had finished his prayers, she became calm and saw him. She directly saw him as Nārāyaṇa (mahāpuruṣa) with four arms. She was surprised, and though fearful of Kaṁsa, offered prayers to her son. Or seeing her son, out of affection she had fear of Kaṁsa and astonishment that this was the Lord. Or she spoke to that son (tam) who appeared with a spiritual form (enam), whom she had long expected.

    Personal Guidance
    Even when assured Kṛṣṇa is supreme, affection makes us tremble for His mission — let that very fear drive us deeper into prayer, not paralysis.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where affection for Kṛṣṇa's movement turns into anxiety about asuric opposition, and convert that worry into a specific prayer.
    • When astonishment at Kṛṣṇa's presence arises in kīrtana or reading, pause and offer a Devakī-style stuti rather than rushing past the moment.
    • Refuse the false comfort of theological certainty alone — bring both your conviction and your fear honestly before Him today.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my devotional life do I, like Devakī, intellectually know Kṛṣṇa is supreme yet still tremble for Him as if He needed my protection from the 'Kaṁsas' of the world?
    • What signs of Kṛṣṇa's lakṣaṇa have I already seen in my own sādhana that I quickly forget the moment fear of the asuric forces around me returns?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When you feel that doubled pull — wonder at something true (a kīrtana that hit, a verse that landed) AND fear that your friend group or Instagram feed will erode it by Monday — name it as suvismitā instead of treating it as weakness, and turn it directly into a short prayer the way Devakī did.
    • Notice the 'Kaṁsa' in your life: the inner critic, the cynical roommate, the exam-stress voice that wants to kill anything tender in you. Don't argue with it; do what Devakī did — upādhāvat, run toward Kṛṣṇa in prayer, even a one-line japa-mālā between classes.
    • Resist the campus pressure to be cool-detached about your sādhana. Devakī was suvismitā — unusually astonished — about her own child. It is okay to still be astonished by Kṛṣṇa at twenty; the people who pretend nothing impresses them are the ones quietly being killed by māyā.
    householder
    • When you look at your own children and feel both awe at the soul entrusted to you and fear at the world's atrocities they will face, recognize this as Devakī's exact bhāva — and let it move you to prayer for them by name each morning, not just to anxious planning.
    • In career and money decisions, distinguish Kaṁsa-fear (worldly threat) from Kṛṣṇa-trust. Devakī held both; you can too. Make the prudent move (Vasudeva crossed the Yamunā) AND offer the prayer (she ran to the Lord) — never substitute one for the other.
    • Protect what is genuinely Kṛṣṇa's in your home — the morning ārati, the prasāda meal, the children's saṁskāras — with the same suvismitā Devakī had. Treat these not as routines but as the mahā-puruṣa-lakṣaṇam quietly appearing in your household, vulnerable to a hostile age.
    senior
    • Devakī's astonishment was at a child she would soon have to release into Vraja. In this season, look at the dharma, the saṅga, the grandchildren you have loved — and practice handing each one to Kṛṣṇa in prayer rather than gripping them with fear of what comes after you.
    • The fear that 'this movement will be killed by the asuras' that Prabhupāda names — examine whether your own version of that fear (about your lineage, your temple, your family's bhakti) is becoming a substitute for trust. Mentor the young, then hand the rest to Him.
    • As the body's transitions accelerate, let suvismitā — wonder — remain. Devakī did not become numb after years of grief in the prison; she was still capable of being unusually astonished. Refuse the senior's temptation toward dry resignation; keep the capacity to be surprised by Kṛṣṇa until the last breath.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating Devakī's fear as a flaw to be dismissed rather than recognizing it as the natural pull of vātsalya-bhāva — and so swinging to a cold, 'detached' posture that has no affection in it at all.
    • Reading 'mahā-puruṣa-lakṣaṇam' as poetic flourish and quietly slipping into the impersonalist habit of seeing Kṛṣṇa as a symbol of the Self, rather than the actual four-armed Personality Devakī beheld with her own eyes.
    • Using suvismitā — astonishment — as an excuse for paralysis: standing dazzled before the Lord's greatness while neglecting the immediate, practical prayer and service that Devakī actually performed in the very next moment.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Devakī sees Kṛṣṇa's four-armed mahā-puruṣa form and is simultaneously astonished AND afraid for His safety. Share a moment when you cognitively knew Kṛṣṇa was in control but your affection still produced fear. Was that fear a defect in your faith, or is it bhakti itself? Where do you and your partner disagree?
    • Prabhupāda extends Devakī's suvismitā to our anxiety about whether 'this movement will be killed by the asuras.' Discuss: is worry about the future of bhakti-institutions a sign of attachment to the Lord's mission, or a sign of forgetting that He protects His own? Press your partner if their answer sounds too clean.
    • Devakī's first response to seeing Kṛṣṇa's divinity is not celebration but prayer born of fear. Many of us were taught that 'real' devotion is fearless. Argue both sides — when is fear a doorway into prayer, and when does it block it?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A plays a new devotee who has just experienced something undeniably real in their sādhana — a moment where Kṛṣṇa felt unmistakably present. But now, a week later, A is afraid the experience will be 'taken away' by their skeptical roommate, by a coming exam season, or by their own wandering mind. Student B plays a senior devotee who must respond — not by dismissing the fear ('just chant more'), and not by inflating the experience ('you're so advanced'), but by helping A see, as Devakī did, that astonishment and fear can coexist and that prayer is the right response to both. Run for 5 minutes, then swap. Debrief: where did the senior devotee slip into platitudes?

    Objections & Responses
    • If Devakī truly recognized Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, her fear of Kaṁsa is irrational. This is just a mother's emotional inconsistency dressed up as theology — the verse undermines the very omnipotence it claims.
      The verse is not embarrassed by this — it names it precisely with suvismitā. Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas read affection (vātsalya-bhāva) not as a defect in knowledge but as a higher relational truth that overrides the calculus of omnipotence. Yaśodā binds Kṛṣṇa with rope; Devakī fears for Him. Aiśvarya-jñāna (knowledge of His majesty) does not abolish prema; prema willingly forgets majesty so the relationship can be tasted. What looks like inconsistency to a logician is the very nectar the ācāryas point to. Kṛṣṇa Himself prefers a mother who fears for Him over a philosopher who correctly catalogs His powers.
    • Prabhupāda's leap from Devakī's fear to anxiety about 'whether this movement will be killed by the asuras' sounds like institutional paranoia. Why import 1970s movement-anxiety into a verse about a mother and child?
      Prabhupāda is doing what every ācārya does — showing that the verse is alive, not archived. The principle is the same: when something genuinely belonging to Kṛṣṇa appears in a hostile world, those who love it feel both wonder and protective fear. That is not paranoia; it is the same vātsalya-bhāva extended to Kṛṣṇa's saṅkīrtana movement, which śāstra calls non-different from Him. The response Prabhupāda models is also the same as Devakī's — not strategic panic, but prayer (upādhāvat). A Gauḍīya teacher would say: if you find yourself afraid for the dharma in your own household or saṅga, do not suppress the fear; let it drive you, like Devakī, into stuti.
    Analogy

    A mother who finds a king's seal-ring in her newborn's hand knows the child is no ordinary baby — and her wonder becomes immediately tactical, because such a child is in danger from rival nobles. Devakī sees the conch, disc, club, lotus on her son and her mother-instinct turns at once to prayer and protection. Recognition and fear arrive in the same breath.

    Stories
    Yaśodā binding the universal child

    Later in the Tenth Canto (10.9), mother Yaśodā would try to bind Kṛṣṇa with a rope and find the rope always two fingers short — until her loving exhaustion was crowned by His own willingness to be bound. The pattern is the same as Devakī's here: a mother sees Kṛṣṇa's divinity, and her response is intensified affection plus protective action.

    Devakī's bhīta-yet-vismitā state — afraid yet astonished — is vātsalya-rasa under threat. The Bhāgavata is teaching us that vātsalya-bhakti does not dissolve in the face of Bhagavān's aiśvarya; it grips tighter.

    Important Words
    • avyaktam — unmanifest
      A- (privative) + vyakta (manifest). Bhagavān is unmanifest to material senses — Prabhupāda glosses with ataḥ śrī-kṛṣṇa-nāmādi na bhaved grāhyam indriyaiḥ (Padma Purāṇa): His name, form, qualities cannot be grasped by material indriyas. Sevonmukha — 'service-facing' — senses alone can perceive Him.
    • brahma — the Supreme Brahman
      Brahman, the impersonal Absolute / the all-pervading. In Gauḍīya theology, Brahman is the bodily effulgence of Bhagavān (brahmajyoti), not a separate or higher reality. Devakī addresses Kṛṣṇa AS brahma — anti-Māyāvāda move: the Person is the source, not the effulgence.
    • nirguṇam — without (material) qualities
      Nir (without) + guṇa. Gauḍīya reading: nirguṇa does NOT mean qualityless (Bhagavān has infinite spiritual qualities — sad-bhuja-īśvara, ṣaḍ-aiśvarya-pūrṇa). It means free of the three MATERIAL modes. Crucial doctrinal precision against Advaita.
    • nirviśeṣam — without distinction (omnipresent)
      Nir (without) + viśeṣa (distinction, particularity). Often Advaitin's favorite word; here read carefully: He is undifferentiated in the sense of being equally present in every heart (Paramātmā). Not 'without form' but 'without locational restriction'.
    • viṣṇuḥ — Viṣṇu
      The name itself — from √viś ('to enter, pervade'). The all-pervading Lord. Devakī's resolution: brahma + jyotiḥ + nirviśeṣam = all aspects converge on Viṣṇu, who is now visibly her child. From three abstractions to one Person.
    • adhyātma-dīpaḥ — the lamp of all transcendental knowledge
      Adhyātma (spiritual) + dīpa (lamp). Bhagavān is the light by which all spiritual knowing happens. Echo of Upaniṣadic yasmin vijñāte sarvam evaṁ vijñātaṁ bhavati — knowing Him, all is known. Personal Lord as epistemic ground.
    Śrī Devakī said: My dear Lord, there are different Vedas, some of which describe You as unperceivable through words and the mind. Yet You are the origin of the entire cosmic manifestation. You are Brahman, the greatest of everything, full of effulgence like the sun. You have no material cause, You are free from change and deviation, and You have no material desires. Thus the Vedas say that You are the substance. Therefore, my Lord, You are directly the origin of all Vedic statements, and by understanding You, one gradually understands everything. You are different from the light of Brahman and Paramātmā, yet You are not different from them. Everything emanates from You. Indeed, You are the cause of all causes, Lord Viṣṇu, the light of all transcendental knowledge.
    Purport

    Viṣṇu is the origin of everything, and there is no difference between Lord Viṣṇu and Lord Kṛṣṇa because both of Them are viṣṇu-tattva. From the Ṛg Veda we understand, oṁ tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṁ padam: the original substance is the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu, who is also Paramātmā and the effulgent Brahman. The living entities are also part and parcel of Viṣṇu, who has various energies ( parāsya śaktir vividhaiva śrūyate svābhāvikī jñāna-bala-kriyā ca ). Viṣṇu, or Kṛṣṇa, is therefore everything. Lord Kṛṣṇa says in the Bhagavad-gītā (10.8) , ahaṁ sarvasya prabhavo mattaḥ sarvaṁ pravartate: “I am the source of all spiritual and material worlds. Everything emanates from Me.” Kṛṣṇa, therefore, is the original cause of everything ( sarva-kāraṇa-kāraṇam ). When Viṣṇu expands in His all-pervading aspect, we should understand Him to be the nirākāra-nirviśeṣa-brahmajyoti. Although everything emanates from Kṛṣṇa, He is ultimately a person. Aham ādir hi devānām: He is the origin of Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara, and from them many other demigods are manifested. Kṛṣṇa therefore says in Bhagavad-gītā (14.27) , brahmaṇo hi pratiṣṭhāham; “Brahman rests upon Me.” The Lord also says: ye ’py anya-devatā-bhaktā yajante śraddhayānvitāḥ te ’pi mām eva kaunteya yajanty avidhi-pūrvakam “Whatever a man may sacrifice to other gods, O son of Kuntī, is really meant for Me alone, but it is offered without true understanding.” ( Bg. 9.23 ) There are many persons who worship different demigods, considering all of them to be separate gods, which in fact they are not. The fact is that every demigod, and every living entity, is part and parcel of Kṛṣṇa ( mamaivāṁśo jīva-loke jīva-bhūtaḥ ). The demigods are also in the category of living entities; they are not separate gods. But men whose knowledge is immature and contaminated by the modes of material nature worship various demigods, according to their intelligence. Therefore they are rebuked in Bhagavad-gītā ( kāmais tais tair hṛta-jñānāḥ prapadyante ’nya-devatāḥ ). Because they are unintelligent and not very advanced and have not properly considered the truth, they take to the worship of various demigods or speculate according to various philosophies, such as the Māyāvāda philosophy. Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, is the actual origin of everything. As stated in the Vedas, yasya bhāṣā sarvam idaṁ vibhāti. The Absolute Truth is described later in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.28.15) as satyaṁ jñānam anantam yad brahma-jyotiḥ sanātanam. The brahmajyoti is sanātana, eternal, yet it is dependent on Kṛṣṇa ( brahmaṇo hi pratiṣṭhāham ). The Brahma-saṁhitā states that the Lord is all-pervading. Aṇḍāntara-stha-paramāṇu-cayāntara-stham: He is within this universe, and He is within the atom as Paramātmā. Yasya prabhā prabhavato jagad-aṇḍa-koṭi-koṭiṣv aśeṣa-vasudhādi-vibhu-ti-bhinnam: Brahman is also not independent of Him. Therefore whatever a philosopher may describe is ultimately Kṛṣṇa, or Lord Viṣṇu ( sarvaṁ khalv idaṁ brahma, paraṁ brahma paraṁ dhāma pavitraṁ paramaṁ bhavān ). According to different phases of understanding, Lord Viṣṇu is differently described, but in fact He is the origin of everything. Because Devakī was an unalloyed devotee, she could understand that the same Lord Viṣṇu had appeared as her son. Therefore, after the prayers of Vasudeva, Devakī offered her prayers. She was very frightened because of her brother’s atrocities. Devakī said, “My dear Lord, Your eternal forms, like Nārāyaṇa, Lord Rāma, Śeṣa, Varāha, Nṛsiṁha, Vāmana, Baladeva, and millions of similar incarnations emanating from Viṣṇu, are described in the Vedic literature as original. You are original because all Your forms as incarnations are outside of this material creation. Your form was existing before this cosmic manifestation was created. Your forms are eternal and all-pervading. They are self-effulgent, changeless and uncontaminated by the material qualities. Such eternal forms are ever-cognizant and full of bliss; they are situated in transcendental goodness and are always engaged in different pastimes. You are not limited to a particular form only; all such transcendental, eternal forms are self-sufficient. I can understand that You are the Supreme Lord Viṣṇu.” We may conclude, therefore, that Lord Viṣṇu is everything, although He is also different from everything. This is the acintya-bhedābheda-tattva philosophy.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śrī Devakī said: My dear Lord, there are different Vedas, some of which describe You as unperceivable through words and the mind. Yet You are the origin of the entire cosmic manifestation. You are Brahman, the greatest of everything, full of effulgence like the sun. You have no material cause, You are free from change and deviation, and You have no material desires. Thus the Vedas say that You are the substance. Therefore, my Lord, You are directly the origin of all Vedic statements, and by understanding You, one gradually understands everything. You are different from the light of Brahman and Paramātmā, yet You are not different from them. Everything emanates from You. Indeed, You are the cause of all causes, Lord Viṣṇu, the light of all transcendental knowledge.
    Commentary

    "As it is well known that the devotees control the Lord by praising him, I will make this child submissive by my prayers and then express my desires." Thinking in this way, she speaks. "O Lord, we are afflicted by fear at every second, but you are not fearful at all." She expresses this in four verses. "The Vedas describe your famous form as avyaka or beyond the material senses, adyam without birth, whose bodily effulgence is without material qualities and unchanging." This statement about Brahman is supported in the scriptures in many places. The sruti says: yasya bhasa sarvam idam vibhati (whose light supports the whole universe...) satyam jnanam anantam yad brahma jyotih santananam Bhagavatam. 10.28.14 Tat param paramam brahma sarvam vibhajate jagat mamaiva tad bhanam tejo jnatum arhasi bharata . I am the supreme Brahman, and the whole universe serves me. You should know that Brahman is my effulgence. Harivamsa (the Lord speaks to Arjuna) Yasya prabha prabhavato jagadanda koti kotisvasesa vasudadhi vibhuti binnam ... Brahma Samhita. Brahmano hi pritisthaham. Gita I am the source of Brahman In relation to the Lord’s vibhuti or powers, Sridha Swami in his commentary on Gita mentions that the impersonal feature of the Lord is called Brahman, indicated by the use of the word param. In Bhagavatam 8.24.38 Matsya speaks: madiyam mahimanam ca param brahmeti sabditam. paratparam brahma ca te vibhutayah The supreme Brahman is your vibhuti. Yamunacarya’s stotra tad brahma krsnayor aikyam mam kiranarkopamayujor The Brahman and Krsna are one as in the example of the rays and the sun. Bhakti rasamrta sindhu. "The associates, devotees, dhama and your forms all arise from the suddha sattva (satta matram). means that you are beyond the particulars of the material world (nirvisesa) You are niriham, without material thirst because you are full and perfect." Or it can mean "You are the person who takes away material desire from the devotee’s heart, and gives that devotee the desire to attain the Lord." Iha means desire, endeavour, thirst in the Amara kosa dictionary. "You are Visnu, adyatma dipah, because You reveal all truths. Though I am ignorant, I have spoken as you have revealed yourself to me."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Śrīdhara Svāmī explains this verse. Avayktam means not visible to anyone. “But it is not possible that an object is invisible to everyone.” You are the cause of everything (ādyam). This means that you are visible in the effects. The small flame does not reveal or burn fire in general. “But all the atoms are invisible and causes. Your definition is not exclusive.” This idea is rejected. No, you are Brahman (the greatest) whereas the collection of atoms of air is not great. “But pradhāna has the qualities of being invisible. It is the cause and spreads everywhere.” No, you are self-manifesting (jyotiḥ). The word jyotiḥ means a conscious entity whereas pradhāna is devoid of consciousness and is revealed by consciousness. Jyotiś caraṇābhidhānāt: light refers to Brahman since he is described as having four feet (three in the spiritual realm and one in matter). (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.25) “Consciousness arises from contact with knowledge. For the Vaiśeṣikas, the soul is essentially unconscious. By arousal of knowledge (part of sattva-guṇa) it becomes conscious. Is Brahman like that?” No, Brahman is nirguṇa. “Is Brahman a transformation of the guṇas, as in Mīmāṁsaka philosophy?” No, it is nirvikāram, without change. “Does Brahman transform, caused by discharge of śakti in the form of knowledge and action, according to Bhāskara?” No, Brahman is existence alone (sattā-mātram). The word sat means that substance is its essence. Brahman is that manifestation of substance alone. It is without transformation. In a joking mood Śrīdhara Svāmī then asks “Is it a combination of all general characteristics (sāmānya). Since it cannot be described by the previous terms it must a combination of all of them, like combining words together--for example hasti-snāna (washing an elephant).” No, it is without particular qualities (nirviśeṣam). Sāmānya depends on qualities. Because of qualities, the sāmānya form does not exist at all times in the past, present or future. Therefore that which is conscious, which can be described in words with true meaning is called sattā, since it reveals all the qualities mentioned. It is called conscious because it is self- revealing. Then again a doubt arises. “Is it full of disturbance because it is the cause?” No, it is without action (nirīham). This means the Lord is the cause by proximity, by his inconceivable śakti arising from his svarūpa. The special meaning is this. “If we analyze things in detail, finally the whole universe is nothing but Brahman. Why are there any qualities at all?” You are directly Viṣṇu. You are not covered by māyā. Therefore you are manifested with six special qualities, transformations of mercy, possessing limbs and other bodily features with graceful movements of hands and feet, a wealth of good qualities. One should consult the Bhagavat-sandarbha for establishment of the Lord’s qualities in his form according to the philosophy of Rāmānuja. Sattā means “having absolute qualities.” Jyotiḥ means self-revealing consciousness. Brahman means the greatest. Ādyam means without birth. That form revealed as a reflection to the jṣānīs by negating faulty qualities which are seen in the material realm, is actually the form of Viṣṇu. You are that form, and do not have the qualities of matter, since faults cannot be seen in you. Because the false concepts are refuted by scriptures which are realized by the learned, the Lord also personally refutes these false conceptions. By appearing directly in Devakī’s womb he refutes the idea that the Lord is unborn. He refutes the idea that qualities limit God, by appearing with his form decorated with ornaments. As well, Viṣṇu in the verse means “all-pervading.” Yaśodā and others make many statements like na cāntar na bahir yasya: he has no inside or outside. (SB 10.9.13) They realized that the Lord contains everything. Then the idea that the Lord manifests or is illuminated by others is refuted with the words adhyātmā-dīpaḥ. Rather you illuminate our intelligence. Like Brahman, you reveal yourself. No one can deceive you. Adhyātma means “depending on the self.” Thus the word can mean ātma-rāma. You also illuminate even the ātmā-rāmas. You give them joy by having them experience the highest bliss. The verse shows that the Lord’s form is superior to Brahman. The word sākṣāt indicates clear difference. Another meaning of the verse is “that form of Viṣṇu is called avyaktam, nirguṇam, free of material guṇas and is also called Parabrahman. That is you, the Supreme Lord (viṣṇuḥ), who pervades by your own powers.” Viṣṇuḥ means the Supreme Lord. Adhyātma-dīpaḥ means the supreme ātmā. Other words have the same meaning.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Another meaning of the verse is “that form of Viṣṇu is called avyaktam, nirguṇam, free of material guṇas and is also called Parabrahman. That is you, the Supreme Lord (viṣṇuḥ), who pervades by your own powers.” Viṣṇuḥ means the Supreme Lord. Adhyātma-dīpaḥ means the supreme ātmā. Other words have the same meaning.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa is Viṣṇu Himself — the personal source of Brahman and Paramātmā; surrender to Him directly, not to an impersonal light.
    Practical Applications
    • When tempted to call Krishna 'the universe' or 'consciousness,' stop and address Him by name as a person you are answering to today.
    • Open your sādhana this morning by acknowledging that the brahmajyoti, the cosmos, and your own self all rest on Kṛṣṇa — then offer one concrete act to Him.
    • Refuse to treat any demigod, ideology, or 'higher power' as parallel to Kṛṣṇa; route every prayer and decision through Him alone.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I quietly worshiping a 'demigod' — career, health, relationship, ideology — as if it were an independent source of refuge, when this verse insists every such shelter is only borrowed effulgence from Kṛṣṇa Himself?
    • Devakī recognized the all-pervading Viṣṇu as her own son — fully personal, in front of her — even while frightened by Kaṁsa; what concrete fear in my life am I keeping abstract precisely because surrendering to Kṛṣṇa as a person, here and now, would demand more of me than worshiping an impersonal 'Absolute'?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Next time you're scrolling Instagram or TikTok and feel that pull of 'I want to be like them,' pause and remember Devakī's verse — every influencer, every aesthetic, every trend is a tiny reflection borrowing its shine from Kṛṣṇa, the original. Worship the source, not the reflections.
    • In your friend group, notice the impulse to say 'the universe is telling me…' or 'trust the vibes' — that's impersonalist drift in your daily speech. For one week, replace those phrases with 'Kṛṣṇa is arranging this' and watch how it changes the way you read events.
    • Before your next exam, instead of praying to 'whatever's out there' for a good result, address Kṛṣṇa specifically as the cause of all causes — and ask not for the marks but for the steadiness to do your part as offering. Then check afterward whether the prayer felt different from the vague kind.
    householder
    • When a major family decision is on the table — a job change, a school for the kids, a financial move — formally name Kṛṣṇa as sarva-kāraṇa-kāraṇam before the discussion begins. This is not ceremony; it reorders the whole conversation away from 'what does the market say' toward 'what serves Him through this family.'
    • Watch the 'demigods' you've quietly enthroned in household life — the boss whose mood runs your week, the in-law whose approval you chase, the bank balance that dictates your peace. Each is a borrowed cause. This week, write down the one you've most over-empowered, and consciously demote it back under Kṛṣṇa.
    • Teach your children, by example, to address Kṛṣṇa as a person, not a concept. When a child asks 'why did this happen,' resist the modern reflex of 'things just happen' or 'the universe.' Say: Kṛṣṇa arranged it, and our work is to respond well. They will inherit your metaphysics whether you intend it or not.
    senior
    • You have watched many 'causes' in your life turn out to be secondary — bosses who seemed all-powerful, illnesses that seemed final, fortunes that seemed permanent. Sit with one of them now and trace it back to Kṛṣṇa as the actual cause. This is not nostalgia; it is the dhīra's review that Devakī models.
    • When mentoring someone younger, refuse the temptation to give 'spiritual but not religious' advice — the vague 'follow your light' kind. Devakī did not console herself with abstractions; she named Viṣṇu directly. Give the next person who comes to you the gift of a personal Absolute, not a comfortable one.
    • As bodily attachments loosen, notice whether you're drifting toward the impersonal — 'I'll merge with the light,' 'I'll dissolve into peace.' Devakī's verse warns against resting there. The brahmajyoti is real but dependent; the destination is Kṛṣṇa Himself. Renew your daily address to Him as a person, by name, especially as the body weakens.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading 'nirguṇaṁ nirviśeṣaṁ' as proof of an impersonal Absolute and slipping into Māyāvāda — missing that the verse climaxes in 'sa tvaṁ sākṣād viṣṇuḥ', the personal Lord standing before Devakī.
    • Using acintya-bhedābheda as an intellectual escape hatch ('everything is Kṛṣṇa, so anything I do is fine') instead of as a call to see Kṛṣṇa as the cause behind every cause and adjust one's daily choices accordingly.
    • Treating Kṛṣṇa as merely one more incarnation alongside Viṣṇu, Rāma, Nṛsiṁha and the demigods — flattening the viṣṇu-tattva hierarchy and quietly demoting Kṛṣṇa to a sectarian deity rather than the origin (ādyam) the verse declares Him to be.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Devakī addresses Kṛṣṇa as both the impersonal Brahman (nirguṇa, nirviśeṣa) AND as Lord Viṣṇu personally present before her. Where in your own practice do you lean toward the impersonal — 'the universe,' 'consciousness,' 'energy' — and where do you actually relate to Kṛṣṇa as a person? Be honest with your partner about which feels more comfortable, and why.
    • The verse says Kṛṣṇa is the cause of all causes (sarva-kāraṇa-kāraṇam), yet most of us live as if our boss, our parents, our circumstances, or random luck are the actual causes in our lives. Name one specific situation this week where you treated a secondary cause as if it were the original cause. What would change if you traced it back to Kṛṣṇa?
    • Prabhupāda warns against worshiping demigods or any 'separate gods' as if they were independent. In modern life, what are the 'demigods' you find yourself worshiping — money, career, health, a guru-figure, a relationship — that you treat as independent sources of welfare rather than as energies of Kṛṣṇa? Push back on each other if the answers stay too abstract.
    Role Play

    Two students. Student A is a devotee preparing for class; Student B is a thoughtful college friend who has just returned from a mindfulness retreat and says, 'I had this incredible experience of merging with pure consciousness — no form, no name, just light. Isn't that exactly what your tradition calls Brahman? So why do you keep insisting on this blue cowherd boy?' Student A must respond using SB 10.3.24 — explaining acintya-bhedābheda-tattva, why the brahmajyoti is dependent on Kṛṣṇa (brahmaṇo hi pratiṣṭhāham), and why the personal form is the source, not a step down from the impersonal. The teacher pauses the role-play whenever Student A drifts into jargon and asks: 'Say that again as if you were her actual friend.'

    Objections & Responses
    • Saying Kṛṣṇa is 'the cause of all causes' sounds exactly like every other religion saying their God is the supreme one. Why should I take this claim more seriously than a Christian saying Christ, or a Muslim saying Allah, is the origin of everything?
      Fair pushback — and the Gauḍīya answer is not 'because we say so.' Devakī's verse points to a specific philosophical claim, not a tribal one: the Absolute must be simultaneously the source of the impersonal effulgence (Brahman), the all-pervading witness (Paramātmā), AND a person — because a source that lacks personality is less than what it produces. Other traditions often stop at one of those three. Test it the way Devakī does: examine whether the Absolute you accept can account for variety, relationship, and love, or whether it has to dissolve those as illusion. The Gauḍīya line, acintya-bhedābheda-tattva, holds all three together. That's not sectarian preference; that's a structural argument you're invited to examine.
    • If Kṛṣṇa is 'free from change and deviation' (nirvikāram) and has 'no material desires' (nirīham), why does He appear, take a body, kill demons, dance with gopīs? That sounds like a lot of activity for someone supposedly beyond all change.
      This is exactly the confusion the verse is pre-empting. Devakī calls Him nirvikāram and nirīham in the same breath that she recognizes Him as her son standing before her — because His activities are not material activities. A material body changes; Kṛṣṇa's form is sac-cid-ānanda, not made of the five elements. Material desire arises from lack; Kṛṣṇa's pastimes arise from fullness (pūrṇa). When you act because you need something, that's vikāra. When Kṛṣṇa acts, nothing is added to or subtracted from Him — the activity is His nature, like sunlight is the sun's nature, not the sun's labor. The verse is naming this paradox, not denying it: He is changeless AND He is the most active person. Acintya — inconceivable to the mundane logic that demands one or the other.
    Analogy

    Light enters a room through three different openings — through a clear window you see the source's form, through a stained-glass pane you see the source's color, through a translucent screen you see only the brightness. Brahman, Paramātmā, Bhagavān are these three openings: the same Sun, three apertures of realization. Devakī addresses Kṛṣṇa as the Sun behind all three.

    Stories
    Caitanya teaching Sanātana the three aspects

    In Caitanya-caritāmṛta, Caitanya Mahāprabhu explicitly teaches Sanātana Gosvāmī the threefold realization of the Absolute: brahmeti paramātmeti bhagavān iti śabdyate (SB 1.2.11). Brahman is the effulgence, Paramātmā the localized in-dweller, Bhagavān the full Person. Same tattva, three depths.

    Devakī's stanza is essentially that catechism in prayer-form. She names brahma, names jyotiḥ (the effulgence), names nirviśeṣam (the indweller-pervasion), and resolves all three in 'saḥ tvam sākṣāt viṣṇuḥ' — that very You, directly Viṣṇu. The Bhāgavatam's own siddhānta delivered through a mother's mouth.

    Important Words
    • dvi-parārdha-avasāne — at the end of the two parārdhas (Brahmā's full life)
      Dvi (two) + parārdha (half of Brahmā's life) + avasāna (end). Bhāgavata cosmology measures time in scales that dwarf human imagination — and Bhagavān outlasts even those. The verse is positioning Him as eternal in the absolute sense, not the relative.
    • kāla-vegena — by the force of time
      Kāla (time) + vega (force, momentum) + instrumental. Time itself is Bhagavān's energy (BG 11.32, kālo'smi). Yet here time is the agent of annihilation — His own potency dissolving His own manifestation. Reflexive cosmic action.
    • ekaḥ — one alone
      Eka — one, alone. Crucial Vaiṣṇava reading: Bhagavān remains 'one' in the sense of being the only existent — but with his eternal sva-rūpa, energies, and associates. NOT 'one' in the Advaitin sense of dissolving difference. Acintya-bhedābheda preserves both eka and ananta.
    • aśeṣa-saṁjñaḥ — known by various names (Ananta, Śeṣa)
      Aśeṣa (without remainder, also a play on the name Śeṣa) + saṁjñā (name, designation). He is named differently in different phases — Ananta-Śeṣa during dissolution. The Vaiṣṇava plurality of holy names is itself a doctrinal fact: He is one, His names are countless, and each name is fully Him.
    After millions of years, at the time of cosmic annihilation, when everything, manifested and unmanifested, is annihilated by the force of time, the five gross elements enter into the subtle conception, and the manifested categories enter into the unmanifested substance. At that time, You alone remain, and You are known as Ananta Śeṣa-nāga.
    Purport

    At the time of annihilation, the five gross elements — earth, water, fire, air and ether — enter into the mind, intelligence and false ego ( ahaṅkāra ), and the entire cosmic manifestation enters into the spiritual energy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who alone remains as the origin of everything. The Lord is therefore known as Śeṣa-nāga, as Ādi-puruṣa and by many other names. Devakī therefore prayed, “After many millions of years, when Lord Brahmā comes to the end of his life, the annihilation of the cosmic manifestation takes place. At that time the five elements — namely earth, water, fire, air and ether — enter into the mahat-tattva. The mahat-tattva again enters, by the force of time, into the nonmanifested total material energy, the total material energy enters into the energetic pradhāna, and the pradhāna enters into You. Therefore after the annihilation of the whole cosmic manifestation, You alone remain with Your transcendental name, form, quality and paraphernalia. “My Lord, I offer my respectful obeisances unto You because You are the director of the unmanifested total energy, and the ultimate reservoir of the material nature. My Lord, the whole cosmic manifestation is under the influence of time, beginning from the moment up to the duration of the year. All act under Your direction. You are the original director of everything and the reservoir of all potent energies.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    After millions of years, at the time of cosmic annihilation, when everything, manifested and unmanifested, is annihilated by the force of time, the five gross elements enter into the subtle conception, and the manifested categories enter into the unmanifested substance. At that time, You alone remain, and You are known as Ananta Śeṣa-nāga.
    Commentary

    For one who is not destroyed during mahapralaya, what is the question of fear? The five elements(mahabhutam) merge into adibhutam or ahankara. Ahankara merges into vyaktam or mahat tattva. The mahat tattva merges into avyakta or prakrti. Then only you remain. Those things mentioned in the previous verse, the forms of Narayan and others, brahma jyoti and the dhama (sattamatram) also remain. The Lord’s associates, place and cloth are all eternal. You are called sesa because you remain (avasesa). This is a way of deriving the name Sesa.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Time is the cause of destruction. You alone remain. Since Vaikuṇṭha is non-different from the Lord it and other spiritual objects are included in the statement. Or you alone remain with those forms designated as unlimited that also remain in Vaikuṇṭha after pralaya. Or the word aśeṣa can also be taken as śeṣa (remain). Thus they inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha also remain after destruction. Or śeṣa can refer to all the objects of Vaikuṇṭha that remain after destruction. You alone, along with the objects of Vaikuṇṭha understood (saṁjṣaḥ) to be non-different from you, remain. You alone exist. This does not include the jīvas of the material world. tattvānāṁ bhagavaṁs teṣāṁ katidhā pratisaṅkramaḥ tatremaṁ ka upāsīran ka u svid anuśerate How many types of destruction are there for the various elements? Who remains serving the Lord during destruction, and who goes to sleep? SB 3.7.37 However the devotees are in a special position: martyo mṛtyu-vyāla-bhītaḥ palāyan lokān sarvān nirbhayaṁ nādhyagacchat tvat pādābjaṁ prāpya yadṛcchayādya susthaḥ śete mṛtyur asmād apaiti No one in this material world has become free from the four principles birth, death, old age and disease, even by fleeing to various planets. But now that you have appeared, my Lord, death is fleeing in fear of you, and the living entities, having obtained shelter at your lotus feet by your mercy, are sleeping in full mental peace. SB 10.3.27

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Even at the time of universal destruction you remain playing with your associates. By the force of time everything is destroyed. At that time the associate Śeṣa remains. This stands for Garuḍa and others as well. They remain or they stand (śiśyate) even at destruction. Or that which is known as śeṣa, because it remains—everything in Vaikuṇṭha—is left. Yatheṣṭa-viniyogārhaṁ śeṣa-śabdena kathyate: all that which is utilized for the Lord’s pleasure is called śeṣa. Those things which are eternally with the Lord are called śeṣa.
