    Personal Guidance
    When all manifestation dissolves at pralaya, Kṛṣṇa alone remains as Ananta Śeṣa — so anchor your shelter in Him today, not in what time will swallow.
    Practical Applications
    • Name three things you are leaning on for security today (job, body, savings) and explicitly hand each one to Kṛṣṇa as borrowed, not owned.
    • When a fear of loss arises, recall that even the five gross elements collapse into Him at annihilation — and offer that fear at His feet.
    • Refuse to invest your identity in any role or possession that pralaya will erase; spend ten minutes in japa rooting your sense of self in Him alone.
    Reflection Questions
    • When I picture the dvi-parārdha dissolution — every gross element folding back into the unmanifest, every category I rely on for identity erased — what part of my present self-conception cannot survive that contraction, and why am I still investing in it?
    • If Kṛṣṇa alone remains as Ananta Śeṣa-nāga when everything else is withdrawn, what would it look like, today, to relate to Him as the one who *will* remain — rather than to the people, roles, and securities that will not?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When your Instagram or college-application persona feels like the most permanent thing about you, sit for two minutes and remember: even pradhāna dissolves. The 'brand' you are building will not survive one cosmic night. Let that loosen the grip — not into laziness, but into honesty about what you are actually here to study and serve.
    • Before your next exam, offer the result formally to Kṛṣṇa as Ananta Śeṣa — the One who remains when even mahat-tattva is gone. Then study harder, not less. Notice how detachment from the score sharpens, rather than dulls, the preparation.
    • When a friendship breaks or a situationship ends and you feel like your world is annihilated, name it accurately: a small dissolution, not THE dissolution. The Self in you that is grieving has already passed through many bodies and many friend groups. Write down three earlier 'endings' you survived — and recognize the same dhīra in you now.
    householder
    • When making the next big family decision (a move, a school choice, a job change), bring it to evening sandhyā and consciously place the outcome at the feet of Ananta Śeṣa — the Lord who alone remains. Decide with full effort and full detachment from the result; this is the householder's karma-yoga, not renunciate's escape.
    • Audit your financial planning this month against the verse: how much of your savings, insurance, and estate-planning anxiety assumes that the structures of this world are more permanent than they are? Keep the prudence; drop the panic. The pradhāna itself dissolves — your 401(k) is even shorter-lived.
    • Teach your children — by what you do, not what you say — that you are training them as eternal souls passing through this stage of life, not as résumés to be optimized. One concrete act this week: skip one achievement-oriented activity and replace it with reading or hearing about Kṛṣṇa together.
    senior
    • Your body, like the five gross elements in the verse, will enter the subtle, and the subtle will enter the unmanifest. Sit with that truth daily for five minutes — not morbidly, but as preparation. The dhīra does not flinch from this passage; he uses the remaining time to deepen surrender.
    • Identify one possession, role, or title you have been quietly clinging to as 'mine forever' — the house, the chair on the board, the position in the family hierarchy. This week, make one concrete act of loosening: hand over a responsibility, give away an heirloom with warm words, name a successor. Practice the dissolution before it is forced.
    • Mentor a younger devotee or family member by speaking plainly about Ananta Śeṣa — the One who remains. Do not philosophize at them; tell them what you have learned about what does and does not survive. Your testimony at this stage carries weight that no book can match.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating cosmic annihilation as a poetic abstraction — admiring the scale of pralaya while never letting it touch one's daily attachments to body, status, or possessions; the verse becomes cosmology instead of vairāgya.
    • Sliding into impersonalism: imagining that what 'remains' at annihilation is a formless light or pure consciousness, rather than the personal Lord with His transcendental name, form, quality, and paraphernalia, as Devakī explicitly prays.
    • Using the inevitability of dissolution as an excuse for fatalism or passivity ('nothing lasts, so nothing matters'), missing that the verse's purpose is to redirect effort toward the one Person who does remain — not to dismiss action altogether.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Devakī describes a moment when even mahat-tattva and pradhāna dissolve into Kṛṣṇa, while He alone remains as Ananta Śeṣa. Share with your partner: what is one 'permanent' structure in your life — a job, a relationship, a body of work — that you have been quietly treating as eternal? Where does the disagreement land between you about whether contemplating its dissolution is liberating or paralyzing?
    • The verse pivots on a personalist claim: at annihilation, what remains is not a luminous void or impersonal Self, but bhavān — You, with name, form, quality and paraphernalia. Discuss: is it harder for you to surrender to a Person than to an abstraction? Push each other on which is intellectual evasion and which is genuine bhakti.
    • Prabhupāda's purport says the entire cosmos enters the spiritual energy of the Supreme. If everything ultimately reposes in Him, does this make daily karma less serious or more serious? Defend opposite positions in your pair before trying to reconcile them through the lens of sva-dharma.
    Role Play

    Two students role-play a hospice scene. Student A is a 78-year-old grandfather who has just received a terminal diagnosis and is panicking that 'everything I built — the company, the house, the family name — will be gone in twenty years.' Student B is a grandchild who has been studying the Bhāgavatam and wants to share the truth of SB 10.3.25 — that at the time of cosmic annihilation, even mahat-tattva dissolves, and only Kṛṣṇa remains as Ananta Śeṣa. Student B must NOT use it to bypass the grandfather's grief or to score philosophical points; they must offer real karuṇā (serving the soul) rather than material compassion (just soothing the body's fear). After 5 minutes, swap roles. Then debrief: where did the verse land as comfort, and where did it land as evasion?

    Objections & Responses
    • This is just cosmic nihilism dressed up in Sanskrit. If everything I love — my children, my work, the planet itself — eventually dissolves into Kṛṣṇa, why bother with any of it? It collapses into apathy.
      Notice the verse does not say everything becomes nothing — it says everything enters Him, and He remains with His transcendental name, form, quality, and paraphernalia. That is not nihilism; that is the opposite. Nothing precious is lost; it is held. Apathy comes from believing things are *unreal* now and *gone* later. The Gauḍīya teaching is that things are real because they rest in Him — and that recognition does not collapse engagement, it purifies it. You serve your children not to make them permanent (you cannot) but because the soul in them is eternal and the service is offered to Kṛṣṇa. That is karma-yoga, not apathy.
    • Modern cosmology gives us the Big Bang, heat death, entropy. Why drape it in mythological language about Brahmā's lifespan and Ananta Śeṣa? Isn't this pre-scientific dressing on facts science already explains better?
      Science describes the *mechanism* of dissolution; it is silent on what, if anything, remains as the substrate and on whether that substrate is personal. SB 10.3.25 is not competing with cosmology — it is answering a question cosmology cannot pose: at the limit of all manifestation, is there a Person, or only equations? Devakī's prayer is empirical in its own register — it comes from a tradition of seers, not speculators. The diacritics and the names (Ananta Śeṣa, Ādi-puruṣa) are not decoration; they are precise designations of what the impersonalist tradition tries to flatten into 'consciousness' or 'the Absolute.' Honor the science where it speaks; do not let it silence the question it cannot answer.
    Analogy

    Consider an ocean: rivers pour into it, waves rise and crash, ice forms and melts. At the end of a kalpa, when the rivers cease and the waves still and the ice has all melted, only the ocean remains, unmoved and one. Ananta-Śeṣa, on whom Viṣṇu reclines after the cosmic dissolution, is exactly this remaining ocean — and Bhagavān reclines upon Himself.

    Stories
    Mārkaṇḍeya's vision of the floodwaters

    The sage Mārkaṇḍeya (SB 12.9) was granted a vision of the cosmic dissolution. He saw the entire universe drowned in water; only a child-form of Bhagavān lay floating on a banyan leaf, the navel-lotus of all creation. Mārkaṇḍeya entered the child's mouth and saw all the worlds within.

    This verse is recalling that state. Beyond duration of any Brahmā's life, beyond the dissolution of mahat-tattva itself, ekaḥ śiṣyate — He alone remains, names changing (Ananta, Śeṣa, Garbhodakaśāyī), but svarūpa the same.

    Important Words
    • kālaḥ — time
      Kāla — time, the divider of being into nimeṣa and vatsara. In Vaiṣṇava theology kāla is one of Bhagavān's principal energies; in BG 11.32 He declares Himself to be kāla directly. Time is not a neutral container but a personal śakti of Bhagavān.
    • avyakta-bandho — O friend of the unmanifest
      Vocative compound: avyakta (unmanifest) + bandhu (friend, kin). Bhagavān is the 'companion' of the unmanifest prakṛti — He sets it in motion. Stunning Sanskrit: not 'overlord' but bandhu, friend. Bhakti's intimacy persists even in cosmological address.
    • kṣema-dhāma — the abode of auspicious welfare
      Kṣema (welfare, security) + dhāma (abode, source). Bhagavān is the source of every good thing — kṣema is what Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa for in BG 9.22 (yoga-kṣemaṁ vahāmy aham). Surrender is intelligent because it puts you in the only address from which kṣema is actually delivered.
    • prapadye — I surrender
      First-person singular of pra-√pad — the verb of śaraṇāgati. Same root as BG 18.66's vraja: prapadye is the active verbal form, the actual doing of surrender. The Gauḍīya tradition makes this verb central — six limbs of prapatti unpack what is folded into this one word.
    O inaugurator of the material energy, this wonderful creation works under the control of powerful time, which is divided into seconds, minutes, hours and years. This element of time, which extends for many millions of years, is but another form of Lord Viṣṇu. For Your pastimes, You act as the controller of time, but You are the reservoir of all good fortune. Let me offer my full surrender unto Your Lordship.
    Purport

    As stated in the Brahma-saṁhitā (5.52) : yac-cakṣur eṣa savitā sakala-grahāṇāṁ rājā samasta-sura-mūrtir aśeṣa-tejāḥ yasyājñayā bhramati saṁbhṛta-kāla-cakro govindam ādi-puruṣaṁ tam ahaṁ bhajāmi “The sun is the king of all planetary systems and has unlimited potency in heat and light. I worship Govinda, the primeval Lord, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, under whose control even the sun, which is considered to be the eye of the Lord, rotates within the fixed orbit of eternal time.” Although we see the cosmic manifestation as gigantic and wonderful, it is within the limitations of kāla, the time factor. This time factor is also controlled by the Supreme Personality of Godhead, as confirmed in Bhagavad-gītā ( mayādhyakṣeṇa prakṛtiḥ sūyate sa-carācaram ). Prakṛti, the cosmic manifestation, is under the control of time. Indeed, everything is under the control of time, and time is controlled by the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Therefore the Supreme Lord has no fear of the onslaughts of time. Time is estimated according to the movements of the sun ( savitā ). Every minute, every second, every day, every night, every month and every year of time can be calculated according to the sun’s movements. But the sun is not independent, for it is under time’s control. Bhramati saṁbhṛta-kāla-cakraḥ: the sun moves within the kāla-cakra, the orbit of time. The sun is under the control of time, and time is controlled by the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Therefore the Lord has no fear of time. The Lord is addressed here as avyakta-bandhu, or the inaugurator of the movements of the entire cosmic manifestation. Sometimes the cosmic manifestation is compared to a potter’s wheel. When a potter’s wheel is spinning, who has set it in motion? It is the potter, of course, although sometimes we can see only the motion of the wheel and cannot see the potter himself. Therefore the Lord, who is behind the motion of the cosmos, is called avyakta-bandhu. Everything is within the limits of time, but time moves under the direction of the Lord, who is therefore not within time’s limit.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O inaugurator of the material energy, this wonderful creation works under the control of powerful time, which is divided into seconds, minutes, hours and years. This element of time, which extends for many millions of years, is but another form of Lord Viṣṇu. For Your pastimes, You act as the controller of time, but You are the reservoir of all good fortune. Let me offer my full surrender unto Your Lordship.
    Commentary

    In the previous verse it appears that time is independent. Thus this verse speaks of time’s origin. It speaks of the cause of time-- who does not fear fearful time? That time is your kriya sakti or cesta. Therefore the Lord is addressed as the instigator of prakriti (avyakta (prakrti) bandho). By the influence of time, the universe runs. What is time? Time is nimesa or moments amounting to years, which again multiply into a day of brahma (dvi prarardha). I surrender to you (tva). Since you are fearless, you can make me fearless.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After the influence of time was mentioned, the independence of time is refuted by Devakī. She rejects fear of time and surrenders to the Lord’s lotus feet out of fear of Kaṁsa. Time, which starts with second and ends with years, which rotate to make the life time of Brahmā (mahīyān), and by which the universe moves, is said to be the movement of you (te) who are of that fearless nature (tasya). Therefore I surrender to you, the Supreme Lord who can destroy the fear of the surrendered, who are the place of fearlessness, and bestower of happiness (kṣema-dhāma). Or, you are the shelter of all auspicious objects.

    Personal Guidance
    Time devours every cosmos but bows to Kṛṣṇa — take shelter of the kṣema-dhāma, the reservoir of all good fortune, today.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice each time anxiety about the future grips you, and inwardly surrender that moment to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of kāla.
    • Spend the first five minutes of your day acknowledging that this day's hours are not yours to command, and offer them to Him.
    • Refuse to treat any deadline, deterioration, or delay as ultimate — trace it back to time, and trace time back to its Controller.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I still pretending to be the controller of time — scheduling, planning, gripping outcomes — when this verse names Kṛṣṇa Himself as the One who moves the cosmic wheel?
    • When the kāla-cakra grinds against me through aging, missed chances, or sudden loss, do I run toward Him as kṣema-dhāma, the reservoir of all good fortune, or do I run toward distractions that promise to stop the wheel?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Before your next exam or deadline, write at the top of the page: 'I am not the potter, I am the wheel — Kṛṣṇa is avyakta-bandhu.' Then study with full effort (udyama), but watch how the panic about results loosens.
    • Audit one week of your social media use against kāla. Every minute is literally a form of Viṣṇu passing through your hand; would you scroll for two hours straight if you could see the Lord in those minutes? Cut one specific app or one specific hour and offer the recovered time as sādhana.
    • When a friend group, a relationship, or a peer ranking makes you feel like your worth depends on it lasting forever, recall that nimeṣa to vatsara — second to year — all dissolve under kāla. Practice one act of vairāgya today: do the right thing in that group even if it costs you status, because status is on a clock anyway.
    householder
    • In your next major family or career decision — a job change, a school for the kids, a financial commitment — name out loud, before deciding, that you are not the controller of the outcome. Do the planning fully (dakṣya), then formally offer the decision and its fruits to Kṛṣṇa before acting.
    • Set up a household practice that honours kāla as the Lord's form: a fixed morning sādhana time and a fixed evening offering of the day, both unmovable for work. The point is not the duration; it is treating time itself as belonging to Him, not to your calendar.
    • When a child, spouse, or parent disappoints you and you feel the urge to tighten control, remember Devakī in the prison cell — she did not control Kaṁsa, she surrendered to kṣema-dhāma. Practice kṣamā in one specific recurring family conflict this week: hold your ground on dharma, release your grip on outcome.
    senior
    • Take stock of what you are still gripping — a property, a title, a grudge, a child's life choice — and name it as a thing you have been pretending to be the avyakta-bandhu of. Choose one and consciously hand it over to Kṛṣṇa this week, in word and in deed.
    • Mortality is not an interruption of your life; it is kāla revealing its identity as Viṣṇu. Spend ten minutes daily reading or chanting with the explicit awareness that the time remaining is a personal gift from Him, not a dwindling resource. Notice how this changes what you choose to do with the afternoon.
    • Mentor one younger person — a grandchild, a junior colleague, a neighbour — not by giving them your accumulated opinions, but by pointing them past you to Kṛṣṇa as kṣema-dhāma. Adambhitva matters here: the goal is that they remember Him, not that they remember how wise you were.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating time-consciousness as mere productivity discipline — squeezing more output from each minute — instead of letting kāla humble the false sense of doership and drive surrender to the avyakta-bandhu behind the wheel.
    • Slipping into impersonal awe of 'cosmic time' or 'the universe' as if time itself were ultimate, forgetting that kāla is only another form of Lord Viṣṇu and that surrender is to Him personally, not to an abstraction.
    • Using the inevitability of time as an excuse for fatalism or inaction — 'everything is in His hands anyway' — rather than performing one's sva-dharma with vairāgya, knowing the Lord directs time but still calls us to right effort (udyama).
    Discussion Prompts
    • Devakī addresses Kṛṣṇa as avyakta-bandhu — the unseen one behind the wheel of time. Share with your partner one area of your life where you have been operating as if you were the potter, not the wheel. Where does the other person see this self-deception more clearly than you do? Push back on each other; do not let either of you off easy.
    • The verse says time is 'another form of Lord Viṣṇu.' For some, this is comforting; for others, it is terrifying — time is not a neutral resource but a personal force already accounting for me. Which response is yours, honestly, and what does the other response in the room see that yours misses?
    • Devakī surrenders to Kṛṣṇa as 'kṣema-dhāma' — the reservoir of all good fortune — at the very moment her seven previous children have been killed by Kaṁsa and this eighth one is in mortal danger. Is calling Him 'kṣema-dhāma' there an act of denial, a forced piety, or the deepest realism? Defend your view against someone who reads it the opposite way.
    Role Play

    A senior software engineer, Ravi, has just been passed over for promotion for the third year running, while a younger colleague was promoted past him. He sits down with a Gauḍīya friend the same evening, furious — 'I have given fifteen years to this company. Time is running out. I am being erased.' One student plays Ravi; another plays the friend. The friend must use the substance of SB 10.3.26 — that kāla is not Ravi's enemy but a form of the Lord, that Ravi is not the avyakta-bandhu behind his career, that surrender to Kṛṣṇa as kṣema-dhāma is the actual response — without quoting the verse cleanly, without sounding pious, and without dismissing Ravi's hurt. After five minutes, swap roles. The class then debates: where did the friend slide into platitude, and where did real consolation land?

    Objections & Responses
    • Saying 'time is controlled by God' is just a coping mechanism for people who feel powerless. In the real world, time management, planning, and seizing opportunity are what produce results — not surrender.
      The verse does not abolish effort; udyama and dakṣya are listed among its values. Devakī is not a passive woman — she is a mother fighting for her child's life inside a tyrant's prison. What she rejects is the illusion that her planning is the cause. Kṛṣṇa Himself in the Gītā says mayādhyakṣeṇa prakṛtiḥ sūyate — prakṛti works under His supervision. A Gauḍīya does not stop planning; he stops imagining the plan is the potter. The result is not less competence but less anxiety, because the outcome was never his to grip. This is the opposite of coping; coping pretends control still exists. Surrender drops the pretence.
    • If kāla is 'another form of Viṣṇu' and everything is under His control, then Kaṁsa's murders of the first six babies are also under His control. That makes God complicit in evil, and the 'reservoir of all good fortune' line sounds obscene right after six infanticides.
      This is the correct place for the objection — Devakī herself is the one speaking, over the bodies of her own children. Notice she does not say Kṛṣṇa caused Kaṁsa's cruelty; she says Kṛṣṇa is the controller of time, and that time has now brought Him into her womb. Kaṁsa acted by his own free will under tamas; the Lord did not script the asura's hatred, but neither is the asura outside His ultimate sovereignty. The personalist line is precise here: Kṛṣṇa is not an impersonal mechanism that 'allows' evil, He is a person who enters the prison Himself. Kṣema-dhāma is not the claim that nothing bad happens; it is the claim that the final shelter is real and personal, and the proof is that He has just arrived in the cell. The objection assumes a deistic god who should have prevented the suffering from a distance. Devakī is worshipping a God who is right there, in the cell, in time, with her.
    Analogy

    A great clockmaker holds the springs and gears of every clock on earth — yet within his own workshop he does not need a clock. He IS the time the clocks measure. Devakī sees that Kṛṣṇa is the source of the very kāla by which we measure our hours, and prapadye, 'I surrender', is the only intelligent response.

    Stories
    Gajendra's surrender

    When the elephant Gajendra was caught by the crocodile in SB 8.2–3, he tried his own strength for a thousand years and finally, exhausted, called out to Bhagavān. His final word was an act of prapatti — full surrender, ātma-nikṣepa. Viṣṇu appeared and saved him.

    Devakī's prapadye echoes Gajendra's cry. The verb is the same; the structure is the same; the moment of recognizing kāla's overwhelming power and one's own helplessness produces the same surrender. The Gauḍīya doctrine of śaraṇāgati is in this single word.

    Bhīṣma's surrender on the bed of arrows

    Bhīṣma, on his bed of arrows in the Mahābhārata, used his last days to glorify Kṛṣṇa and offer extended prayers. Knowing he had power to choose the hour of his death (icchā-mṛtyu), he chose to wait for the auspicious uttarāyaṇa — and surrendered as kāla took him.

    The pattern: even those who command time at a local level recognize that they do not control kāla absolutely; Bhagavān does. Prapadye is the answer to that recognition.

    Important Words
    • mṛtyu-vyāla-bhītaḥ — afraid of the serpent of death
      Mṛtyu (death) + vyāla (serpent) + bhīta (afraid). Death as a snake — sudden, venomous, inescapable by running. The image makes the next verb (palāyan, running) intelligible: people genuinely try to flee, and the verse names every running place — lokān sarvān, every world.
    • tvat-pāda-abjam — Your lotus feet
      Tvat (You) + pāda (foot) + abja (lotus). The 'lotus feet' image is the most concentrated symbol of śaraṇāgati in Vaiṣṇava poetry — feet (because surrender is at the feet) of lotus (because they are tender, fragrant, transcendental, and the seat of bhakti).
    • yadṛcchayā — by chance / by His mercy
      Yadṛcchayā — apparently 'by chance', but in Gauḍīya reading, what looks like chance is actually kṛṣṇa-kṛpā and guru-kṛpā operating beneath the surface. Prabhupāda's gloss: nothing is truly 'by chance' — every contact with Bhagavān comes through His causeless mercy.
    • śete — sleeps (peacefully)
      Third-person singular of √śī — to sleep, lie down. Same root as Ananta-Śeṣa-śayana. Once at His lotus feet, one 'sleeps' — that is, rests in non-anxiety. Cessation of mṛtyu-vyāla-bhīta agitation.
    • apaiti — flees (death itself flees)
      Apa (away) + √i (go). Death, the chaser, becomes the chased. Once one shelters at His feet, mṛtyu reverses direction. This is bhakti's eschatological promise: not 'death is conquered by knowledge' but 'death itself runs from where Bhagavān is the shelter'.
    No one in this material world has become free from the four principles birth, death, old age and disease, even by fleeing to various planets. But now that You have appeared, My Lord, death is fleeing in fear of You, and the living entities, having obtained shelter at Your lotus feet by Your mercy, are sleeping in full mental peace.
    Purport

    There are different categories of living entities, but everyone is afraid of death. The highest aim of the karmīs is to be promoted to the higher, heavenly planets, where the duration of life is very long. As stated in Bhagavad-gītā (8.17) , sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ: one day of Brahmā equals 1,000 yugas, and each yuga consists of 4,300,000 years. Similarly, Brahmā has a night of 1,000 times 4,300,000 years. In this way, we may calculate Brahmā’s month and year, but even Brahmā, who lives for millions and millions of years ( dvi-parārdha-kāla ), also must die. According to Vedic śāstra, the inhabitants of the higher planetary systems live for 10,000 years, and just as Brahmā’s day is calculated to equal 4,300,000,000 of our years, one day in the higher planetary systems equals six of our months. Karmīs, therefore, try for promotion to the higher planetary systems, but this cannot free them from death. In this material world, everyone from Brahmā to the insignificant ant must die. Therefore this world is called martya-loka. As Kṛṣṇa says in Bhagavad-gītā (8.16) , ābrahma-bhuvanāl lokāḥ punar āvartino ’rjuna: as long as one is within this material world, either on Brahmaloka or on any other loka within this universe, one must undergo the kāla-cakra of one life after another ( bhūtvā bhūtvā pralīyate ). But if one returns to the Supreme Personality of Godhead ( yad gatvā na nivartante ), one need not reenter the limits of time. Therefore, devotees who have taken shelter of the lotus feet of the Supreme Lord can sleep very peacefully with this assurance from the Supreme Personality of Godhead. As confirmed in Bhagavad-gītā (4.9) , tyaktvā dehaṁ punar janma naiti: after giving up the present body, a devotee who has understood Kṛṣṇa as He is need not return to this material world. The constitutional position for the living entity is eternity ( na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre, nityaḥ śāśvato ’yam ). Every living entity is eternal. But because of having fallen into this material world, one wanders within the universe, continually changing from one body to another. Caitanya Mahāprabhu says: brahmāṇḍa bhramite kona bhāgyavān jīva guru-kṛṣṇa-prasāde pāya bhakti-latā-bīja (Cc. Madhya 19.151) Everyone is wandering up and down within this universe, but one who is sufficiently fortunate comes in contact with Kṛṣṇa consciousness, by the mercy of the spiritual master, and takes to the path of devotional service. Then one is assured of eternal life, with no fear of death. When Kṛṣṇa appears, everyone is freed from fear of death, yet Devakī felt, “We are still afraid of Kaṁsa, although You have appeared as our son.” She was more or less bewildered as to why this should be so, and she appealed to the Lord to free her and Vasudeva from this fear. In this connection, it may be noted that the moon is one of the heavenly planets. From the Vedic literature we understand that one who goes to the moon receives a life with a duration of ten thousand years in which to enjoy the fruits of pious activities. If our so-called scientists are going to the moon, why should they come back here? We must conclude without a doubt that they have never gone to the moon. To go to the moon, one must have the qualification of pious activities. Then one may go there and live. If one has gone to the moon, why should he return to this planet, where life is of a very short duration?

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    No one in this material world has become free from the four principles birth, death, old age and disease, even by fleeing to various planets. But now that You have appeared, My Lord, death is fleeing in fear of You, and the living entities, having obtained shelter at Your lotus feet by Your mercy, are sleeping in full mental peace.
    Commentary

    Since those who take shelter of your lotus feet become fearless, what to speak of those who meet you face to face. Wandering throughout the universe, one cannot become free from fear. By the devotion attained by great mercy (yadrcchaya), one attains your lotus feet which are abjam or Dhanvatari, Lord of medicine. By this medicine the person becomes healthy. (Medini says that abja means lotus, dhanvantari, conch and moon.) "O Lord, origin of all, though I am your devotee, and have been accepted by you as your mother, I am still afflicted by fear of Kamsa."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Taking shelter of your feet one becomes fearless. Thus one becomes happy. That is expressed in this verse. No one qualified with death (martyaḥ) can attain freedom from fear of death. You are the best of all people (ādya,) since you are the controller of death! Attaining your lotus feet, one becomes fearless (susthaḥ) and tranquil (śete). Death flees from your lotus feet or from the peaceful person. Mention of lotus feet suggests that the Lord is the highest goal. Just by his influence, fear disappears. There is another meaning. Today (adya), now that you have appeared, all people will become fearless and tranquil. Present tense is used for the near future. This is because death flees from you. The rest is the same. It is also suggested that Kṛṣṇa is Parabrahman. Her fearlessness is emphasized by what she expresses. Because you remain at pralaya and because of your control of time causing all destruction, you destroy death for those who surrender to you. How can it not be possible? In accordance with the common theme of her prayers, verse 24 does not show that she has attraction for impersonal Brahman.

    Personal Guidance
    No planet, no plan, no power escapes mṛtyu — only shelter at Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet lets the soul sleep without fear.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one 'higher planet' you are secretly chasing — promotion, longevity, security — and refuse to treat it as your refuge today.
    • Before sleep tonight, place the day and the body explicitly at Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet and rest in the assurance that mṛtyu has no claim on the surrendered soul.
    • When fear of loss, illness, or death surfaces, stop and chant Kṛṣṇa's name once aloud instead of reaching for the next distraction.
    Reflection Questions
    • To which 'higher planet' — promotion, security, longevity, even a spiritual achievement — am I still fleeing in the hope it will exempt me from death, instead of taking shelter at Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet?
    • Where in my life do I sleep restlessly because I have not surrendered that domain to Him — and what would it look like to actually 'sleep peacefully' there, knowing mṛtyu has fled in His presence?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the next time you 'flee to another loka' — a new app, a new friend group, transferring colleges, swapping majors — to escape a fear you haven't named. Pause and ask: am I running toward something, or just away?
    • Before exams or a big interview this week, take two minutes to formally place the outcome at Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet. Not as a magic-trick request to pass, but as the actual relinquishing of the fear that your worth equals your result.
    • Audit one feed (Instagram, LinkedIn, whatever) for 'higher-loka' promises — the influencer life, the FAANG offer, the perfect aesthetic. Name out loud that even those lokas end in death, and unfollow three accounts that quietly preach otherwise.
    householder
    • When making the next big family decision — school district, job change, mortgage, medical choice for a parent — explicitly distinguish: am I optimizing for a longer or richer stay in martya-loka, or am I making a choice that also serves the soul of everyone involved? Write both answers down before deciding.
    • Build a household practice — even five minutes after dinner — where the family together offers the day's actions and worries to Kṛṣṇa. Children learn shelter (tvat-pādābjaṁ prāpya) by watching parents take it, not by being lectured about it.
    • Examine your insurance, savings, and retirement planning honestly. Provide responsibly — that is sva-dharma — but notice where the planning has quietly become a project of conquering death through spreadsheets. Cap the worry; do not cap the duty.
    senior
    • Each morning, name one attachment — a possession, a role, an opinion about how children should live — that you are ready to loosen this week. Loosening now is gentler than having it pried from you later.
    • Mentor at least one younger person specifically on the difference between material compassion (smoothing their bodily life) and real compassion (pointing them to shelter). Your age gives you authority to say what a peer cannot.
    • Instead of fearing the body's decline, treat each new limitation as Kṛṣṇa's quiet instruction to transfer weight from the body's projects to the soul's shelter — more japa, more hearing, more remembrance, less rearranging of a house death will empty anyway.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating 'fearlessness of death' as a psychological mood to cultivate rather than the natural fruit of taking shelter at Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet — manufacturing calm instead of surrendering.
    • Reading mṛtyur asmād apaiti as a promise of bodily safety or worldly insulation, and then feeling betrayed when difficulties still come, rather than understanding it as freedom from punar-janma.
    • Misusing 'sleeping in peace' as license for spiritual complacency — neglecting sādhana on the assumption that shelter has already been secured, when shelter is something to be taken daily, not banked.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Devakī says death itself flees in fear of Kṛṣṇa, yet she still trembles before Kaṁsa. Where in your life do you intellectually accept Kṛṣṇa's protection while practically still organizing your day around fear? Be specific — name the fear, name the hedge.
    • Prabhupāda is blunt: the so-called scientists never went to the moon, because no one returns from a 10,000-year pious-life destination to this short-lived planet. Does this reading offend, amuse, or persuade you? What does your reaction reveal about whose authority — śāstra or modern consensus — actually governs your worldview?
    • The verse contrasts running between lokas (palāyan) with taking shelter at the lotus feet (tvat-pādābjaṁ prāpya). In the last month, where have you been running — switching jobs, cities, relationships, apps, identities — under the illusion that the next loka will solve what only surrender can solve?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A plays a recently retired professional who has just received a serious medical diagnosis and is panicking — booking experimental treatments, researching life-extension protocols, considering a move to a 'healthier' country. Student B plays a Gauḍīya friend who has been invited over for tea. Without preaching, dismissing the medical reality, or offering cheap comfort, Student B must help Student A see the difference between fleeing to another loka (palāyan) and taking shelter at the lotus feet (tvat-pādābjaṁ prāpya) — and must distinguish material compassion (just calm them about the body) from real compassion (serve the soul). Swap roles after seven minutes. Debrief: where did the 'helper' slip into platitudes, and where did real shelter get pointed to?

    Objections & Responses
    • This verse is escapism. 'Death flees in fear of You' is wishful thinking — devotees still die of cancer, accidents, and old age just like everyone else. Calling this 'freedom from death' is a semantic trick.
      The verse never claims the devotee's body becomes immortal — martya-loka remains martya-loka. What it claims is that the soul, having taken shelter (tvat-pādābjaṁ prāpya), no longer reenters the kāla-cakra: tyaktvā dehaṁ punar janma naiti (BG 4.9). 'Death flees' means the death that matters — the forced rebirth into another body, another womb, another cycle of forgetting — loses its grip. The body still drops; the bondage does not return. That is not a semantic trick; it is a precise distinction between the death of the costume and the death of the wearer. Compare BG 2.21: how can one who knows the soul as imperishable kill or be killed?
    • Telling people 'sleep peacefully because Kṛṣṇa will save you' sounds like the same opiate Marx criticized — a way to make oppressed people stop fighting their actual conditions. Kaṁsa is still on the throne; why are we telling Devakī to relax?
      Look at the verse carefully: Devakī is not told to relax about Kaṁsa. She herself names her continuing fear in the very next breath, and the Lord does act — Kaṁsa is killed. Surrender in the Gauḍīya line is not passivity; it is the reordering of whom you ultimately depend on. The karmī fights Kaṁsa hoping a longer life on a higher loka will solve the death problem — and dies anyway. The devotee fights Kaṁsa too (Kṛṣṇa Himself does), but without the delusion that political victory is final victory. The peace Prabhupāda points to is not the peace of giving up the struggle; it is the peace of no longer mistaking the struggle for the goal. That is the opposite of opium — opium numbs you to reality; this wakes you up to which reality is actually permanent.
    Analogy

    A frightened bird flies from rooftop to rooftop trying to escape the falcon — until it finally lands on the falconer's wrist itself, the one place the falcon will not strike. Lokān sarvān — all the planets — the bird could try; only at Bhagavān's lotus feet does mṛtyu actually flee. The shelter is not a place; it is a Person.

    Stories
    Citraketu's tour of the worlds

    SB 6.14–17 tells of King Citraketu, who through Aṅgirā's blessing got a son, lost him to a poisoning, and was led by Nārada through demonstrations of how no realm — heavenly or earthly — escapes death. Only when he turned to bhakti did he attain Vidyādhara status, and ultimately Vaikuṇṭha.

    The verse compresses Citraketu's whole arc: martyaḥ, mṛtyu-bhīta, palāyan lokān sarvān — running to every world — nirbhayam na adhyagacchat — finds no fearlessness — until tvat-pāda-abjam prāpya — receiving Your lotus feet — śete, sleeps peacefully.

    Ajāmila's last moment

    Ajāmila (SB 6.1–3), at the moment of death, called for his son Nārāyaṇa — and by that one utterance of the holy name, the Viṣṇudūtas arrived and snatched him from the noose of the Yamadūtas. Even an unintentional invocation of Bhagavān's name dispels mṛtyu's grip.

    This verse is naming the same dynamic at the level of doctrine: the shelter of Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet is the only refuge from mṛtyu. Ajāmila found it accidentally; the wise find it deliberately.

    Important Words
    • trāhi — kindly protect
      Imperative of √trā — 'to protect, save'. The cry of trāhi-māṁ runs through Vaiṣṇava prayer literature (Stotra-ratna, Bhāgavatam, etc.). Imperative form indicates dependent intimacy — only one who knows you can save addresses you this way.
    • bhṛtya-vitrāsa-hā asi — You are the destroyer of Your servants' fear
      Bhṛtya (servant) + vitrāsa (terror) + hā (slayer) + asi (You are). Bhagavān's very nature is named: He is the slayer of His devotees' fear. Compound used as a SVN — a name that compresses a doctrine. Bhakti's reasonable confidence rests on this svabhāva.
    • pauruṣam — the form of the Supreme Person
      From puruṣa. The aiśvarya-form (four-armed Viṣṇu) that establishes who He is. Devakī asks Him to withdraw this puruṣatva — not because she rejects His personhood but because the demonic eyes around her cannot bear it without weaponizing.
    • dhyāna-dhiṣṇyam — the seat of meditation
      Dhyāna (meditation) + dhiṣṇya (seat, abode). The form on which yogīs meditate. The same form Kaṁsa would profane if seen. The verse silently affirms the four-armed Viṣṇu-mūrti as the legitimate object of dhyāna — pratimā-upāsana with Vedic warrant.
    • māṁsa-dṛśām — of those who see with flesh eyes
      Māṁsa (flesh) + dṛś (sight) + genitive plural. Sharp Sanskrit: 'flesh-eyes' — eyes that perceive only the material. Kaṁsa's vision. To see Bhagavān truly requires dīkṣā-saṁskāra — eyes anointed by guru and bhakti.
    My Lord, because You dispel all the fear of Your devotees, I request You to save us and give us protection from the terrible fear of Kaṁsa. Your form as Viṣṇu, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, is appreciated by yogīs in meditation. Please make this form invisible to those who see with material eyes.
    Purport

    The word dhyāna-dhiṣṇyam is significant in this verse because the form of Lord Viṣṇu is meditated upon by yogīs ( dhyānāvasthita-tad-gatena manasā paśyanti yaṁ yoginaḥ ). Devakī requested the Lord, who had appeared as Viṣṇu, to conceal that form, for she wanted to see the Lord as an ordinary child, like a child appreciated by persons who have material eyes. Devakī wanted to see whether the Supreme Personality of Godhead had factually appeared or she was dreaming the Viṣṇu form. If Kaṁsa were to come, she thought, upon seeing the Viṣṇu form he would immediately kill the child, but if he saw a human child, he might reconsider. Devakī was afraid of Ugrasena-ātmaja; that is, she was afraid not of Ugrasena and his men, but of the son of Ugrasena. Thus she requested the Lord to dissipate that fear, since He is always ready to give protection ( abhayam ) to His devotees. “My Lord,” she prayed, “I request You to save me from the cruel hands of the son of Ugrasena, Kaṁsa. I am praying to Your Lordship to please rescue me from this fearful condition because You are always ready to give protection to Your servitors.” The Lord has confirmed this statement in the Bhagavad-gītā by assuring Arjuna, “You may declare to the world, My devotee shall never be vanquished.” While thus praying to the Lord for rescue, mother Devakī expressed her motherly affection: “I understand that this transcendental form is generally perceived in meditation by the great sages, but I am still afraid because as soon as Kaṁsa understands that You have appeared, he might harm You. So I request that for the time being You become invisible to our material eyes.” In other words, she requested the Lord to assume the form of an ordinary child. “My only cause of fear from my brother Kaṁsa is due to Your appearance. My Lord Madhusūdana, Kaṁsa may know that You are already born. Therefore I request You to conceal this four-armed form of Your Lordship, which holds the four symbols of Viṣṇu — namely the conchshell, the disc, the club and the lotus flower. My dear Lord, at the end of the annihilation of the cosmic manifestation, You put the whole universe within Your abdomen; still, by Your unalloyed mercy, You have appeared in my womb. I am surprised that You imitate the activities of ordinary human beings just to please Your devotee.” Devakī was so afraid of Kaṁsa that she could not believe that Kaṁsa would be unable to kill Lord Viṣṇu, who was personally present. Out of motherly affection, therefore, she requested the Supreme Personality of Godhead to disappear. Although because of the Lord’s disappearance Kaṁsa would harass her more and more, thinking that the child born of her was hidden somewhere, she did not want the transcendental child to be harassed and killed. Therefore she requested Lord Viṣṇu to disappear. Later, when harassed, she would think of Him within her mind.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    My Lord, because You dispel all the fear of Your devotees, I request You to save us and give us protection from the terrible fear of Kaṁsa. Your form as Viṣṇu, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, is appreciated by yogīs in meditation. Please make this form invisible to those who see with material eyes.
    Commentary

    "You are fearless and your devotees are fearless. Then why, o Lord, do you keep your mother and father in fear?" This is the intention of this verse. Ghora here means great fear. Out of fear she does not mention the name of Kamsa directly but uses the word Ugrasena atmaja, son of Ugrasena. "You destroy the fears of your devotees, but why do you not remove our fear?" "O mother, I have appeared to kill Kamsa. Bring Kamsa here and I will kill him before your eyes." Fearing such talk from Krsna, Devaki, out of motherly affection, thinking that her small child could not kill Kamsa, and rather worrying about harm coming to the child from Kamsa, became more fearful. Her body began shaking. "It is not suitable to follow the strategy of showing fear before my child who is showing himself as God. Rather using sweet words is a better policy." Thinking in this way, she began to reason in another way in order to get her child to change his form. "O master, this splendid form, which is the object of meditation, should not be visible to human eyes."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Since you can produce fearlessness and have appeared as my son, please protect us. Kaṁsa’s men will directly attack you since they have no attraction for you, being your enemies. And Kaṁsa is the most ferocious, as indicated in verse 22, referring to Kaṁsa as the uncivilized one and suggested in this verse by calling him the son of Ugrasena (ferocious leader). And because he had thrown his father in prison the words “son of Ugrasena” further suggest his fearsome nature. It is also suggested that Kaṁsa was more fearful for appearing in his father’s line, since it is said that fear arising from friends relatives destroys the root . Therefore she says “Save us.” She speaks with compassion for she does not request the Lord to kill Kaṁsa. The word bho indicates extreme suffering. Out of motherly affection she speaks of some way to make the child disappear since she fears for the child also. Since the form of the Lord is the antaryāmī situated in all beings with four arms the child is also famous as the object of meditation (dhyāna-dhiṣṇyam) for those situated in the material world. The two armed form as the object of meditation is also seen but more rarely. Gūḍhaṁ paraṁ brahma manuṣya-liṅgam: Supreme Brahman personally resides in your houses in a human form. (SB 7.10.48) Gopāla-tāpanī Upaniṣad also says śṛṅga-veṇu-dharam: he holds a horn and flute. Hide that from ignorant people (māṁsa-dṛśām) because they are unqualified. The reason is later explained in verse 31: people will ridicule her when it is said that she gave birth to the Lord.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Protect persons like us (naḥ), terrified of Kaṁsa, the son of Ugrasena--he whose associates (sena) were fierce (ugra). This hints at Kaṁsa’s fierce nature. It is also suggested that Kaṁsa was more fearsome due to appearing in his father’s line, since it is said that fear arising from friends and relatives destroys the root. Or protect us, but do not kill Kaṁsa since he is the son of Ugrasena, a maternal uncle. “Why are you afraid?” He is ferocious (ghorāt). Bho indicates great pain. The method of deliverance is suggested. You have a smile which destroys your servants’ fears (bhṛtya-vitrāsa-hāsi). Do not show your form to the ignorant (māṁsa-ḍṛśām) or to those like Kaṁsa who see only to eat (māṁsa-dṛśām). Why? That form is the object of meditation for sages only (dhyāna-dhiṣṇyam). We will not be fearful if he does not know about your birth, being unable to see the attractive form. Or simply disappear. Not showing the form means the person should disappear. This is a prayer made out of affection.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa is the abhayam-giver — when fear closes in, beg Him to meet you in the form your trembling heart can hold today.
    Practical Applications
    • Name the specific 'Kaṁsa' you fear today — a person, outcome, or threat — and place it openly before Kṛṣṇa as Devakī did, asking for protection.
    • Refuse the impersonalist temptation to abstract Kṛṣṇa into 'the Self'; speak to Him directly, by name, the way a frightened mother speaks to her child's protector.
    • When His four-armed splendor feels too distant, ask Him to come close as the simple, holdable form your bhakti can actually serve right now.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I, like Devakī, asking Kṛṣṇa to 'tone down' His full presence because His undisguised reality threatens the safety I have built around a 'Kaṁsa' I still fear?
    • Whose 'māṁsa-dṛśā' — material gaze — am I unconsciously protecting Kṛṣṇa from in my own practice: relatives, colleagues, my own skeptical mind? And what does that hiding cost the depth of my relationship with Him?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Identify one place online — a group chat, a feed, a comment thread — where revealing your actual sādhana (japa, deity worship, scripture study) would invite ridicule from a 'Kaṁsa-ātmaja' figure; practice Devakī's discretion this week and keep that part of your life dhyāna-dhiṣṇyam, internal, while not denying it if directly asked.
    • When exam fear or peer-rejection fear spikes, name the specific person or outcome you actually fear (not the vague 'pressure'); then pray exactly as Devakī did — 'trāhi trastān' — naming Kṛṣṇa as bhṛtya-vitrāsa-hāsi, the one who removes a servant's fear, not as a generic universe.
    • Notice the temptation to want Kṛṣṇa to show up dramatically — a viral post, a miraculous result, an obvious sign — and instead train your eye to see Him in the 'ordinary child' form: the steady friend, the un-glamorous duty done, the quiet answer to prayer that nobody else would even register.
    householder
    • In family decisions where you are tempted to broadcast your devotion (in-laws, colleagues, school parents), ask Devakī's question first: would the four-armed form serve them, or would the ordinary child? Calibrate disclosure to the listener's adhikāra, not to your need to be seen as devout.
    • Identify the specific 'Kaṁsa' in your professional or financial life — a particular person, deal, or dependency whose hostility you actually fear — and stop laundering it as generic stress; bring that named fear into your morning prayer and let Kṛṣṇa be the protector of that exact relationship, not an abstract refuge.
    • When raising children, resist the urge to make Kṛṣṇa flashy to compete with their entertainment; let Him appear in your home as an ordinary, daily presence — meals offered, a small altar, a verse at bedtime — trusting that what looks unimpressive to māṁsa-dṛś eyes is precisely the form that will lodge in their hearts.
    senior
    • As bodily strength loosens, deliberately let your sādhana become more dhyāna-dhiṣṇyam and less performative — fewer external duties, more internal worship; the form of the Lord that meets you now is the one yogīs see in meditation, and that interior chamber is exactly what this stage is for.
    • Name your actual remaining fears — a specific illness, a particular grandchild's future, a legacy concern — rather than the polite 'fear of death'; bring each named fear to Kṛṣṇa as Devakī did, asking Him precisely as bhṛtya-vitrāsa-hāsi, the destroyer of the servant's fear, and notice which fears dissolve and which expose remaining attachment.
    • When mentoring younger family or students, practice Devakī's restraint: do not display the 'four-armed form' of all you have realized; offer them the ordinary-child form they can actually hold — a simple instruction, a shared meal, a verse — and trust the Lord to reveal more when their eyes are ready.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking Devakī's request for the Lord to conceal His four-armed form as scriptural license for impersonalism — as though the 'ordinary child' form were a metaphor for a formless Absolute, when in fact both forms are Kṛṣṇa personally and the verse honors His personhood, not its dissolution.
    • Reading 'bhṛtya-vitrāsa-hāsi' (He who dispels His devotees' fear) as a guarantee of material safety — expecting Kṛṣṇa to remove every external 'Kaṁsa' from one's life — rather than as the inward abhayam He grants the surrendered soul, which Devakī herself receives even while continuing to be harassed.
    • Imitating Devakī's protective concealment without her bhakti — keeping one's sādhana, japa, tilaka, or Kṛṣṇa-conscious convictions hidden from the world out of social fear, and calling that discretion 'humility,' when it is actually the māṁsa-dṛśā of others ruling one's own devotional life.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Devakī asks Kṛṣṇa to hide His four-armed Viṣṇu form so He looks like an ordinary child. Was this a lapse of faith — she should have trusted His protection — or was it a higher expression of vātsalya-rasa? Defend your answer to a partner who takes the opposite view.
    • Prabhupāda says Devakī feared not Ugrasena but the son of Ugrasena (Kaṁsa-ātmaja). In your own life, where does fear actually originate — circumstances, or specific persons whose intent threatens you? Share a concrete instance and let the group press you on whether you have correctly identified the real source.
    • The verse holds two truths in tension: the Lord's form is dhyāna-dhiṣṇyam (only for yogīs in meditation) yet He stands present before material eyes. Discuss with one other person: where in your sādhana do you actually want Kṛṣṇa to remain hidden, and why? Surface a real disagreement, not a polite agreement.
    Role Play

    Two students sit across from each other. Student A is 'Devakī' — the Lord has just manifested in their life as something obviously transcendental (an undeniable answer to prayer, a clear instruction from guru, a protection in crisis). Student B is 'a relative-Kaṁsa' — a skeptical, powerful family member who would mock, sabotage, or exploit this manifestation if they recognized it. Student A must explain to Student B what happened, while deciding in real time how much of Kṛṣṇa's hand to reveal and how much to 'conceal as an ordinary child.' After five minutes, switch roles. Then the class discusses: when is concealment bhakti-yukta discretion, and when is it a failure of nerve?

    Objections & Responses
    • Why would the Supreme Personality of Godhead need His mother to ask Him to hide? An omnipotent God would not require coaching from a frightened devotee — this reads like a folk story projected onto the divine.
      Precisely the point a Gauḍīya teacher would lean into. Kṛṣṇa is not a remote omnipotence to be defended philosophically — He is a person who relishes being managed by His devotees. He becomes bhṛtya-vitrāsa-hāsi (destroyer of the servant's fear) by responding to her cry, not by overriding it. His omnipotence includes the freedom to be guided by vātsalya. To strip the exchange of its personalism in the name of protecting God's dignity is the impersonalist mistake — it makes the Absolute smaller, not greater.
    • Asking Kṛṣṇa to become 'invisible to material eyes' sounds like religious privacy theater — keep the mystical stuff hidden so outsiders cannot scoff. Is bhakti really about concealment from non-believers?
      Devakī is not protecting the Lord's reputation; she is protecting the unprepared eye from a vision it would weaponize. Kaṁsa seeing Viṣṇu would not produce surrender — it would produce homicidal panic, because māṁsa-dṛśāḥ, fleshly eyes, cannot receive what dhyāna-dhiṣṇyam discloses. The principle is not secrecy but adhikāra: the same sun that ripens fruit blisters bare skin. A Gauḍīya teacher applies this to today — we do not parade kīrtana, deity-worship, or guru-instruction in front of those who can only ridicule, not because the truth is fragile, but because we owe them a doorway sized to their eyes.
    Analogy

    A jeweler shows a rare diamond to a discerning king who knows what he holds; the king then asks the jeweler to wrap it before the crowd of admirers arrives, lest greedy fingers see and grasp. Devakī asks Kṛṣṇa to fold away the four-armed Viṣṇu form before Kaṁsa's eyes can find Him. The form that yogīs meditate upon must not be made available to māṁsa-dṛśām, eyes of flesh.

    Stories
    Kṛṣṇa concealing His divinity in Vraja

    Through nearly all of Kṛṣṇa's Vraja-līlā in Canto 10, He appears as an ordinary cowherd boy. The gopīs love Him without metaphysical knowledge that He is svayaṁ bhagavān; the wrestling matches and butter-thefts are sweet precisely because the aiśvarya is veiled.

    Devakī's request in this verse anticipates the entire Vraja program: 'pratyakṣaṁ mā māṁsa-dṛśām' — please don't be directly visible (as four-armed Viṣṇu) to material eyes. Yoga-māyā will obey her request and keep Kṛṣṇa's full identity concealed even from Yaśodā for years.

    Important Words
    • madhusūdana — O slayer of Madhu
      Vocative — Madhu (a demon slain by Viṣṇu) + sūdana (slayer). Devakī addresses Kṛṣṇa by His asura-slaying name precisely because she fears another asura. The choice of epithet is theologically purposeful — she invokes the protective svarūpa appropriate to the threat.
    • samudvije — I am full of anxiety
      Sam (fully) + ud (up) + √vij (to tremble). Tremor that rises from within. Devakī names her actual emotional state — bhakti does not require pretending equanimity one does not feel; honest report of the heart is part of stuti.
    • bhavat-hetoḥ — because of You
      Bhavat (Your Lordship) + hetu (cause) + ablative. The cause of her anxiety is Bhagavān's very appearance — not Kaṁsa's threat in isolation. Striking honesty: His coming is what places Him in danger. Bhakti can name this paradox without losing devotion.
    • adhīra-dhīḥ — with unsteady intelligence
      A- (privative) + dhīra (steady) + dhī (intelligence). 'Unsteady-minded'. Devakī self-diagnoses; she is not pretending to philosophical calm. The Bhāgavata's psychological realism: even the Lord's mother registers terror at the cost of His descent.
    O Madhusūdana, because of Your appearance, I am becoming more and more anxious in fear of Kaṁsa. Therefore, please arrange for that sinful Kaṁsa to be unable to understand that You have taken birth from my womb.
    Purport

    Devakī addressed the Supreme Personality of Godhead as Madhusūdana. She was aware that the Lord had killed many demons like Madhu who were hundreds and thousands of times more powerful than Kaṁsa, yet because of affection for the transcendental child, she believed that Kaṁsa could kill Him. Instead of thinking of the unlimited power of the Lord, she thought of the Lord with affection, and therefore she requested the transcendental child to disappear.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O Madhusūdana, because of Your appearance, I am becoming more and more anxious in fear of Kaṁsa. Therefore, please arrange for that sinful Kaṁsa to be unable to understand that You have taken birth from my womb.
    Commentary

    "O mother, if I make this four armed form disappear, when Kamsa comes he will ask, ‘Where is the child?’" And thinking you have stolen the child, he will commit violence against you, will he not?" To answer this Devaki replies "I have no fear of that." Thus she speaks this verse. "Do something so Kamsa (papa) will not know that you have taken birth from me". "Having killed the Madhu demon, is it necessary that I kill Kamsa?" Fearing this question Devaki says, "O Madhusudana, Kamsa at present is thousands of times more powerful than Madhu of the past. Let Kamsa beat me for my offense. But I am desiring only your safety." "You have spoken of my powers in the previous verses, but was all that emply words?" She answers, "Truly, o son, as your mother I am unsteady of mind (adhira dhih). Do not be sad. This is my fault. I take responsibility. But out of affection for your mother, please withdraw your form."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “What is your fear, O mother? If I disappear you will have fear that he will steal your future children.” Fearing such a statement, Devakī speaks. I fear for you, not for myself. Though you cannot have fear of insignificant Kaṁsa since you are the killer of the Madhu demon, my mind is suddenly unsteady because of your great mercy to me. She says this with great desire that the child should not be taken away by Kaṁsa’s men.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    “Your pregnancy was clear. Being born, the child has been taken away somewhere by his father.” Thinking in this way, Kaṁsa will then kill the child, who was promised to him. Fearing this, Devakī prays. He should not know of your birth from me. O killer of the great demon Madhu! Though you and your devotees have no fear, I have strong fear of the wicked Kaṁsa for your sake since I have no steadiness because of my great affection (adhīra-dhīḥ).

    Personal Guidance
    Devakī's plea shows that even pure devotees, gripped by vātsalya, forget Kṛṣṇa's unlimited power — affection is real, but never mistake Him for vulnerable.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice when your affection for Kṛṣṇa or His devotees slides into anxious protectiveness, and recall that He is Madhusūdana — slayer of demons far greater than your fears.
    • When fear of a 'Kaṁsa' in your life rises today — a boss, illness, deadline — pause and name three times Kṛṣṇa has already removed obstacles you could not.
    • Refuse to let bodily-platform anxiety dictate your sādhana; chant one extra round today specifically as an offering of trust in His protection.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where, like Devakī, has my affection for what I love made me forget Kṛṣṇa's unlimited power — and start treating Him as something I must protect rather than surrender to?
    • Which 'Kaṁsa' in my life — what specific fear of a hostile force — am I quietly negotiating with by asking Kṛṣṇa to stay hidden, instead of trusting Him to act as Madhusūdana?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the 'Kaṁsa' in your own life — the friend group, the algorithm, the professor whose opinion you fear more than you fear forgetting Kṛṣṇa. Today, name that Kaṁsa specifically in your journal; do not let it stay vague.
    • When you feel adhīra-dhīḥ before an exam or a hard conversation, pause and remember Madhusūdana — the Lord who has already defeated demons far worse than your circumstance. Chant one round of japa before walking in.
    • Devakī protects the newborn bhakti in her heart. If your sādhana — chanting, reading, prasāda — is new and fragile, do not broadcast it on social media for validation. Hide it like a flame in cupped hands until it can withstand wind.
    householder
    • Recognize the affection-trap: Devakī forgets Kṛṣṇa's power because she loves Him as her child. Where in your family — for a spouse, a child, an aging parent — has affection made you forget that Kṛṣṇa, not you, is the actual protector? Today, consciously hand one specific worry back to Him.
    • Identify the 'Kaṁsa' threatening your household's spiritual life — the work demand, the in-law's pressure, the financial fear — and make a concrete plan this week to limit its access, not by fighting it, but by quietly protecting the family's morning sādhana from its reach.
    • Practice Madhusūdana-smaraṇa during decision-making: before signing the contract, before the difficult parenting conversation, audibly say 'O Madhusūdana' once. Let the name reset your adhīra-dhīḥ into trust.
    senior
    • Devakī's prayer is to *protect* what is precious by *concealing* it. In this stage, practice deliberate withdrawal — fewer opinions, fewer public roles — so that the bhakti you have cultivated is not consumed by the Kaṁsa of social performance in your final years.
    • Mortality itself is the great Kaṁsa from which no Devakī-like cleverness can hide the body. Use this verse to redirect: stop trying to hide the body from death, and start protecting the soul's remembrance of Kṛṣṇa for the moment of departure. Increase japa now, not later.
    • When mentoring younger devotees or grandchildren, do not make them adhīra-dhīḥ by transmitting your own anxieties about their future. Speak as one who has seen Madhusūdana defeat many demons across a lifetime, and let that steadiness be your legacy.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Mistaking Devakī's request for the Lord to disappear as a model of humility, rather than recognizing it as the bewilderment of vātsalya-rasa that the verse itself names as adhīra-dhīḥ — an unsteady intelligence overwhelmed by affectionate fear.
    • Reading 'I am becoming more and more anxious' as ordinary material anxiety, and using the verse to validate one's own fear-based avoidance, instead of seeing it as transcendental affection in which the devotee forgets the Lord's omnipotence out of love.
    • Concluding that one should 'hide' Kṛṣṇa from hostile environments — keeping devotion private to avoid the modern Kaṁsas of ridicule or career risk — when the verse is actually exposing how affection can eclipse faith in His protective power as Madhusūdana, slayer of demons far greater than Kaṁsa.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Devakī, beholding the four-armed Lord, still trembles for Kaṁsa — knowing the Madhusūdana power that destroyed Madhu. Share with your partner: where in your own life do you intellectually know Kṛṣṇa is in control, yet emotionally still strategize as if everything depends on you? Push back if your partner makes it sound easy.
    • Is Devakī's adhīra-dhīḥ (unsteady intelligence) a fault, or is it the very vātsalya (parental affection) that Kṛṣṇa cherishes? Argue both sides honestly — does bhakti make us *more* anxious for Him, not less? Where is the line between affection and forgetfulness of His aiśvarya?
    • She asks the Lord to *hide* — to withdraw His own appearance. Is this a higher prayer, or a lower one, than 'reveal Yourself'? Disagree with each other: when is concealing Kṛṣṇa (in our families, jobs, social feeds) genuine protection of bhakti, and when is it our own fear of Kaṁsa-like opinion?
    Role Play

    Two students. Student A has just told their non-devotee parents they are taking initiation, planning to chant sixteen rounds and follow the four regulative principles. The parents (Student B plays the senior parent) are not violent but are 'Kaṁsa-like' in their power over the household — they control finances, social standing, and the family's reputation in the community. Student B must press hard: 'You're ruining your career. What will people say? Hide this nonsense.' Student A must respond from the verse — feeling Devakī's exact tension: wanting to protect the bhakti-bhāva that has just been born in their heart, while neither denying Kṛṣṇa nor inviting needless conflict. After five minutes, swap roles. Then the class debriefs: where did Student A act from adhīra-dhīḥ (unsteady fear), and where from genuine, dhīra discrimination about when to speak and when to wait?

    Objections & Responses
    • This is exactly the problem with theistic religion — even the mother of God is reduced to a frightened woman begging her own child to hide. It infantilizes the devotee and makes God seem weak. A mature spirituality wouldn't need this melodrama.
      The 'melodrama' is the point, not the embarrassment. Prabhupāda explains in the purport that Devakī *knew* the Lord had killed Madhu and demons thousands of times more powerful than Kaṁsa — her fear is not theological ignorance, it is vātsalya-rasa, the relationship of parental love. Kṛṣṇa is not interested in being worshipped only as the all-powerful Absolute; He relishes being loved as a vulnerable child. The impersonalist wants a God who cannot be loved this intimately — but that is a poorer conception, not a higher one. Mature bhakti does not transcend affection; it deepens into it.
    • If Kṛṣṇa is really the Supreme Personality of Godhead, why does He need His mother to hide Him from Kaṁsa? Either He's omnipotent or He isn't — you can't have it both ways.
      He is fully omnipotent — Devakī's request is honored not because He needs protection, but because He reciprocates with His devotee's bhāva. He came to fulfill her prayer (the previous verses describe her tapasyā across lifetimes for this child), so He plays the role her love asks Him to play. This is the Gauḍīya understanding: Kṛṣṇa is controlled by prema. He is svayam bhagavān precisely because He has the freedom to *appear* dependent in the embrace of His devotees, without ever ceasing to be the cause of all causes. The 'contradiction' you're naming is actually His highest aiśvarya — that supreme power chooses to be bound by love.
    Analogy

    A mother nursing her baby in the next room from a violent husband holds her breath at every footstep — 'let him not know, let him not enter'. Devakī's prayer here is exactly this domestic terror raised to cosmic stakes. The husband is Kaṁsa; the baby is the Supreme Person; the only insurance is that Bhagavān Himself veil His own identity.

    Stories
    Yaśodā tying Kṛṣṇa with the rope (foreshadowed)

    Mother Yaśodā in SB 10.9 would, out of vātsalya, try to tie Kṛṣṇa to a mortar — and the rope would always be two fingers short. Eventually Kṛṣṇa permitted Himself to be bound, because vātsalya-rasa requires the Lord to accept the postures the mother needs.

    Devakī here is asking for a different form of the same concession: 'don't be visibly Viṣṇu; be coverable, be hideable.' Bhagavān accepts the mother's structuring of the relationship — He is bound by Yaśodā's rope and concealed by Devakī's plea, both out of love.

    Important Words
    • upasaṁhara — withdraw
      Upa-saṁ-√hṛ — 'to gather in, withdraw'. Imperative. The same verb used at the end of Bhagavān's Viśvarūpa-darśana (BG 11.45 — Arjuna asking Him to withdraw the cosmic form). The Bhāgavata reuses the verb here — a mother making the same request a warrior made on Kurukṣetra.
    • viśvātman — O Soul of the universe
      Vocative — viśva (universe) + ātman (self). Bhagavān is the inner self of the entire cosmos. Devakī's address simultaneously acknowledges His cosmic identity AND asks Him to hide it — the paradox is the point. Bhakti can hold both.
    • alaukikam — unnatural in this world
      A- (privative) + laukika (worldly). The four-armed form is alaukika — beyond worldly norm. The word does double duty: it is unworldly in being transcendental, AND it is unworldly in being conspicuous to material eyes. Both senses inform Devakī's request.
    • śaṅkha-cakra-gadā-padma — conch, disc, club, lotus
      The four divine emblems of Viṣṇu, named individually. Each is a tattva: śaṅkha (the Veda's sound), cakra (kāla, sudarśana), gadā (the smashing of pride), padma (the lotus heart). Together they identify Him unmistakably — which is precisely the problem.
    • catuḥ-bhujam — four-armed
      Catuḥ (four) + bhuja (arm). The signature mark of Viṣṇu-tattva. Note: Kṛṣṇa in Vraja will be dvi-bhuja (two-armed); the four arms are the aiśvarya-form. Gauḍīya line: Kṛṣṇa is dvi-bhuja in His svarūpa, four-armed only when displaying aiśvarya. Devakī asks Him to revert to dvi-bhuja.
    O my Lord, You are the all-pervading Supreme Personality of Godhead, and Your transcendental four-armed form, holding conchshell, disc, club and lotus, is unnatural for this world. Please withdraw this form [and become just like a natural human child so that I may try to hide You somewhere].
    Purport

    Devakī was thinking of hiding the Supreme Personality of Godhead and not handing Him over to Kaṁsa as she had all her previous children. Although Vasudeva had promised to hand over every child to Kaṁsa, this time he wanted to break his promise and hide the child somewhere. But because of the Lord’s appearance in this surprising four-armed form, He would be impossible to hide.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O my Lord, You are the all-pervading Supreme Personality of Godhead, and Your transcendental four-armed form, holding conchshell, disc, club and lotus, is unnatural for this world. Please withdraw this form [and become just like a natural human child so that I may try to hide You somewhere].
    Commentary

    "As you pervade the whole universe and I reside within the universe, you also reside within me. How then has this weakness of heart arisen in me? It must be your fault." Thus she addresses the Lord as visvatma, soul of the universe. "Withdraw this uncommon form and assume a form of a normal human baby, and I will quickly hide you."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Doubting that he will agree to her request, she speaks again, unable to tolerate Kaṁsa. Hide that particular form with four arms decorated with conch, cakra, club and lotus. Show a different form. You cannot hide your present form from the people anywhere. O soul of the universe! Since you show unlimited forms simultaneously, this is not impossible for you! Hiding two of your arms and your Kaustubha and other ornaments, show a concealed form like that of other people. Then you will be able to hide anywhere among the people.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Withdraw this form since it is extraordinary. O soul of the universe, this is possible for you to do. The extraordinary form is described. It is endowed with the beauty of conch etc. Or it should be withdrawn because it is extraordinary, with the beauty of clothing etc. and conch, cakra, lotus and club. The deep meaning is this: it is possible to protect you by hiding you somewhere in the world. Or the reason for hiding is given in the previous verse. He should not know, because by not knowing about your birth (bhavad-dhetoḥ), he will not harm us. “Should I disappear completely?” This verse answers. No, just withdraw this particular form.
