    Personal Guidance
    Sustained tapas only bears fruit when fixed in Kṛṣṇa-consciousness — austerity without Him is exhausting; austerity with Him divinizes time itself.
    Practical Applications
    • Choose one austerity today (a fast, silence, or screen-restraint) and explicitly dedicate it to Kṛṣṇa before beginning, not as self-improvement.
    • Notice when your discipline is fueled by ego or self-image, and quietly re-aim it toward mad-ātmanoḥ — 'with Me at the center'.
    • Refuse to abandon a sādhana commitment today because results feel slow; remember the twelve thousand celestial years of Vasudeva and Devakī.
    Reflection Questions
    • Twelve thousand celestial years of tapas were sustained by mad-ātmanoḥ — consciousness fixed on Kṛṣṇa. Where in my own sādhana do I rely on willpower or self-image to endure austerity, instead of letting consciousness of Him be the sustaining force?
    • What single discipline have I abandoned because the result did not arrive on my timeline — and what would change if I measured tapas not by visible fruit but by the depth of remembrance of Kṛṣṇa during the effort?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Pick one tapas for this semester — phone off after 9pm, or no scrolling before japa, or one weekly fast — and hold it through finals, breakups, and group-chat FOMO. The point is not the rule; it is mad-ātmanoḥ — staying fixed in consciousness of Kṛṣṇa when your friends are not.
    • When peers mock your discipline ('why are you like this now?'), do not argue and do not preach — just continue. Pṛśni and Sutapā did not post about their tapas; they sustained it for twelve thousand years because Kṛṣṇa was the audience.
    • During exam season, instead of bargaining with God for marks, perform your study itself as tapas — offered to Kṛṣṇa, with regulated sleep and food — and let the result come as His arrangement, not your transaction.
    householder
    • Choose one austerity that fits the gṛhastha-āśrama — a fixed japa count before the family wakes, a weekly ekādaśī, a budget cap on personal indulgences — and hold it across job changes, school admissions, and in-law visits. Tapas in family life is consistency under interruption.
    • Reframe parenting and earning themselves as parama-duṣkaram tapas: the difficult, daily, unglamorous work of raising children and meeting deadlines, performed in consciousness of Kṛṣṇa, not as obstacles to spiritual life but as its very field.
    • When a family decision tempts you toward comfort over principle (a dishonest shortcut at work, a status-driven purchase, skipping sādhana for a social weekend), remember twelve thousand years — your one decision today is a vanishing fraction of the arc, and tapas is built decision by decision.
    senior
    • The body is loosening its grip — let that be tapas, not loss. Each comfort the body can no longer demand (rich food, late nights, vigorous travel) is a viṣaya naturally renounced; receive it as Kṛṣṇa's gift of vairāgya rather than a deprivation.
    • Move from accumulation to mentoring: your remaining years are a concentrated tapas of giving away — wisdom to the young, possessions to those who need them, attachments back to Kṛṣṇa. Twelve thousand celestial years compresses, in old age, into the sharpened austerity of letting go cleanly.
    • Make daily remembrance of Kṛṣṇa your one non-negotiable — japa at fixed hours, hearing from Bhāgavatam, association with devotees — so that when the final transition comes, mad-ātmā is not a verse you once read but the actual posture of your mind.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating tapas as a transactional bargain with the Lord — performing austerity to extract a boon, rather than as an offering rooted in mad-ātmanoḥ, consciousness of Him.
    • Mistaking dry self-denial in the mode of tamas or rajas (fasting to punish the body, ascetic display, willful deprivation) for genuine tapas in sattva that is anchored in Kṛṣṇa consciousness.
    • Expecting quick results and quitting early — forgetting that the verse highlights twelve thousand celestial years of sustained effort, and that real tapas is measured in steady duration, not intensity of a single burst.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Twelve thousand celestial years of tapasya — and the fruit was not a boon but the darśana of Kṛṣṇa Himself. Share with your partner: when have you performed a 'tapas' (a fast, a discipline, a sacrifice) and felt cheated because the outcome was not what you bargained for? Was the tapas itself flawed, or was the bargain?
    • Modern life calls almost everything 'discipline' — gym routines, productivity systems, dopamine fasts. Discuss in your group: what genuinely separates these from tapas in the Gauḍīya sense (mad-ātmanoḥ — fixed in consciousness of Kṛṣṇa)? Push back on each other; do not settle for 'intention' as the only difference.
    • Pṛśni and Sutapā performed tapas not to escape the world but to receive Kṛṣṇa as their son. Debate: is it legitimate to perform austerity for a *personal* relationship with Kṛṣṇa, or does that contaminate the austerity with kāma? Where do you and your partner disagree?
    Role Play

    Two students take roles. Student A is a college roommate who has just begun a serious sādhana — early rising, japa, restricted diet, no late-night socials. Student B is the close friend who feels abandoned and accuses A of becoming 'cold,' 'rigid,' and 'performatively spiritual.' B presses: 'You used to be fun. Now you're just doing this for points with your guru.' A must respond from the spirit of SB 10.3.36 — tapas held over the long arc, fixed in consciousness of Kṛṣṇa, not for show and not for human approval — without becoming defensive or preachy. After five minutes, swap roles. Then debrief: where did A slip into self-righteousness? Where did B name something real?

    Objections & Responses
    • Twelve thousand celestial years of austerity sounds like spiritual masochism. Isn't this exactly the kind of life-denying religion that drives modern people away — punishing the body to please a distant God?
      Tapas in the Gauḍīya line is not punishment of the body; it is the voluntary regulation of the senses (viṣaya) so that the soul can remember Kṛṣṇa. The verse says mad-ātmanoḥ — their consciousness was fixed in Kṛṣṇa the entire time. That is what made the duration bearable and even sweet. Compare it to an athlete's training or a mother's sleepless nights for her child — discipline endured for love is not masochism; it is the natural shape of devotion. The Gītā (17.5–6) explicitly condemns austerity performed to torture the body without proper aim. What Pṛśni and Sutapā did was the opposite: tapas saturated with bhakti, aimed at Kṛṣṇa Himself.
    • Twelve thousand celestial years is obviously mythological exaggeration. If we cannot take the number literally, why should we take the lesson seriously?
      A Gauḍīya teacher does not require you to first settle the cosmology before you can take the lesson. But notice what the number is doing: it is stretching your imagination past any tapas you would ever attempt, so that your own small disciplines stop seeming heroic. The point is the *quality* of consciousness sustained across an unimaginable span — parama-duṣkaram, supremely difficult — not the arithmetic. Even within one human life, sādhana is a long arc, not a weekend retreat. If twelve thousand divine years feels unreal, then ask: can I sustain mad-ātmā — Kṛṣṇa-consciousness — for the next twelve hours? The verse calibrates ambition, not chronology.
    Analogy

    A devoted student studies one subject without interruption for twelve years — by the end, the subject and the student have become one. Pṛśni and Sutapā meditated on Kṛṣṇa for twelve thousand celestial years; by the end, His likeness was their only memory. The verse names the duration so that we will not imagine cheap shortcuts to vātsalya-rasa with Bhagavān.

    Stories
    Vālmīki composing the Rāmāyaṇa

    Sage Vālmīki, after meditating on Rāma's name long enough to undergo total transformation (the famous 'marā marā' inversion to 'Rāma Rāma'), composed the Rāmāyaṇa in twenty-four thousand verses. His composition was downloaded; the duration of his tapas earned that direct vision.

    The Bhāgavata is consistent: extended, exclusive absorption produces unmistakable darśana. Twelve thousand divya-years is the price-tag for receiving Bhagavān as son. The Bhāgavata never trades on devotional sentimentalism that pretends easier access.

    Important Words
    • parituṣṭaḥ aham — I was fully satisfied
      Pari (around, fully) + tuṣṭa (satisfied) + aham (I). Bhagavān's complete satisfaction with their tapas. Reading: His satisfaction (parituṣṭi) is what produces His appearance — bhakti pleases the Lord, and His pleasure is then visibly given as Himself.
    • śraddhayā — with faith
      Instrumental of śraddhā. Without śraddhā tapas is mere athletics. Caitanya-caritāmṛta defines śraddhā as the confidence that by serving Kṛṣṇa, all other duties are automatically performed (śraddhā śabde — viśvāsa kahe sudṛḍha niścaya). Foundation of bhakti.
    • bhaktyā — by devotional service
      Instrumental of bhakti. Crucial: their tapas was bhakti-yukta, not jñāna-mārga or yoga-mārga. The same actions performed with bhakti produce different fruit than performed for liberation. The verb's instrumental marks the means by which Bhagavān is reached — bhakti and bhakti alone.
    • vara-da-rāṭ — the king among benediction-givers
      Vara (boon) + da (giver) + rāṭ (king). The supreme bestower of boons. Bhagavān names Himself: not 'a' giver of benedictions but the best of them. Sambandha: knowing who gives is half of asking rightly.
    • mādṛśaḥ — (a son) like Me
      Mā (Me) + dṛśa (likeness). The famous request — 'a son like You'. Bhagavān's compassionate correction (verse 41): finding no one truly equal to Himself, He gave Himself instead. The bhakta's request reaches further than the bhakta knew.
    • vṛtaḥ — was asked for
      Past participle of √vṛ — 'to choose, ask for'. Same root as vara (boon). The shape of their request: they CHOSE Him. Bhakti is a chosen relation, not a metaphysical necessity. The Bhāgavata stresses this — surrender is voluntary, and Bhagavān reciprocates accordingly.
    O sinless mother Devakī, after the expiry of twelve thousand celestial years, in which you constantly contemplated Me within the core of your heart with great faith, devotion and austerity, I was very much satisfied with you. Since I am the best of all bestowers of benediction, I appeared in this same form as Kṛṣṇa to ask you to take from Me the benediction you desired. You then expressed your desire to have a son exactly like Me.
    Purport

    Twelve thousand years on the celestial planets is not a very long time for those who live in the upper planetary system, although it may be very long for those who live on this planet. Sutapā was the son of Brahmā, and as we have already understood from Bhagavad-gītā (8.17) , one day of Brahmā equals many millions of years according to our calculation ( sahasra-yuga-paryantam ahar yad brahmaṇo viduḥ ). We should be careful to understand that to get Kṛṣṇa as one’s son, one must undergo such great austerities. If we want to get the Supreme Personality of Godhead to become one of us in this material world, this requires great penance, but if we want to go back to Kṛṣṇa ( tyaktvā dehaṁ punar janma naiti mām eti so ’rjuna ), we need only understand Him and love Him. Through love only, we can very easily go back home, back to Godhead. Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu therefore declared, premā pum-artho mahān: love of Godhead is the highest achievement for anyone. As we have explained, in worship of the Lord there are three stages — jñāna, jñānamayī and rati, or love. Sutapā and his wife, Pṛśni, inaugurated their devotional activities on the basis of full knowledge. Gradually they developed love for the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and when this love was mature, the Lord appeared as Viṣṇu, although Devakī then requested Him to assume the form of Kṛṣṇa. To love the Supreme Personality of Godhead more, we want a form of the Lord like Kṛṣṇa or Rāma. We can engage in loving transactions with Kṛṣṇa especially. In this age, we are all fallen, but the Supreme Personality of Godhead has appeared as Caitanya Mahāprabhu to bestow upon us love of Godhead directly. This was appreciated by the associates of Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu. Rūpa Gosvāmī said: namo mahā-vadānyāya kṛṣṇa-prema-pradāya te kṛṣṇāya kṛṣṇa-caitanya- nāmne gaura-tviṣe namaḥ In this verse, Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu is described as mahā-vadānya, the most munificent of charitable persons, because He gives Kṛṣṇa so easily that one can attain Kṛṣṇa simply by chanting the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahā-mantra. We should therefore take advantage of the benediction given by Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu, and when by chanting the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra we are cleansed of all dirty things ( ceto-darpaṇa-mārjanam ), we shall be able to understand very easily that Kṛṣṇa is the only object of love ( kīrtanād eva kṛṣṇasya mukta-saṅgaḥ paraṁ vrajet ). Therefore, one need not undergo severe penances for many thousands of years; one need only learn how to love Kṛṣṇa and be always engaged in His service ( sevonmukhe hi jihvādau svayam eva sphuraty adaḥ ). Then one can very easily go back home, back to Godhead. Instead of bringing the Lord here for some material purpose, to have a son or whatever else, if we go back home, back to Godhead, our real relationship with the Lord is revealed, and we eternally engage in our eternal relationship. By chanting the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra, we gradually develop our eternal relationship with the Supreme Person and thus attain the perfection called svarūpa-siddhi. We should take advantage of this benediction and go back home, back to Godhead. Śrīla Narottama dāsa Ṭhākura has therefore sung, patita-pāvana-hetu tava avatāra: Caitanya Mahāprabhu appeared as an incarnation to deliver all fallen souls like us and directly bestow upon us love of Godhead. We must take advantage of this great benediction of the great Personality of Godhead.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O sinless mother Devakī, after the expiry of twelve thousand celestial years, in which you constantly contemplated Me within the core of your heart with great faith, devotion and austerity, I was very much satisfied with you. Since I am the best of all bestowers of benediction, I appeared in this same form as Kṛṣṇa to ask you to take from Me the benediction you desired. You then expressed your desire to have a son exactly like Me.
    Commentary

    "Because of your meditation on me, I am very pleased. I appeared in that form (four handed)." The austerity performed was constant meditation on the Lord with devotion and faith. The use of the three words, bhakti, sraddha and nitya indicate that the devotion was not merely an anga of yoga practice. Rather it was absorption in the Lord. That by itself leads to perfection; it is a cause of prema. Their bhakti was mixed however with jnana and aisvarya because of practice of yoga and austerity. Some also reason that since nitya siddha Vasudeva and Devaki had nitya siddha aisvarya-jnana mixed bhakti, their amsas Prsni and Sutapa also had mixed bhakti. The tapa and yoga practice were therefore incidental. In this verse the word bhavita is used instead of cintata. Their meditation was filled with bhava. In other words they had genuine bhakti for the Lord.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    O Devakī, devoid of aparādhas (anaghe)! This indicates her faultless austerity. Seeing you, I was satisfied. The affix pari denotes repeated action. I was satisfied with you, birth after birth. “But the Lord is satisfied with bhakti, not austerity.” That is true. Successive causes are shown. From austerity meant to please me faith in nine types of bhakti was produced. From faith came bhakti. By that bhakti, I was attained constantly in your hearts, with effort (bhāvitaḥ). The word ca indicates that then, by prema I was attained without effort. Their prema was filled with loving the Lord as their son. I was satisfied completely and have been obtained in your hearts. I, Kṛṣṇa (amunā vapuṣā), was the cause of this. Instrumental case expresses cause. Varada-raṭ is explained by Śrīdhara Svāmī. I give great results for those who do austerities. I give greater results for those having faith. I give greatest results for those having bhakti and prema. I said you should ask for a benediction. You asked for a son like me. They did not ask for the Lord directly, out of shyness.

      His Grace Padaseva Prabhu· Oriya
    Personal Guidance
    Devakī's twelve thousand years of tapas brought Kṛṣṇa as her son — but Caitanya Mahāprabhu now gives that same Kṛṣṇa freely through the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra.
    Practical Applications
    • Chant a fixed number of Hare Kṛṣṇa rounds today as your sādhana — receive directly what Devakī earned through twelve thousand years of austerity.
    • Refuse the impulse to bargain with Kṛṣṇa for some material 'son' — a result, a promotion, a relationship — and instead pray only to go back home to Him.
    • Speak Caitanya Mahāprabhu's name once today with gratitude as the mahā-vadānya who delivered kṛṣṇa-prema to fallen souls like you.
    Reflection Questions
    • Sutapā and Pṛśni performed twelve thousand celestial years of tapas just to have the Lord come down as their son — what am I attempting to drag Kṛṣṇa into my world to obtain, instead of letting Him draw me back to His?
    • When I sit to chant or contemplate, am I cultivating love for Kṛṣṇa Himself, or am I quietly bargaining for a specific 'benediction' I would name if He asked vriyatāṁ varam?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Audit one prayer you have actually prayed this semester — for a grade, an admit, a crush, a follower count. Ask honestly: was I asking Kṛṣṇa to come into my plan, or asking Him to take me into His? Write the answer down, do not just feel it.
    • Pick one tapas-sized commitment for the next thirty days that costs you something real on campus — chanting one round before opening your phone in the morning, or skipping one weekend party to read Kṛṣṇa book. Twelve thousand celestial years are not on offer; thirty days are.
    • Notice the next time you treat sādhana like a transaction with God ('I chanted, so the exam should go well'). Catch it, name it, and replace it with one line — 'Kṛṣṇa, I want You, not Your arrangements' — before you go to sleep.
    householder
    • Sutapā and Pṛśni did tapas together as a couple before Kṛṣṇa came as their child. This week, sit with your spouse for fifteen minutes a day in shared sādhana — japa, reading, or kīrtana. Treat the household itself as the tapovana.
    • Examine the boons you are currently asking from Kṛṣṇa through your work and parenting — promotion, the right school for the kids, a bigger home. For each one, ask: am I asking Him to bless my material project, or am I using this project to take my family back to Him? Re-aim one decision this week accordingly.
    • Each evening, before sleep, formally offer the day's actions — the meetings, the school run, the difficult conversation with your child — to Kṛṣṇa. Do not bargain for outcomes; just hand the day over. This is the householder's version of twelve thousand years.
    senior
    • You have already lived through several 'bodies' — student, professional, parent. Sit quietly today and trace the continuity of the same self through them. Then ask: what tapas is appropriate for this final āśrama, and am I doing it, or am I still performing the householder's tapas out of habit?
    • Identify one attachment — a possession, a role, an opinion you are known for — that you are still asking Kṛṣṇa to preserve for you. Begin the practice of offering it back. Sutapā's prayer was 'come to me'; the senior's prayer ripens into 'take me to You.'
    • Mentor one younger devotee or family member this month not by giving advice but by quietly modeling chanting and remembrance. Prabhupāda's whole point in this purport is that Caitanya Mahāprabhu's gift travels through living examples, not lectures. Be one.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading Devakī's request as the ideal — modeling one's sādhana on 'getting Kṛṣṇa as my son/asset/answer' rather than on going back to Him, when Prabhupāda explicitly contrasts the two and recommends the latter.
    • Concluding that because twelve thousand celestial years of tapas were required, sincere bhakti now is futile — and missing Caitanya Mahāprabhu's mahā-vadānya gift of kṛṣṇa-prema through the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahā-mantra in this age.
    • Treating chanting as a shortcut technique to skip discipline, while neglecting the śraddhā, nityaṁ, and bhaktyā that the verse names as the very texture of Sutapā's contemplation hṛdi bhāvitaḥ — chanting without that inner orientation becomes mechanical, not ceto-darpaṇa-mārjanam.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Sutapā and Pṛśni performed twelve thousand celestial years of tapas just to have Kṛṣṇa as their son — yet Prabhupāda says we today need only chant and love. Is this a real shortcut, or are we minimizing what bhakti actually costs? Where does each of you land, and why?
    • Devakī asked the Lord to appear as her son — a personal, almost 'material' request. Prabhupāda gently reframes: better to go back to Him than bring Him here. Share a benediction you have actually asked Kṛṣṇa for. Was it a 'bring Him here' prayer or a 'take me there' prayer? Be honest with each other.
    • The verse holds together two things modern devotees often split: severe tapas and intimate love. In your sādhana right now, which one are you neglecting — the austerity or the affection? Push back on each other's diagnosis.
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A is a sincere new bhakta who has just decided to chant sixteen rounds and follow the four regulative principles strictly, and is privately hoping this 'austerity' will produce a specific result — a marriage, a child, a job, healing for a parent. Student B is a slightly senior devotee who notices the transactional undertone in A's sādhana. B must, in the spirit of this verse, neither crush A's enthusiasm (Sutapā and Pṛśni's tapas was honored by Kṛṣṇa) nor leave the misunderstanding intact (Prabhupāda warns: don't bring Him here for material purposes; go back to Him). Play it for five minutes, then switch. Afterward the class discusses: where did the conversation get stuck, and what would Prabhupāda have said?

    Objections & Responses
    • Twelve thousand celestial years of austerity to earn a son is mythology, not spirituality. This kind of story makes bhakti sound like a cosmic vending machine — insert tapas, receive boon. Why should a thinking modern person take it seriously?
      Read the verse again with Prabhupāda. He is not selling vending-machine spirituality — he is dismantling it. He explicitly says: if you want Kṛṣṇa as a son in this material world, yes, that costs twelve thousand years of tapas. But if you want to go back to Him, you need only love Him, and Caitanya Mahāprabhu has made even that available through the Hare Kṛṣṇa mantra. The story is not a prescription for transactional religion; it is a measuring stick that shows how absurdly cheap our path actually is. The 'mythology' is doing the opposite of what the objector thinks — it is exposing how unwilling we are to pay even the small price of chanting attentively.
    • Prabhupāda says we should not bring Kṛṣṇa here 'for some material purpose, to have a son or whatever else.' But Devakī did exactly that and is celebrated for it. Isn't this a contradiction — we're praising her and being warned against being like her?
      It is not a contradiction; it is the Gauḍīya pivot itself. Devakī's desire was material in form but personalist in substance — she wanted Kṛṣṇa Himself, not wealth or power. Even her 'lower' prayer was infinitely closer to bhakti than the impersonal liberation many seekers chase. Prabhupāda is honoring her while also showing us a higher option that her own son later opened up: instead of asking the Lord to come into our temporary family, ask to be brought into His eternal one. Same Person, deeper relationship. That is svarūpa-siddhi, and it is the destination Caitanya Mahāprabhu came to give us directly.
    Analogy

    A great patron, hearing of a generation of artisans who have labored for years to produce a single masterwork in his honor, comes personally to their workshop and says, 'Ask anything.' Their answer is not 'wealth' or 'fame' but 'a son like yourself, who will live with us.' Bhagavān is the patron; Pṛśni and Sutapā are the artisans; their request — sutaḥ mādṛśaḥ — is the perfect mistake.

    Stories
    The gopīs' Kātyāyanī-vrata

    The Vraja-gopīs (SB 10.22) undertook the Kātyāyanī-vrata to obtain Kṛṣṇa as husband. Bhagavān fulfilled their request by ultimately giving them Himself in mādhurya-rasa. The principle is the same: prolonged worship of Kṛṣṇa with a specific relational request results in His granting exactly that relationship.

    Pṛśni and Sutapā asked for vātsalya — a son like Me; the gopīs asked for mādhurya — a beloved who is Me. Each received what they asked. Bhakti's reciprocity is exact.

    Yaśodā and Nanda's prior tapas

    Caitanya-caritāmṛta and various Purāṇic accounts indicate that Yaśodā and Nanda are eternal vātsalya-rasa associates of Kṛṣṇa, and that Droṇa and Dharā (their pre-incarnations) underwent austerities to receive Him as their son. The Vraja-vātsalya is the more intimate; the Mathurā-vātsalya here is its preface.

    Bhagavān has two sets of parents in Canto 10 — Devakī-Vasudeva (aiśvarya-mixed vātsalya) and Yaśodā-Nanda (pure vātsalya). Both pairs earned their place. The Bhāgavatam is naming Devakī-Vasudeva's earning here.

    Important Words
    • ajuṣṭa-grāmya-viṣayau — engaged in marital relation (for the sake of a son like Me)
      A + juṣṭa (engaged) + grāmya (worldly, village-life) + viṣaya (sense-objects). Even apparently ordinary marital activity, when motivated by desire for Bhagavān as son, becomes part of bhakti. Gauḍīya principle: the action is the same; the antaḥkaraṇa changes its tattva.
    • apavargam — liberation
      Apa (away) + varga (class, condition) — literally 'apart from class', i.e., free from saṁsāra. Standard term for mukti. Crucial: they REFUSED apavargam. The Vaiṣṇava ideal is not liberation but nitya-seva. Caitanya's siddhānta: prema is higher than mukti.
    • deva-māyayā — by transcendental love
      Deva (divine) + māyā (here, the favorable internal energy, NOT the deluding external one). Compare the two māyās in Gauḍīya theology — bahiraṅga-māyā that deludes and svarūpa-śakti / yoga-māyā that orchestrates līlā. Their 'desire' was the operation of His own internal energy fixing them in vātsalya-bhakti.
    • mohitau — captivated
      Past participle dual of √muh — 'to be enchanted'. The Gauḍīya reading: this is bhakti-moha, not avidyā-moha. To be captivated by Bhagavān is not bondage but the highest freedom. Vraja-residents in Canto 10 will live in deepest deva-māyā-moha and be praised for it.
    Being husband and wife but always sonless, you were attracted by sexual desires, for by the influence of devamāyā, transcendental love, you wanted to have Me as your son. Therefore you never desired to be liberated from this material world.
    Purport

    Vasudeva and Devakī had been dam-patī, husband and wife, since the time of Sutapā and Pṛśni, and they wanted to remain husband and wife in order to have the Supreme Personality of Godhead as their son. This attachment came about by the influence of devamāyā. Loving Kṛṣṇa as one’s son is a Vedic principle. Vasudeva and Devakī never desired anything but to have the Lord as their son, yet for this purpose they apparently wanted to live like ordinary gṛhasthas for sexual indulgence. Although this was a transaction of spiritual potency, their desire appears like attachment for sex in conjugal life. If one wants to return home, back to Godhead, one must give up such desires. This is possible only when one develops intense love for the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu has said: niṣkiñcanasya bhagavad-bhajanonmukhasya pāraṁ paraṁ jigamiṣor bhava-sāgarasya (Cc. Madhya 11.8) If one wants to go back home, back to Godhead, one must be niṣkiñcana, free from all material desires. Therefore, instead of desiring to have the Lord come here and become one’s son, one should desire to become free from all material desires ( anyābhilāṣitā-śūnyam ) and go back home, back to Godhead. Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu teaches us in His Śikṣāṣṭaka: na dhanaṁ na janaṁ na sundarīṁ kavitāṁ vā jagad-īśa kāmaye mama janmani janmanīśvare bhavatād bhaktir ahaitukī tvayi “O almighty Lord, I have no desire to accumulate wealth, nor do I desire beautiful women, nor do I want any number of followers. I only want Your causeless devotional service, birth after birth.” One should not ask the Lord to fulfill any materially tainted desires.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Being husband and wife but always sonless, you were attracted by sexual desires, for by the influence of devamāyā, transcendental love, you wanted to have Me as your son. Therefore you never desired to be liberated from this material world.
    Commentary

    Maya here refers to affection for their son, for Bhagavatam 10.8.43 says: Vaisnavi vyatanon mayam putra sneha mayim vibhur (Krsna spread out his maya in the form of affection for a son)P. Mohitau here means that they were overcome with bliss. "Being childless and detached from material enjoyment, but overcome with bliss by parental affection, you did not pray for liberation."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Because of your love for me, you did not have any interest in other objects. But not only that, you had no interest in liberation, though you were qualified and though I could have given it to you. That is expressed in this verse. You had no desire for material pleasures. You were devoid of conceptions of body and place which are based on ahaṅkāra. You were without children. You had no possessiveness. You had conduct suitable for libration. Verse 34 mentioned that they were completely purified of contamination. This indicates that liberation was possible for them since only the Lord gives liberation. The Lord was called “king of benedictors” in verse 38. You, though qualified for liberation, did not ask me, who am qualified to give liberation. The cause is explained. You were bewildered by my mercy (māyayā), which suddenly produced affection in you for having me as your child. Or you were bewildered by my mercy which made me desire to be pampered as your son. Other sentiments are derided. An example is the following verse. ālokya-sārṣṭi-sāmīpya- sārūpyaikatvam apy uta dīyamānaṁ na gṛhṇanti vinā mat-sevanaṁ janāḥ A pure devotee does not accept any kind of liberation—sālokya, sārṣṭi, sāmīpya, sārūpya or ekatva—even though they are offered by the Lord. SB 3.29.13

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    You did not accept liberation. Since you were detached from material objects, without developing renunciation, you did not have a taste for liberation. Or even though you did not enjoy material objects, and did not have children, you accept me as a son, and not material enjoyment or many children. And you did not even accept liberation. The cause of all this was that you were not bewildered (amohitau) by māyā. Liberation is accepted by persons under illusion.

    Personal Guidance
    Even the desire to possess Kṛṣṇa as 'mine' through gṛhastha attachment is a covering — true return home requires niṣkiñcana surrender, not curated wishes.
    Practical Applications
    • Audit one 'spiritualized' desire today — a relationship, role, or comfort you've quietly wrapped in Kṛṣṇa's name — and name the material attachment hiding inside it.
    • Before japa, recite Caitanya Mahāprabhu's na dhanaṁ na janaṁ na sundarīṁ verse aloud and renounce one specific thing you were planning to ask Kṛṣṇa for.
    • Refuse the bargain of treating bhakti as a means to keep your present life intact; offer one indulgence (food, scrolling, conjugal fantasy) up today as evidence you want Him, not His gifts.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I dressing up a material attachment as a spiritual aspiration — wanting Kṛṣṇa to enter my situation rather than wanting to leave the situation for Him?
    • What 'sonless' ache am I trying to fill through gṛhastha indulgence, and what would it look like to bring that same longing directly to the Lord as niṣkiñcana, asking for nothing but His service?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Audit your prayer life this week: when you ask Kṛṣṇa for help with an exam, a crush, an internship, or peer acceptance, are you asking Him to be a delivery service for the life you already want, or are you asking Him to make you His? Write down one prayer in each category and notice the ratio.
    • Identify the one 'sacred-sounding' want you use to justify normal teenage cravings — 'I want to be famous so I can preach,' 'I want this relationship because we'll do bhakti together,' 'I want money so I can donate.' Name it honestly to one trusted friend today; do not let yourself off the hook with the spiritual veneer.
    • Pick one social-media stream you scroll for viṣaya — bodies, status, lifestyle envy — and fast from it for seven days. Each time you reach for it, replace it with one verse of Caitanya's Śikṣāṣṭaka (start with na dhanaṁ na janaṁ). Track what changes in your mind by day seven.
    householder
    • This week, sit with your spouse and ask: 'What are we really raising this family for?' If the honest answer is comfort, status, or legacy, name it. Then together draft one concrete change — a daily family kīrtana, a fixed donation, a service commitment — that reorients the household toward Kṛṣṇa rather than around Him.
    • Examine the next big family decision on your table — a house, a school, a career move, a child's marriage. Apply the niṣkiñcana test: would you make this same choice if it brought you no security, no prestige, no future return — only the chance to please Kṛṣṇa? If not, find the smaller version of the choice that passes the test, and make that one.
    • Stop using your children's well-being as a reason to defer your own sādhana. Vasudeva and Devakī's example shows that even the most exalted parental love is not a substitute for surrender. Fix a non-negotiable morning sādhana — japa, reading, ārati — and let your children see a parent who serves Kṛṣṇa first; that itself is the highest gift you give them.
    senior
    • Make a written list of every material desire still alive in you — a grandchild, a paid-off house, a final achievement, a particular kind of death. Read Caitanya's prayer aloud over the list: na dhanaṁ na janaṁ na sundarīṁ. Cross off, one by one, what you are willing to release this year. Keep the list where you will see it daily.
    • Choose one younger devotee — a child, grandchild, or student — and instead of bequeathing advice about worldly success, transmit one specific instruction from this verse: do not ask the Lord to fulfill materially tainted desires. Tell them how you learned this the hard way. Legacy as warning, not as trophy.
    • Begin a weekly practice of 'loosening the grip': each week, give away one possession, one role, or one expectation you have been holding. Offer it consciously to Kṛṣṇa as a small rehearsal for the final letting-go. By the time the body's transition comes, surrender should not be a sudden act but a long-practiced posture.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating Vasudeva and Devakī's desire as a license for one's own sense gratification — forgetting that their 'attachment' was devamāyā operating in pure devotees, not a template for ordinary conjugal indulgence.
    • Praying to Kṛṣṇa to fulfill materially tainted desires (a child, a spouse, wealth, success) and calling it bhakti, when the verse explicitly warns that even wanting the Lord Himself as a means to material life keeps one bound.
    • Misreading niṣkiñcana as outward poverty or renunciation of duties, rather than the inner emptying of all desires except ahaitukī bhakti — leading to either showy renunciation or quiet resentment of one's āśrama responsibilities.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Vasudeva and Devakī's desire to have Kṛṣṇa as their son is praised as devamāyā, yet Prabhupāda still says one must give up such desires to go back to Godhead. In your own life, where is the line between a sacred attachment that draws you toward Kṛṣṇa and a material attachment dressed up in spiritual language? Bring a real example and let your partner push back.
    • The verse names them as 'ajuṣṭa-grāmya-viṣayau' — engaged in conjugal life, yet without ordinary sons. Discuss honestly: in modern gṛhastha life, can sex and family life be a transaction of spiritual potency, or is that almost always a self-flattering rationalization? Where does each of you actually land, and why?
    • Caitanya Mahāprabhu's prayer asks for nothing — na dhanaṁ, na janaṁ, na sundarīṁ — only ahaitukī bhakti. If you prayed that prayer with full honesty tonight, which specific item on your current 'asking list' would you have to drop first? Share it; do not let your partner let you off easy.
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A is a sincere devotee who has been praying for years for a specific outcome — a child, a marriage, a job, the recovery of a parent — and frames it as 'I am asking Kṛṣṇa for this so I can serve Him better.' Student B is a senior Vaiṣṇava friend who has just heard SB 10.3.39 in class. B must lovingly but firmly probe whether A's prayer is truly devamāyā (like Pṛśni and Sutapā wanting the Lord as son) or anyābhilāṣa wearing devotional clothes. A must defend the prayer; B must apply niṣkiñcana and ahaitukī bhakti as the test. After 6 minutes, swap roles with a different 'sacred wish.' Then debrief: where did the test bite? What did each of you concede?

    Objections & Responses
    • This verse sounds like it shames a married couple for wanting children and a normal sex life. Isn't that a regressive, life-denying message — especially coming to householders who are already doing their dharma?
      Read the verse carefully — Kṛṣṇa is not shaming Vasudeva and Devakī; He is revealing the inner mechanics of devamāyā so they can now move past it. Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism does not reject gṛhastha life; it honors it as one of the four āśramas. What the verse critiques is not marriage or children but the subtle clinging that keeps even great devotees circling back into material existence. Prabhupāda's point is structural, not moralistic: every desire other than ahaitukī bhakti — however refined, however 'spiritual' it looks — is still a tether. Householders are not asked to abandon family; they are asked to stop secretly bargaining with Kṛṣṇa using their family life as currency.
    • If wanting Kṛṣṇa as your son is itself an obstacle to liberation, then nothing personal — no relationship, no love, no specificity — is safe. This collapses into impersonalism: just want nothing, be nothing.
      Exactly the opposite. The verse does not tell Vasudeva and Devakī to stop loving Kṛṣṇa as their son — that vātsalya-rasa is eternal and is one of the highest reciprocations in the spiritual world. It corrects the framing that this loving relationship requires the apparatus of material gṛhastha life to continue. In the spiritual realm, the same personal love between them and Kṛṣṇa goes on forever, more intensely, without the mortal bodies, the sonlessness, the longing. Gauḍīya siddhānta is the most personalist of all schools: the goal is not to dissolve into 'the Self' but to recover one's eternal personal relationship with Kṛṣṇa — as servant, friend, parent, or beloved. Niṣkiñcana means free of material desires, not free of love.
    Analogy

    A couple loves a particular master so deeply that they cannot bear to leave his service for any reward — even liberation. Offered freedom from work, they ask instead for a child who looks just like him, so the master's face will be in their home forever. Pṛśni and Sutapā's deva-māyā is bhakti-bound attachment, not material lust; their 'sex desire' is a vector toward Kṛṣṇa, not away.

    Stories
    Hanumān refusing liberation

    When Rāma offered Hanumān any benediction, Hanumān asked only to continue serving — not mokṣa. Tradition records that Hanumān actively refuses liberation, preferring eternal dāsya. The same logic operates in this verse: Pṛśni and Sutapā refuse apavargam (liberation) because mukti would end their seva.

    Gauḍīya theology celebrates this refusal: nitya-dāsya is higher than mukti; eternal service is the goal, not impersonal merging. Pṛśni and Sutapā are operating with the topmost siddhānta even before formally hearing it.

    Important Words
    • gate mayi — when I had departed
      Gata (gone) + mayi (in Me — locative absolute). Locative absolute construction: 'When I had gone'. Bhagavān describes His own withdrawal after granting the benediction. He goes; the fruit ripens; He returns. Pattern of līlā: descent, dispatch, return.
    • mat-sadṛśam — exactly like Me
      Mat (Me) + sadṛśa (similar to). Their precise request. Verse 41 will reveal that no one is truly sadṛśa to Bhagavān except Himself — so He fulfilled the request by becoming their son in person. The literal answer was higher than the literal request.
    • grāmyān bhogān — ordinary worldly enjoyments
      Grāmya (village, worldly) + bhoga (enjoyment) + accusative plural. Sex life, family life, household enjoyments. The Bhāgavata does not romanticize this; it names it plainly. Yet because their orientation was mat-cittatva, the same grāmya-bhoga produced Bhagavān as fruit.
    • manorathau — the desire of their hearts (fulfilled)
      Manas (mind) + ratha (chariot) — literally 'the chariot of the mind', i.e., the heart's deepest movement. Dual: both husband and wife shared one manoratha. Gauḍīya principle: when both partners share kṛṣṇa-manoratha, the union itself becomes seva.
    After you received that benediction and I disappeared, you engaged yourselves in sex to have a son like Me, and I fulfilled your desire.
    Purport

    According to the Sanskrit dictionary Amara-kośa, sex life is also called grāmya-dharma, material desire, but in spiritual life this grāmya-dharma, the material desire for sex, is not very much appreciated. If one has a tinge of attachment for the material enjoyments of eating, sleeping, mating and defending, one is not niṣkiñcana. But one really should be niṣkiñcana. Therefore, one should be free from the desire to beget a child like Kṛṣṇa by sexual enjoyment. This is indirectly hinted at in this verse.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    After you received that benediction and I disappeared, you engaged yourselves in sex to have a son like Me, and I fulfilled your desire.
    Commentary

    Desiring in this way for a son, you then engaged in sexual intercourse. Vyavyah means sex act according to the amara kosa.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    I arranged that you became slack in renunciation in order to fulfill my purpose. With joyful minds, you then collected material objects with a desire to be qualified for a wealthy son like me. You (yuvām) began enjoying objects previously enjoyed because you (yuvām) had a desire. The first yuvām can also mean yuvām mayi gate: when I left you. The word dattvā instead of labdhvā is seen in Śrīdhara’s commentary but that version is not seen anywhere. The meaning would be “having given the boon and departed.” The word varam indicates the means. Having attained the means of getting a son like me, you engaged in material life.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The benediction is described: having a son like me. Later you enjoyed material life because your desire was fulfilled. You had no fear at all. Or as ingredients for the birth of a son, you gathered items like oil, betel nut, bed, and cloth.

    Personal Guidance
    Even a desire as noble as wanting a son like Kṛṣṇa is still grāmya-dharma — the niṣkiñcana surrenders even sacred desires to Him.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today the one 'spiritual' desire you secretly use to justify material enjoyment, and offer it honestly to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Refuse to measure your sādhana by what you receive — eat, sleep, and work today as a niṣkiñcana, claiming nothing as your own.
    • Speak Kṛṣṇa's names once today with no petition attached — not for a son, a result, or a benediction, only for Him.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I treating a benediction from Kṛṣṇa as license for grāmya-bhoga — using a spiritual gift to ratify a material craving I had not yet renounced?
    • What attachment to eating, sleeping, mating, or defending am I still rationalizing as 'natural,' and what would it cost me to recognize that even one such tinge keeps me from being niṣkiñcana?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the moments this week when 'I want to do something meaningful' quietly collapses into 'I want to look impressive on Instagram, get into the right friend group, or land the right internship' — that slide from sevā-language into grāmya-bhoga is the exact move SB 10.3.40 is naming.
    • Pick one form of viṣaya that runs your day — late-night scrolling, hookup culture talk in the group chat, snack-and-Netflix loops during exam stress — and practice one week of explicit ahaṅkāra-checking: 'Am I the body wanting this, or the soul?' Write the answer down each night.
    • Before you next say 'I want a relationship so I can grow spiritually together,' sit with the verse: even Devakī and Vasudeva's desire for a son like Kṛṣṇa is gently called grāmya-dharma. Ask honestly whether you want a partner, or want bhakti, and don't let the two collapse into one excuse.
    householder
    • When you make the next big family decision — second child, bigger house, a new car, a school upgrade — write down the actual driver in one honest sentence before reaching for the devotional justification. SB 10.3.40 trains you to see that even 'for Kṛṣṇa' can be grāmya-bhoga in disguise.
    • Run a quarterly money-and-time audit with your spouse: what fraction of household resources actually flows toward sādhana, dāna, and serving Vaiṣṇavas, versus eating, sleeping, mating, defending? Don't aim for guilt — aim for accuracy, and shift one concrete percentage point this quarter.
    • Raise children inside gṛhastha-dharma without selling them the lie that family life is the spiritual summit. Tell them, in age-appropriate language, that mom and dad are also still working toward niṣkiñcana — model the direction, not just the role.
    senior
    • Take inventory of the grāmya-bhoga you are still quietly defending in late life — the favorite food, the comfortable chair, the grandchild-attachment dressed as love — and pick one to consciously loosen this month as tapas, not as deprivation.
    • When mentoring younger devotees or family members, do not romanticize your own gṛhastha years as the high point. Tell the truth: the children, the house, the career were grāmya-bhoga sanctified by duty, and the real work was always bhakti — and still is.
    • Use the nearness of mortality as the verse uses Kṛṣṇa's disappearance: the benediction has been received, the household chapter is closing, what remains is direct surrender. Each evening, formally hand the day's remaining attachments to Kṛṣṇa before sleep.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the verse as a sentimental story about Devakī and Vasudeva 'getting their wish,' and missing Prabhupāda's pointed warning that desiring even a Kṛṣṇa-like son through sex is still grāmya-dharma to be transcended.
    • Mistaking niṣkiñcana for outward poverty or ascetic theatrics, while quietly nursing the same household appetites — clinging to the fruits of bhoga while wearing the costume of vairāgya.
    • Twisting the verse into a blanket condemnation of family life or procreation, instead of hearing its real edge: that any tinge of attachment to material enjoyment, however refined or 'spiritualized,' disqualifies one from full surrender.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Prabhupāda says even the desire to beget a son like Kṛṣṇa through sex life is not appreciated for one who would be niṣkiñcana. Share with your partner: where in your own life have you tried to baptize a grāmya-bhoga (eating, sleeping, mating, defending) by attaching a 'spiritual' purpose to it? Be specific. Push back if your partner's example sounds too clean.
    • Devakī and Vasudeva were given the supreme benediction — Kṛṣṇa Himself as son — yet the verse gently points out that the means was still grāmya-dharma. Discuss: does this verse imply that even sanctified family life is a concession, not the ideal? Does your group disagree on this? Where does the disagreement actually sit — on śāstra, or on personal stake?
    • The purport contrasts the niṣkiñcana with one who has 'a tinge of attachment' to bodily enjoyments. Most of us have far more than a tinge. Pair up and name one specific viṣaya you would not be willing to give up today even if a sādhu told you to. Then ask each other honestly: is that attachment serving bhakti, or being protected by bhakti-language?
    Role Play

    Two students play a married couple in their early thirties. They have one child. They are seriously practicing devotees and now considering a second child, and they tell themselves the reason is 'to raise another devotee for Kṛṣṇa.' A third student plays a senior Vaiṣṇava friend who has just heard them say this and gently challenges the framing — referencing SB 10.3.40 and Prabhupāda's note on grāmya-dharma. The couple must defend their reasoning honestly without hiding behind devotional vocabulary; the senior friend must distinguish between condemning gṛhastha life (which is not the point) and exposing self-deception about grāmya-bhoga dressed up as sevā. Run for eight minutes, then swap roles.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds anti-family and anti-sex. Devakī and Vasudeva were married, they had a child, and that child was Kṛṣṇa Himself — so why does Prabhupāda turn around and say even their desire was not 'very much appreciated'? It feels like the tradition can never let householders simply be householders.
      The verse and purport are not condemning Devakī and Vasudeva — Kṛṣṇa is in fact fulfilling their desire, and gṛhastha-āśrama is one of the four legitimate āśramas in varṇāśrama. What Prabhupāda is naming is a finer point: even the most sanctified material desire is still a material desire, and the niṣkiñcana stage lies beyond it. Householder life is not being rejected; the romanticization of householder life as the spiritual summit is being rejected. A Gauḍīya teacher upholds gṛhastha-dharma fully and at the same time refuses to let the student mistake grāmya-dharma for the goal. Both can be true.
    • The framing of sex as grāmya-dharma — 'village-dharma,' something low — is exactly the kind of body-shaming, sex-negative religion modern people are walking away from. Why should anyone today take this seriously?
      Grāmya-dharma is not a moral insult; it is a precise diagnostic term from the Amara-kośa. It names the level at which an activity functions — the level of bodily, common-to-all-creatures life (eating, sleeping, mating, defending). The Gītā's whole project is to ask: am I the body, or am I the soul situated in this body? If I am the soul, then organizing my entire life around bodily enjoyments — even with a partner I love, even with children I love — leaves the actual self un-fed. This is not shame; it is accuracy. A Gauḍīya teacher does not tell the student to hate the body or hate the spouse. The teacher tells the student: do not mistake the menu of grāmya-bhoga for the food of the soul, which is bhakti to Kṛṣṇa.
    Analogy

    An artisan, after receiving a master's promise, returns to his workshop and resumes the very work that always seemed mundane — but now every motion is filled with new meaning, because the master himself will inhabit the next piece. Pṛśni and Sutapā's grāmya-bhoga, after the boon, is artisanal: ordinary action saturated with divine purpose.

    Stories
    Prahlāda's birth from Hiraṇyakaśipu and Kayādhū

    Prahlāda was born when Nārada had instructed his mother Kayādhū during pregnancy — the child in the womb absorbed bhakti directly. The mechanism: parental orientation and the bhāva at the time of conception shape the soul that arrives.

    The Bhāgavata is here naming the same mechanism positively. Pṛśni and Sutapā's union, undertaken with mat-cittatva, prepared the field for Bhagavān Himself to arrive. The Gauḍīya line takes this seriously: sambandha matters in physical generation as much as in spiritual.

    Important Words
    • adṛṣṭvā — not seeing/finding
      Gerund of √dṛś — 'not having seen'. Bhagavān searched and did not find an equal. The Sanskrit acknowledges His own uniqueness: no second person matches Him. Personalist theology: He is sui generis.
    • śīla-audārya-guṇaiḥ — in the qualities of character and magnanimity
      Śīla (good character) + audārya (magnanimity, breadth) + guṇa + instrumental plural. The specific dimensions on which Pṛśni and Sutapā were unmatched. Note: not 'spiritual achievement' but character. The Bhāgavata-line cares about śīla.
    • pṛśni-garbhaḥ — born of Pṛśni's womb
      Pṛśni (Devakī's prior name) + garbha (womb) + ḥ (one whose). One of Bhagavān's many descent-names — Pṛśnigarbha. Each avatāra has names indexed to the parents who hosted Him. Bhagavān is named by His relations as much as by His acts.
    Since I found no one else as highly elevated as you in simplicity and other qualities of good character, I appeared in this world as Pṛśnigarbha, or one who is celebrated as having taken birth from Pṛśni.
    Purport

    In the Tretā-yuga the Lord appeared as Pṛśnigarbha. Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura says, pṛśnigarbha iti so ’yaṁ tretā-yugāvatāro lakṣyate.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Since I found no one else as highly elevated as you in simplicity and other qualities of good character, I appeared in this world as Pṛśnigarbha, or one who is celebrated as having taken birth from Pṛśni.
    Commentary

    "In my first birth I appeared as Prsnigarbha." This refers to the treta yuga avatara, for this is mentioned in the eleventh canto visnu yajnah prsni garbha...

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Moved by your skilful words, later on considering the matter, I fulfilled your desires. I did not see anyone in the world (and even myself) equal to you in good character (śila) and great (āudārya) qualities. For this reason I was merciful. Instead of śrutaḥ sometimes smṛtaḥ is seen. It means “well known.” Pṛṣnigarbha became the overseer of Tretā-yuga. viṣṇur yajṣaḥ pṛśnigarbhaḥ sarvadeva urukramaḥ vṛṣākapir jayantaś ca urugāya itīryate In Tretā-yuga the Lord is glorified by the names Viṣṇu, Yajṣa, Pṛśnigarbha, Sarvadeva, Urukrama, Vṛṣākapi, Jayanta and Urugāya.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    There was no one else equal to me in nature (śīla), generosity (audārya) and qualities like mercy. I was known as Pṛśnigarbha. He was famous by that name.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa descends personally where ārjava and pure character shine — cultivate simplicity today, and you become a place He chooses to appear.
    Practical Applications
    • Strip one piece of pretense from your day — speak plainly to someone you usually impress, and notice the relief of ārjava.
    • Identify a relationship where you are performing rather than being straightforward, and offer a single honest sentence instead of a polished one.
    • Before sleep, ask Kṛṣṇa to make your character — not your achievements — the thing that draws Him near, and name one quality you will guard tomorrow.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life do I posture with elaborate qualities while quietly lacking the simple, straightforward śīla and ārjava that actually drew the Lord to Pṛśni and Sutapā?
    • If Kṛṣṇa Himself looks across the world for simplicity of character before choosing where to appear, what hidden duplicity in my speech, dealings, or sādhana is keeping Him at a distance from my heart?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • On your next exam or assignment, refuse the small dishonesties everyone normalizes — inflated participation claims, padded resumes, 'borrowed' answers. The verse says the Lord notices ārjava; let one assignment this week be conducted as if He were the grader.
    • In your friend group or on social media, catch yourself once today performing a version of you that is more impressive than the real one — a curated photo, a name-dropped book you didn't read, a strategic humblebrag. Delete it or correct it. Practice adambhitva in the medium where dambha is rewarded most.
    • Pick the friend in your circle who is plain, unstrategic, and a little 'uncool' in their straightforwardness. Spend real time with them this week. Kṛṣṇa came to Pṛśni for that quality; train your own taste to recognize it.
    householder
    • In one financial decision this month — a negotiation, a tax filing, a transaction with a vendor — take the path of full disclosure even where partial disclosure is legal and customary. Tell your spouse afterward; let asteya become a shared family standard, not a private virtue.
    • When raising your children, stop rewarding cleverness over candor. The next time your child confesses something inconvenient honestly, praise the honesty more loudly than you would have punished the act. You are shaping the kind of household the Lord describes in this verse.
    • In your career, identify one place where you are managing your image — a meeting where you posture, a relationship you cultivate strategically, a credit you quietly take. Drop it for one week and observe what actually happens. Test whether ārjava is, as the verse implies, the qualification the Lord watches for, or whether you still secretly believe dambha is what pays.
    senior
    • In conversations with grandchildren or younger relatives, stop curating the sanitized version of your life. Tell one true story this month about a failure or a regret, named plainly. Let your legacy be ārjava, not a polished myth — this is the simplicity Kṛṣṇa came for.
    • Review your will, your possessions, and your unspoken expectations of your children. Where are you still holding leverage, hinting, or 'managing' the family through your estate? Loosen one such grip this season. Asteya at this stage means not stealing from your heirs the freedom to grieve and decide cleanly.
    • Mentor at least one younger devotee or family member without strategic intent — no grooming them to carry your name, no shaping them into your mirror. Serve their svarūpa as Sutapā and Pṛśni served the Lord's: by being straightforward, undemanding, and simple in their presence.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating ārjava (simplicity) as a personality trait or temperament one is born with, rather than a daily, deliberate refusal to be crooked in thought, word, and deed.
    • Cultivating outward simplicity as a spiritual aesthetic — plain dress, soft speech, humble posture — while inwardly trafficking in calculation, image-management, and hidden agendas (the very dambha this verse implicitly rejects).
    • Reading the verse as a story about Pṛśni and Sutapā being uniquely special long ago, and concluding that Kṛṣṇa's choice of where to appear has nothing to do with the quality of one's own character today.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Kṛṣṇa says He chose Sutapā and Pṛśni because He found no one else equal to them in śīla (simplicity, good character) and udārya (magnanimity). Share with your partner: in your own life, who are the two or three people whose ārjava (straightforwardness) has actually attracted real responsibility, trust, or affection toward them — and what does that tell you about how the Lord chooses His servants? Be ready to disagree if your partner romanticizes 'cleverness' over simplicity.
    • The verse claims that simplicity and good qualities — not power, intelligence, or position — are what made these two parents 'fit' to receive the Lord. In a world that rewards self-promotion, dambha (showmanship), and strategic positioning, do you actually believe ārjava is a competitive virtue, or is it a liability you tolerate because scripture commends it? Push each other; do not settle for the pious answer.
    • Pṛśnigarbha is the Tretā-yuga avatāra; the Lord literally takes a name that means 'born of Pṛśni' — His identity in that descent is bound up with the simplicity of His mother. Discuss: where in your sādhana are you trying to attract Kṛṣṇa through what you do (japa counts, service hours, knowledge), versus through who you are quietly becoming in private? Where does the group disagree on which matters more?
    Role Play

    Two students play a hiring panel at a Vaiṣṇava-run organization. A third student plays a candidate who is technically average but unusually straightforward — admits weaknesses in the interview, refuses to inflate accomplishments, declines to bad-mouth a previous employer even when prompted. A fourth student plays a candidate who is polished, strategically vague, and impressive on paper. The panel must decide whom to hire and justify it in light of SB 10.3.41 — that the Lord Himself selected parents on the basis of śīla and ārjava, not capability. After the role-play, reverse the framing: would the panel apply the same standard if it were their own money or their own child's marriage? Surface the gap.

    Objections & Responses
    • Isn't this just a story Vasudeva tells himself to feel chosen? Every parent thinks their child is special; calling Kṛṣṇa your son because of your 'simplicity' sounds like spiritualized self-flattery.
      Notice who is speaking in this verse — it is Kṛṣṇa Himself, addressing Vasudeva and Devakī, telling them why He came. It is not the parents claiming distinction; it is the Lord disclosing His own criterion. And His criterion is striking precisely because it is the opposite of self-flattery: He names ārjava and śīla — qualities that by their nature cannot be self-advertised without being destroyed. The moment you boast of your simplicity, you have lost it. So the verse is not flattery; it is a quiet warning that the Lord watches for the very qualities our culture trains us to hide or outgrow.
    • Picking parents based on 'good character' sounds quaint. In real life, character is shaped by circumstance — trauma, class, opportunity. Isn't this verse just rewarding those who got lucky enough to be raised well?
      The Gauḍīya line does not treat śīla as a lottery of birth. Ārjava, asteya, adambhitva — these are practiced, not inherited; many born into refinement lose them, and many born into hardship cultivate them through sādhana and saṅga. Sutapā and Pṛśni in their previous birth performed long austerity to become fit — character here is the fruit of deliberate effort across lifetimes, not a prize for being born comfortable. The verse is in fact deeply democratic: whatever your beginnings, the Lord's attention is drawn by qualities you can begin building today — straightforwardness in speech, honesty in dealings, refusal of pretense. Nothing about that requires luck.
    Analogy

    An emperor, told that a craftsman in his realm has fashioned an empty throne in his honor and is now waiting for a king to fill it, finds that no other king is grand enough for the throne — and so he occupies it himself. Pṛśni and Sutapā asked for a son like Bhagavān; not finding any other being equal to Himself, Bhagavān became their son.

    Stories
    Bhagavān as Upendra-Vāmana (next verse's same logic)

    When Aditi and Kaśyapa, in a later millennium, performed tapas seeking a son like Bhagavān, He again came personally — this time as Vāmana, the dwarf-avatāra. The same pattern: tapas + request for a son like Me + Bhagavān's own appearance as son.

    The Bhāgavata's narrative grammar: when the request is mādṛśaḥ ('like Me'), Bhagavān fulfills it Himself. He does not delegate. The boon's literal exactness is preserved only by His personal coming.

    Important Words
    • adityām — in (the womb of) Aditi
      Locative of Aditi — mother of the ādityas, here the prior incarnation of Pṛśni-Devakī. The Bhāgavata is naming Devakī's second avatāra-motherhood. Sambandha continues across cosmic cycles.
    • kaśyapāt — from Kaśyapa
      Ablative of Kaśyapa — the prior incarnation of Sutapā-Vasudeva. Vasudeva is identified with Kaśyapa-prajāpati. The chain Sutapā → Kaśyapa → Vasudeva makes Bhagavān's fathers a single eternal associate appearing under different names.
    • upendraḥ — Upendra (younger brother of Indra)
      Upa (under, alongside) + Indra. Vāmana was younger brother to Indra — hence Upendra. The name marks His functional position in that līlā as Indra's protector. Bhagavān takes names that fit the līlā's social structure.
    • vāmanaḥ — Vāmana, the dwarf
      Vāmana — dwarf. The form that, by being small, could expand to trivikrama. The name marks the contraction-expansion paradox. Bhagavān is sometimes large (Viśvarūpa), sometimes small (Vāmana, infant Kṛṣṇa) — His size is His choice.
    In the next millennium, I again appeared from the two of you, who appeared as My mother, Aditi, and My father, Kaśyapa. I was known as Upendra, and because of being a dwarf, I was also known as Vāmana.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    In the next millennium, I again appeared from the two of you, who appeared as My mother, Aditi, and My father, Kaśyapa. I was known as Upendra, and because of being a dwarf, I was also known as Vāmana.
    Commentary

    "He who appeared as Vamana to Aditi and Kasyapa has now appeared as your son, as myself."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Śṛīdhara Svāmī explains the verse. When Vāmana appeared (āsa) in Aditi from Kaśyapa, I appeared (the verb āsam is missing by poetic license) a second time to you. The full meaning is “When Vāmāna called by that name because he was short, and also known as Upendra, appeared in Aditi, I appeared to you a second time.” Or the verb āsa can be taken with aham if aham stands for saḥ. He who is I (aham) appeared (āsa) a second time.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Āsa should be āsam (I became). It is poetic licence, or the “I” is taken in an indirect sense like “he.” I was known as Vāmana.

    Personal Guidance
    As Vāmana, Kṛṣṇa enters as the small, humble form to claim everything for the devotee — surrender to His personal descent, not an abstract Absolute.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one place today where you are dismissing something as 'too small to matter' — and treat it with the reverence due to Kṛṣṇa's vāmana-form.
    • Offer three steps of your day — morning, work, evening — explicitly to Upendra, the Lord who appears as the younger brother of the demigods to protect His devotee.
    • Refuse to flatten Kṛṣṇa into 'the universal Self'; speak of Him today as a person with a mother (Aditi) and father (Kaśyapa), with a name and a form.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I refusing to 'become small' — like Vāmana — to recover what has been usurped, insisting instead that my full stature be acknowledged before I act?
    • Kṛṣṇa took birth as Upendra, the younger brother of Indra, deliberately accepting a subordinate position to serve a devotee — where am I unwilling to take the 'younger' seat in service to someone I outrank?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • This week, when someone 'small' in your social hierarchy — a quiet classmate, a younger sibling, a service worker on campus — makes a small request, treat it as Vāmana at your door and give without calculating the social cost.
    • Audit your Instagram or LinkedIn for one hour: where are you performing largeness (followers, internships, achievements) the way Bali ruled three worlds? Pick one boast you will quietly retire this week as your offering to Upendra.
    • Before your next exam or interview, recite this verse once and offer the result in advance to Krishna — not to do worse, but to do your best without claiming the outcome as 'mine.'
    householder
    • Identify the 'three steps' Krishna is currently asking of you in your household — perhaps time for sādhana, money for service, or space in a decision where you are used to being king — and concretely give one step this week.
    • Teach your children the Vāmana pastime this week, in your own words, and let them see you treat a humble guest, delivery worker, or relative as you would treat the Lord arriving in a small form.
    • Review your career and finances through Bali's lens: which 'kingdom' (a title, a property, a savings target) have you started defending as ultimately yours? Name it aloud to your spouse and re-vow it as Krishna's, held in trust.
    senior
    • Begin handing over your 'three worlds' deliberately — assets, authority in the family, decision-making — to the next generation as conscious offering, not as reluctant loss, before Vāmana arrives unannounced.
    • Each evening, meditate on Vāmana standing on Bali's head as the supreme benediction at the end of life, and pray that whatever the Lord removes from you in your final years He removes by His own foot, not by your clinging.
    • Mentor at least one younger devotee or family member by telling them, plainly, what you wish you had surrendered earlier — let your hindsight become their śraddhā, and your loosening attachments their inheritance.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the dwarf form as mere divine cleverness or trickery, rather than as Kṛṣṇa's tenderness toward Aditi's vow and Bali's eventual elevation — turning a pastime of relationship into a story about strategy.
    • Concluding that because Kṛṣṇa appears repeatedly through Aditi and Kaśyapa, the parents are interchangeable vessels — missing that the Lord honors specific bhakti-bonds and returns to the same devotees across millennia.
    • Romanticizing 'smallness' as a generic spiritual virtue (humility-as-aesthetic), when Vāmanatva here is purposeful, surgical, and undertaken to protect a devotee — not a posture of self-effacement for its own sake.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Vāmana, the Lord Himself, took the form of a small dwarf brāhmaṇa to approach Bali. Where in your own life have you confused largeness of form with largeness of spirit, and missed the Lord because He came in a small package?
    • Aditi performed severe penance to receive Krishna as her son; the Lord 'again appeared from the two of you.' Discuss whether parenthood today is treated as a right, a project, or a sādhana — and what would change in your home if you held your children as Aditi held Vāmana.
    • Bali was generous, truthful, and devoted — yet Vāmana came specifically to take everything from him. Where do you sense Krishna may be moving to take something from you precisely because of, not in spite of, your good qualities? Share something concrete you suspect He is asking for.
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A plays a sincere, hard-working young professional who has just received a major promotion — more salary, more status, more 'territory.' Student B plays a small, unimpressive-looking guest (a brāhmaṇa, a junior colleague, a relative no one takes seriously) who shows up and asks for 'just three steps' worth of A's time, attention, or resources — something that, if honestly given, will cost A the very thing they were celebrating. A must decide in real time: refuse politely, bargain, or surrender like Bali. Run it twice, swapping roles, then debrief: where did the ahaṅkāra speak loudest, and where did śraddhā actually show up?

    Objections & Responses
    • Vāmana taking everything from a generous, truthful king like Bali sounds unjust — Krishna rewards bad behavior and punishes good behavior in this story.
      Look again at what Bali actually loses and gains. He loses three worlds of opaque kingship; he gains Vāmana standing personally on his head as the greatest benediction in the universe. The Lord does not strip Bali — He extracts Bali from a position that, however righteous, was still rooted in proprietorship. Real compassion serves the soul, not the ego's sense of fairness. What looks like injustice is the Lord performing the one surgery only He can perform: removing the last refined layer of 'mine' from a devotee good enough to bear it. We should pray for such 'injustice.'
    • An infinite God shrinking into a dwarf body to trick a king out of his kingdom is mythology, not theology. Why should a thinking modern person take this literally?
      Two things to hold together. First, Krishna is the supreme Personality of Godhead — personal, willful, and free to appear in any form He chooses; the dwarf form is not a limitation imposed on Him but a līlā chosen by Him, and 'vāmanatvāc ca vāmanaḥ' is His own self-description through Kaśyapa. Second, the so-called trick is the opposite of deception: Vāmana asks openly, Bali agrees freely, and the Lord fulfills the contract exactly. What offends the modern reader is not dishonesty but the scale — that the Absolute would condescend to ask, to bargain, to walk three steps. That condescension is precisely the news of the Gauḍīya tradition: the supreme is not impersonal vastness but a Person small enough to stand at your door and ask. Discriminative wisdom (viveka) accepts the avatāra on the strength of śāstra, sādhu, and guru — not because it flatters the modern mind, but because it does not.
    Analogy

    A great teacher promises a student: 'I will come to your house every generation as long as you and your wife perform real tapas.' He keeps the promise — as Pṛśnigarbha first, as Upendra-Vāmana next, as Kṛṣṇa now. Three appearances, one Person, one couple. Bhakti's long arc is the relationship across cosmic time.

    Stories
    Bali's encounter with Vāmana

    Vāmana, Aditi's son, approached Bali Mahārāja and asked for three steps of land. With those three steps He measured the universe. Bali surrendered the third step by offering his own head, and was placed in Sutala — given the highest possible honor.

    This verse names that same Vāmana as Pṛśni/Aditi and Sutapā/Kaśyapa's son — completing the genealogy across yugas. Bhagavān as Vāmana-Upendra is the same Person now arriving as Kṛṣṇa. The connection between Bali's surrender and Devakī's prison is family-resemblance in the truest sense.

    Important Words
    • tṛtīye — for the third time
      Locative of tṛtīya — third. The numbering is precise: Pṛśnigarbha (first), Upendra-Vāmana (second), Kṛṣṇa (third). Bhagavān's appearances are countable, not vague. Each is a distinct historical event in a distinct sarga.
    • asmin bhave — in this appearance
      Asmin (this) + bhava (appearance, becoming) + locative. Bhāva here means 'manifest appearance'. The same root as the bhāva of bhāva-bhakti. Bhagavān's bhāvas are His self-manifestations into history.
    • satyam-me-vyāhṛtam — My speech is truth
      Satyam (truth) + me (My) + vyāhṛta (spoken). The Bhāgavata explicitly grounds the historicity claim in Bhagavān's own truth-speech. He is not mistaken; He is not exaggerating. Take this as truth, He says. Caitanya tradition takes it so.
    • sati — O chaste one
      Vocative of satī. Echoes verse 32. Bhagavān addresses Devakī as satī in both the opening and closing of His narration — establishing her qualification through repetition. The framing names what she is throughout: faithful, true.
    O supremely chaste mother, I, the same personality, have now appeared of you both as your son for the third time. Take My words as the truth.
    Purport

    The Supreme Personality of Godhead chooses a mother and father from whom to take birth again and again. The Lord took birth originally from Sutapā and Pṛśni, then from Kaśyapa and Aditi, and again from the same father and mother, Vasudeva and Devakī. “In other appearances also,” the Lord said, “I took the form of an ordinary child just to become your son so that we could reciprocate eternal love.” Jīva Gosvāmī has explained this verse in his Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha, Ninety-sixth Chapter, where he notes that in text 37 the Lord says, amunā vapuṣa, meaning “by this same form.” In other words, the Lord told Devakī, “This time I have appeared in My original form as Śrī Kṛṣṇa.” Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī says that the other forms were partial expansions of the Lord’s original form, but because of the intense love developed by Pṛśni and Sutapā, the Lord appeared from Devakī and Vasudeva in His full opulence as Śrī Kṛṣṇa. In this verse the Lord confirms, “I am the same Supreme Personality of Godhead, but I appear in full opulence as Śrī Kṛṣṇa.” This is the purport of the words tenaiva vapuṣā. When the Lord mentioned the birth of Pṛśnigarbha, He did not say tenaiva vapuṣā, but He assured Devakī that in the third birth the Supreme Personality of Godhead Kṛṣṇa had appeared, not His partial expansion. Pṛśnigarbha and Vāmana were partial expansions of Kṛṣṇa, but in this third birth Kṛṣṇa Himself appeared. This is the explanation given in Śrī Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha by Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O supremely chaste mother, I, the same personality, have now appeared of you both as your son for the third time. Take My words as the truth.
    Commentary

    "In the present birth I have been born with four arms. I was born in the first birth as Prsnigarbha, and in the second birth as Vamana. In the third birth I am born." This indicates that the birth as Krsna is the full,complete form and the previous two are his amsas. In verse 31 the Lord says to Devaki, "You were previously Prsni" but he did not say "Prsni is you." In verse 45 he says, "After thinking of me as your son in this you will go to my spiritual abode." By these evidences it is shown that Prsni and Sutapa are expansions of Devaki and Vasudeva.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    When the Lord appeared as Pṛśnigarbha and Vāmana to them, he did not say tena vapuśā (by the form that you see now, Kṛṣṇa). Thus those forms are his aṁśas as expressed in the verse ete cāṁśa-kalāḥ purṁsaḥ kṛṣṇās tu bhagavān svayam: these are all aṁśas or kalās but Kṛṣṇa is Svayam Bhagavān. But now he appeared in svayam rūpa. The distinction is made in the following verse. pṛśnigarbhas tu te buddhim ātmānaṁ bhagavān paraḥ May Pṛśnigarbha protect your intelligence, and may the Supreme Bhagavān protect your soul. SB 10.6.25 That is the subtle implication of the present verse. The word vai expresses certainty. The Lord’s promise became true in his third appearance, fulfilling that they would have a son like the Lord they saw at the beginning (Kṛṣṇa with four arms).
