    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa Himself — not a partial expansion — comes as son to those whose love for Him has matured across lifetimes; trust His personal word.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one relationship where you have settled for an 'expansion' of Kṛṣṇa — a concept, a feeling, an impersonal Absolute — and today address Him by name in prayer instead.
    • Recall a promise Kṛṣṇa makes in śāstra that you have been quietly doubting, and act on it once today as if satyaṁ me vyāhṛtam — His word is true.
    • Reflect on the bhakti Pṛśni and Sutapā cultivated across three births and commit to one sādhana you will not skip today, however small.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I treating Kṛṣṇa as a partial expansion — useful for some needs, kept at a distance for others — instead of receiving Him in His full opulence as Sutapā and Pṛśni did?
    • What intensity of love would He need to see in me before He would consent to appear in my life as Himself, and what am I currently substituting for that intensity?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the friendships and family bonds you currently treat as 'temporary' — the roommate you'll lose touch with, the parent you barely call. Pick one and act this week as if the soul-connection will outlast graduation, the breakup, even this body.
    • Before your next exam or audition, instead of begging Kṛṣṇa for the result, offer the effort itself as a small reciprocation — the way Pṛśni and Sutapā offered tapasyā long before they got Kṛṣṇa as their son. Long before, not in exchange for.
    • When social media tempts you to perform a self for likes, remember Kṛṣṇa's tenaiva vapuṣā — 'this same form.' Practice one act of being who you actually are, in front of someone whose approval you don't need.
    householder
    • Look at your spouse and children today as souls Kṛṣṇa Himself may have brought into your home across multiple lifetimes — not as roles or obligations. Make one decision this week (a financial sacrifice, a postponed promotion, a hard conversation) that treats the relationship as eternal rather than transactional.
    • When raising children, don't merely manage their behavior — cultivate the kind of love Pṛśni and Sutapā cultivated, the love that draws Kṛṣṇa Himself. Read or chant something of Kṛṣṇa with your child this week, even five minutes, knowing the soul in front of you is who the Lord came for.
    • In career and money decisions, ask whether you are accumulating for this body alone or building a household where Kṛṣṇa would willingly take birth. Adjust one specific expenditure or commitment accordingly.
    senior
    • Reflect on the bodies you have already passed through — child, youth, householder — and feel the same I that Kṛṣṇa points to when He says 'I, the same personality.' Use this as the steadying anchor for facing the next transition.
    • Mentor a younger sādhaka not as a transmission of opinions but as an offering of the love that has accrued in you across decades; that accrued love, like Pṛśni's, is what draws Kṛṣṇa near, into your life and theirs.
    • Loosen one specific attachment this month — a possession, a grudge, a prestige — and consciously redirect that energy toward fixing the mind on Kṛṣṇa as svayam bhagavān, the complete Person, so that whatever body comes next is chosen by Him, not by lingering desires.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading 'I have come as your son for the third time' as mythology to admire rather than as a personal assurance that the Supreme Personality keeps His word across lifetimes — and therefore failing to trust His promises now.
    • Flattening Kṛṣṇa's specific appearance from Devakī into a generic 'divine within everyone,' losing the personalist truth that He chooses particular parents, particular forms, and particular relationships.
    • Treating Pṛśnigarbha, Vāmana, and Kṛṣṇa as interchangeable — missing Jīva Gosvāmī's careful distinction that only here, after sustained tapasyā and love, did Kṛṣṇa appear in His original form rather than as a partial expansion.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Kṛṣṇa says He chose Devakī and Vasudeva as parents repeatedly because of the love cultivated by Pṛśni and Sutapā across lifetimes. Where in your life do you treat relationships as one-shot encounters rather than as ongoing reciprocations the soul carries forward? Share one relationship you'd reconsider if you took this verse seriously.
    • Jīva Gosvāmī distinguishes between the partial expansions (Pṛśnigarbha, Vāmana) and Kṛṣṇa Himself appearing in full opulence here. What is the practical, lived difference for a sādhaka between worshipping a partial conception of God and surrendering to Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Personality? Does that distinction actually change your daily sādhana, or is it only theological?
    • The Lord's words satyaṁ me vyāhṛtaṁ sati — 'take My words as the truth' — are the Supreme Person personally vouching for what He says. In an age trained to distrust all authority, where do you find yourself instinctively doubting Kṛṣṇa's plain statements in śāstra, and what would it cost you to drop that doubt for a week?
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A is Devakī, who has just heard Kṛṣṇa reveal that He has appeared as her son for the third time across cosmic ages, confirming an unbroken thread of love. Student B is Devakī's modern-day skeptical relative visiting the prison cell, who insists this is wishful storytelling and that the 'baby is just a baby.' Student A must respond — not by argument but by the conviction of one who has heard the Lord's own assurance — and articulate how she now sees her relationship with this child, her past lives, and her present suffering. After 5 minutes, switch roles. Debrief: what shifted in you when you had to speak as Devakī rather than as the skeptic?

    Objections & Responses
    • Reincarnation across specific parent-child pairs sounds like a fairy tale. Why should a thoughtful modern reader accept that Kṛṣṇa 'chose' Sutapā and Pṛśni, then Kaśyapa and Aditi, then Vasudeva and Devakī as the same couple across yugas?
      We are not asked to accept it as folklore but on the authority of the Supreme Person Himself, who declares satyaṁ me vyāhṛtaṁ — 'My words are truth.' The Gauḍīya line, through Jīva Gosvāmī's Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha, treats this not as poetic flourish but as a precise statement: love cultivated through long tapasyā draws the Lord personally into a reciprocal relationship. The 'modern' instinct to flatten this into metaphor is itself a faith position — faith in materialism. The verse asks you to consider another faith: that personal love between souls and Kṛṣṇa is real, durable across bodies, and the actual fabric of existence. You don't have to accept it on day one; you have to be honest that rejecting it is also a choice, not neutrality.
    • If Kṛṣṇa is the same as Pṛśnigarbha and Vāmana, why does Jīva Gosvāmī make such a fuss about Kṛṣṇa appearing 'in full opulence' here? Isn't this just sectarian one-upmanship — Gauḍīyas elevating their iṣṭa-deva over other forms?
      It is not sectarian; it is precise. The Lord's own word tenaiva vapuṣā in this verse — used here and not when Pṛśnigarbha was mentioned — is the textual evidence Jīva Gosvāmī rests on. The other forms were aṁśa, partial expansions; Kṛṣṇa is svayam bhagavān, the source. The distinction matters practically because the bhāva you cultivate depends on whom you are relating to: a sādhaka who knows Kṛṣṇa is the complete Person can offer complete love, not hedged worship of an aspect. Far from one-upmanship, honoring this distinction is what allows the intimacy Devakī and Vasudeva earned across three births. To blur it is to refuse the gift the verse is offering.
    Analogy

    A master craftsman has returned to the same family three times across the centuries — first as a gem-cutter, then as a painter, now as a sculptor — each visit producing a different masterpiece in their home. He says, 'This is the third time I have come to you. Believe my words.' Bhagavān has been Pṛśnigarbha, Vāmana, and now Kṛṣṇa to the same couple — three appearances, one familial bond.

    Stories
    Kṛṣṇa's vow of repeated descent in BG 4

    In Bhagavad-gītā 4.7–8, Kṛṣṇa declares: 'Whenever there is decline of dharma… I appear, age after age.' The plurality of descents is Bhagavān's own promise.

    This verse instances that promise concretely for one couple. The Gauḍīya line takes BG 4.7 not as poetic exaggeration but as historical commitment: Bhagavān actually does descend, multiply, into specifiable historical moments. The Bhāgavata records the moments; the Gītā names the principle.

    Important Words
    • prāk-janma — previous births
      Prāk (former, eastern, prior) + janma. Bhagavān's prior 'births' — the appearances as Pṛśnigarbha and Vāmana. Note: He uses janma colloquially though He is ajan-māne, unborn. Even Bhagavān adopts the language of birth to communicate intimately.
    • smaraṇāya — for the purpose of remembering
      Smaraṇa (remembrance, smṛti) + dative. The purpose of the form-display is smaraṇa. Smaraṇaṁ is the third of the nine limbs of bhakti — remembering Kṛṣṇa. Bhagavān deliberately triggers smaraṇa in Devakī by showing the Viṣṇu-form.
    • martya-liṅgena — with the mark of a mortal
      Martya (mortal) + liṅga (mark, sign, form) + instrumental. The 'mark' of mortality — ordinary infant body. The word liṅga here means distinguishing sign, not gender; Bhagavān is wearing the disguise of mortality.
    • jñānam — this knowledge
      Jñāna — knowledge, specifically the recognition of who He is. Without the four-armed display, this specific jñāna would not have arisen. Gauḍīya distinction: vaidha-bhakti needs jñāna of who Bhagavān is; rāga-bhakti in Vraja proceeds without explicit jñāna — both paths are valid, and this is the vaidha-aiśvarya-mixed branch.
    I have shown you this form of Viṣṇu just to remind you of My previous births. Otherwise, if I appeared like an ordinary human child, you would not believe that the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Viṣṇu, has indeed appeared.
    Purport

    Devakī did not need to be reminded that the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Viṣṇu, had appeared as her son; she already accepted this. Nonetheless, she was anxious, thinking that if her neighbors heard that Viṣṇu had appeared as her son, none of them would believe it. Therefore she wanted Lord Viṣṇu to transform Himself into a human child. On the other hand, the Supreme Lord was also anxious, thinking that if He appeared as an ordinary child, she would not believe that Lord Viṣṇu had appeared. Such are the dealings between devotees and the Lord. The Lord deals with His devotees exactly like a human being, but this does not mean that the Lord is one of the human beings, for this is the conclusion of nondevotees ( avajānanti māṁ mūḍhā mānuṣīṁ tanum āśritam ). Devotees know the Supreme Personality of Godhead under any circumstances. This is the difference between a devotee and a nondevotee. The Lord says, man-manā bhava mad-bhakto mad-yājī māṁ namaskuru: “Engage your mind always in thinking of Me, become My devotee, offer obeisances and worship Me.” A nondevotee cannot believe that simply by thinking of one person, one can achieve liberation from this material world and go back home, back to Godhead. But this is a fact. The Lord comes as a human being, and if one becomes attached to the Lord on the platform of loving service, one’s promotion to the transcendental world is assured.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    I have shown you this form of Viṣṇu just to remind you of My previous births. Otherwise, if I appeared like an ordinary human child, you would not believe that the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Viṣṇu, has indeed appeared.
    Commentary

    I have appeared in the four armed form because you would not recognize me as God if I appeared in my complete, original, two armed human-like form.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Bhava means “that in which something exists” or in other words an object. There would be no discernment (jṣānam) of me as the object of your previous worship. Instead of jāyate sometimes janyate is seen. Or bhava can mean the form with four arms shown so that they would remember the Lord’s three appearances to fulfill the boon. This indicates that this form is not the principle form. My form is Svayam Bhagavān, parambrahma with human form. My birth (bhava) would not be recognized by another method (anyathā), by appearing with human characteristics and two arms as the secret parabrahman in a human form. Though it is my chief form with either two or four arms, I did not show it first. That this is the chief form is shown in the following verses. Brahmā speaks the following: adyaiva tvad ṛte ’sya kiṁ mama na te māyātvam ādarśitam eko ’si prathamaṁ tato vraja-suhṛd-vatsāḥ samastā api tāvanto ’si catur-bhujās tad akhilaiḥ sākaṁ mayopāsitās tāvanty eva jaganty abhūs tad amitaṁ brahmādvayaṁ śiṣyate Have you not shown me today that both you yourself and everything within this creation are manifestations of your inconceivable potency? First you appeared alone, and then you manifested yourself as all of Vṛndāvana’s calves and cowherd boys, your friends. Next you appeared as an equal number of four-handed Viṣṇu forms, who were worshiped by all living beings, including me, and after that you appeared as an equal number of complete universes. Finally, you have now returned to your unlimited form as the Supreme Absolute Truth, one without a second. SB 10.14.18 Śukadeva speaks: na cāntar na bahir yasya na pūrvaṁ nāpi cāparam pūrvāparaṁ bahiś cāntar jagato yo jagac ca yaḥ The Supreme Lord has no beginning and no end, no exterior and no interior, no front and no rear. In other words, he is all-pervading. Because He is not under the influence of the element of time, for him there is no difference between past, present and future; he exists in his own transcendental form at all times. SB 10.9.13 Śukadeva speaks, with realization of Kṛṣṇa’s sweetness: gopyas tapaḥ kim acaran yad amuṣya rūpaṁ lāvaṇya-sāram asamordhvam ananya-siddham dṛgbhiḥ pibanty anusavābhinavaṁ durāpam ekānta-dhāma yaśasaḥ śrīya aiśvarasya What austerities must the gopīs have performed! With their eyes they always drink the nectar of Kṛṣṇa’s form, which is the essence of loveliness and is not to be equaled or surpassed. That loveliness is the only abode of beauty, fame and opulence. It is self-perfect, ever fresh and extremely rare. SB 10.44.14 The women of Mathurā speak: yan martya-līlaupayikaṁ sva-yoga- māyā-balaṁ darśayatā gṛhītam vismāpanaṁ svasya ca saubhagarddheḥ paraṁ padaṁ bhūṣaṇa-bhūṣaṇāṅgam Kṛṣṇa possesses that form suitable for human pastimes to show the full capacity of his yoga-māyā. That form astonishes even the lord of Vaikuṇṭha. It is the pinnacle of auspicious qualities and enhances the beauty of his ornaments. SB 3.2.12 Uddhava also makes similar statements.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    You would not understand my birth (mad-bhavam). Citsukha explains ahaṁ jāto ‘smīti jṣānaṁ manuṣya-rūpeṇa na syāj janmataḥ: knowledge that I have been born would not arise if I had a human form from birth.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa reveals His Viṣṇu form to confirm He is the Supreme Person, not an ordinary child — devotees recognize Him under every disguise.
    Practical Applications
    • When the mind whispers 'Kṛṣṇa is just a charming village boy,' refuse the demotion and remember: this is the same Lord who showed Devakī His four-armed Viṣṇu form.
    • Notice today where you avajānanti — quietly downgrade the Lord into a symbol, an idea, or 'one path among many' — and correct that drift in your next round of japa.
    • Speak about Kṛṣṇa to one person today as a Person, not a principle, holding the conviction Devakī held: my Lord has personally come.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my sādhana am I quietly demanding that Kṛṣṇa show me a four-armed Viṣṇu form before I will trust Him — refusing to recognize Him in the 'ordinary human child' shape He has actually given me (the holy name, the Deity, the words of the ācārya)?
    • When Kṛṣṇa's dealings in my life feel too human, too coincidental, too unspectacular to be Him — what is the avajānanti māṁ mūḍhā reflex inside me that needs the spectacular before it will bow?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When you post or share something about your sādhana online and get one mocking comment, notice the pull to delete it or soften the next post. That pull is the same fear Devakī had about her neighbors. Choose one place this week — a class discussion, a chat, a story — to keep your conviction visible without arguing about it.
    • In your friend group there is probably one person everyone has quietly reduced to a stereotype ('the religious one,' 'the intense one'). You have done to them what nondevotees do to Kṛṣṇa — flattened a person into a category because of how they appear. Spend one real conversation this week looking past the label.
    • Before an exam or a high-stakes audition, you are tempted to hide that you pray, chant, or offer your work — because peers will think it is a crutch. Do it anyway, privately if needed. Kṛṣṇa showed the four-armed form so the connection to His earlier appearances would not be lost; you offer your effort so the connection to Him is not lost in the pressure.
    householder
    • Your children watch how seriously you treat the deity, the altar, the Bhāgavatam — and they will calibrate their śraddhā to yours. Do not domesticate Kṛṣṇa into 'just a nice family tradition' for their comfort. Let one practice in the home this month be unmistakably reverent — full ārati, full prostration, full attention — so they see Viṣṇu, not just a baby.
    • In a work or money decision this week, you will be tempted to present your reasoning in purely secular terms to a spouse, partner, or colleague because you fear the devotional reasoning will not land. Try the harder thing: name the actual reason. 'I am not taking this contract because the work conflicts with my sādhana' — said plainly, not apologetically.
    • When relatives reduce your guru, your tradition, or Kṛṣṇa to 'one path among many' at the dinner table, you usually let it slide for peace. That is the avajānanti mistake happening at your table. You don't need to argue — but do not nod along either. Silence that looks like agreement teaches your children the wrong thing.
    senior
    • You have lived through enough bodies-within-this-body — child, youth, parent, professional — to know experientially that the self has continued through each. Use this verse's prāg-janma-smaraṇa principle to do the inverse: trace the continuity backward through THIS life as preparation for trusting it across the next transition.
    • Your grandchildren and younger relatives will receive their first impression of Kṛṣṇa from how you, the elder, speak of Him. Do not collapse Him into vague 'God talk' to seem broad-minded. Speak of Him personally — by name, with specifics from līlā you actually know — so the next generation inherits a Person, not an abstraction.
    • As physical capacity narrows, the temptation is to let sādhana also narrow into something private and sentimental. Resist. Keep one practice publicly visible in the household — chanting aloud, offering food, daily Bhāgavatam reading — so that when you depart, those around you remember not a quiet old devotee but a clear witness to Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Person.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating the four-armed Viṣṇu darśana as the 'real' Kṛṣṇa and the human-like form as a lesser concession — inverting the verse, which actually shows that the human-like dealings are the intimate norm and the opulent form is the reminder given for our weak faith.
    • Concluding from 'the Lord deals like a human being' that Kṛṣṇa is therefore one of us — a great soul, an avatar among avatars, a symbol — instead of holding both: fully approachable and fully the Supreme Personality of Godhead.
    • Waiting for a personal four-armed vision before committing to man-manā bhava mad-bhakto, as if surrender required prior proof — when the verse teaches that the proof was given once for the devotee's sake and the practice of remembrance must now proceed on śraddhā, not on spectacle.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Devakī asks Kṛṣṇa to hide His four-armed form because she fears the neighbors will not believe. Where in your own life have you softened or hidden your devotional convictions because you feared others would not believe? Was that protective wisdom, or was it a quiet betrayal of śraddhā? Push back on each other — don't let your partner off easy.
    • Prabhupāda says nondevotees, seeing the Lord act like a human, conclude He IS one of the human beings (avajānanti māṁ mūḍhāḥ). Discuss a concrete moment when YOU made that mistake — reduced Kṛṣṇa, the guru, or a sādhu to merely human because of how they appeared. What did it cost you? Disagree if you think this 'reduction' is sometimes appropriate humility.
    • The verse turns on a paradox: without the four-armed darśana, mad-bhavaṁ jñānaṁ (knowledge of My nature) does not arise through ordinary human appearance. Yet today we have no such darśana — only books, deity, and the holy name. Argue with each other: is our situation harder than Devakī's, or easier? Where do you actually disagree?
    Role Play

    Two students play the scene immediately after this verse. Student A is Devakī, who has just been shown the four-armed Viṣṇu form and asked Kṛṣṇa to become an ordinary child. A neighbor (Student B) walks in the next morning and asks, 'I heard something strange happened in your room last night — were you chanting too loudly again?' Devakī must respond: she knows what she saw, but she also knows the neighbor will dismiss any literal account. Does she tell the truth and accept ridicule? Does she deflect to protect the secret? Does she try to plant a seed without revealing everything? Run the scene twice, swapping roles, then debrief: where in your own life are you 'Devakī the morning after' — holding a conviction nobody around you will accept?

    Objections & Responses
    • This whole verse is just retroactive mythology — the storytellers needed to explain why Kṛṣṇa looked like a normal baby in every other story, so they invented a 'He showed His Viṣṇu form first, then became a child' transition. It is a narrative patch, not a revelation.
      Notice what the objection assumes: that the text is a human composition trying to be internally consistent. The Gauḍīya line receives Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam as Vyāsa's mature revelation, the ripened fruit of the Vedic tree, spoken by Śuka to Parīkṣit at the moment of his death — not a stitched-together folk tradition. But set aside the source-claim for a moment and look at the verse's own logic: Kṛṣṇa Himself names the problem the objector is raising. He says, in effect, 'If I had appeared as an ordinary child, you would not believe.' The verse anticipates the very skepticism the objector now voices about the verse. That is not the structure of a patch; that is the structure of a teaching that knows its audience. Sit with that before dismissing it.
    • Why does an all-powerful God need to convince His own mother by a special effects display? If Devakī is truly His devotee, faith should be enough — the four-armed form is a crutch, and the verse exposes a God who is insecure about being recognized.
      Read the verse alongside the purport. Prabhupāda points out that BOTH parties were anxious — Devakī about the neighbors, Kṛṣṇa about her. This is not insecurity; this is the dealings between devotees and the Lord, where the Lord voluntarily participates in the mood of reciprocation. Kṛṣṇa is not proving Himself; He is meeting Devakī in her vātsalya-bhāva, where she relates to Him as a mother. A mother needs to remember her son across births — that is the concern of the verse (prāg-janma-smaraṇāya). The 'crutch' framing imports a transactional, prove-it-to-me model of faith. The Gauḍīya understanding is that the Lord's appearances and concealments are līlā — loving exchange, not evidence-gathering. The objection mistakes intimacy for inadequacy.
    Analogy

    A teacher reveals to her returning students the full diploma she will award them at the end of the course — not to keep it on display, but so they will trust the curriculum that follows. Bhagavān showed the four-armed Viṣṇu-form to Devakī precisely so she would believe what came next; otherwise, the ordinary infant in her arms could not be recognized as Lord.

    Stories
    Kṛṣṇa showing the Viśvarūpa to Arjuna

    In BG 11, Kṛṣṇa showed Arjuna the cosmic form — but only briefly, then returned to His two-armed Pārtha-sārathi form, the one Arjuna preferred. The display was for credentialing; the relationship was sustained through the ordinary form.

    Devakī's situation is exactly parallel. The four-armed Viṣṇu-form was the credential; the human-child form is the relationship. Aiśvarya establishes who; mādhurya/vātsalya sustains the love. The Bhāgavatam knows this rhythm by heart.

    Important Words
    • putra-bhāvena — with the conception of a son
      Putra (son) + bhāva (mood, conception) + instrumental. The relational mood of parent-toward-child. In rasa-śāstra this is vātsalya-bhāva. Kṛṣṇa is instructing them to PRESERVE the vātsalya, not transcend it. The aiśvarya-knowledge is added, not substituted.
    • brahma-bhāvena — with the conception of Brahman/Supreme
      Brahma (Brahman, Supreme) + bhāva + instrumental. The mood of awareness of His ultimate nature. The verse instructs the simultaneous holding of putra-bhāva and brahma-bhāva — a hallmark of aiśvarya-miśra-bhakti, the bhakti-mood appropriate to Devakī-Vasudeva.
    • asakṛt — constantly, repeatedly
      A- + sakṛt (once). Not 'once' but 'again and again, without intermission'. Continuous remembrance — the standard for nitya-smaraṇa. Bhakti is not occasional; it is the continuous shape of consciousness.
    • kṛta-snehau — having developed affection
      Kṛta (made, having done) + sneha (affection) + dual. Sneha is the foundational bhāva of vātsalya in rasa-śāstra. Kṛṣṇa says: develop and maintain sneha; do not retreat into bare cognition. Affection IS the path, not its bypass.
    • mat-gatim-parām — My supreme abode
      Mat (My) + gati (destination, attainment) + parām (supreme). Echoes BG 8.21 — paramāṁ gatim. The 'supreme destination' in Gauḍīya theology is not Brahman but Goloka Vṛndāvana, the personal abode of Kṛṣṇa. Reached through eternal seva, not through merging.
    Both of you, husband and wife, constantly think of Me as your son, but always know that I am the Supreme Personality of Godhead. By thus thinking of Me constantly with love and affection, you will achieve the highest perfection: returning home, back to Godhead.
    Purport

    This instruction by the Supreme Personality of Godhead to His father and mother, who are eternally connected with Him, is especially intended for persons eager to return home, back to Godhead. One should never think of the Supreme Personality of Godhead as an ordinary human being, as nondevotees do. Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, personally appeared and left His instructions for the benefit of all human society, but fools and rascals unfortunately think of Him as an ordinary human being and twist the instructions of Bhagavad-gītā for the satisfaction of their senses. Practically everyone commenting on Bhagavad-gītā interprets it for sense gratification. It has become especially fashionable for modern scholars and politicians to interpret Bhagavad-gītā as if it were something fictitious, and by their wrong interpretations they are spoiling their own careers and the careers of others. The Kṛṣṇa consciousness movement, however, is fighting against this principle of regarding Kṛṣṇa as a fictitious person and of accepting that there was no Battle of Kurukṣetra, that everything is symbolic, and that nothing in Bhagavad-gītā is true. In any case, if one truly wants to be successful, one can do so by reading the text of Bhagavad-gītā as it is. Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu especially stressed the instructions of Bhagavad-gītā: yāre dekha, tāre kaha ‘kṛṣṇa’-upadeśa. If one wants to achieve the highest success in life, one must accept Bhagavad-gītā as spoken by the Supreme Lord. By accepting Bhagavad-gītā in this way, all of human society can become perfect and happy. It is to be noted that because Vasudeva and Devakī would be separated from Kṛṣṇa when He was carried to Gokula, the residence of Nanda Mahārāja, the Lord personally instructed them that they should always think of Him as their son and as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. That would keep them in touch with Him. After eleven years, the Lord would return to Mathurā to be their son, and therefore there was no question of separation.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Both of you, husband and wife, constantly think of Me as your son, but always know that I am the Supreme Personality of Godhead. By thus thinking of Me constantly with love and affection, you will achieve the highest perfection: returning home, back to Godhead.
    Commentary

    In the scriptures indicating worship of Krsna through mantras, Vasudeva is mentioned as the father of Krsna. Therefore this shows without doubt that Vasudeva is eternally in that position. But in order to increase their bliss by promising perfection of their sadhana in this birth, their nitya siddha status is hidden in this verse. "By thinking of me you will attain me." The actual meaning of the verse however is: "I will now go to my most excellent eternal dhama Gokula. After eleven years, I will return to Mathura and you will attain me there at that time. But now I will be separated from you."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The word vā (instead of ca) can mean a comparison or an alternative. You developed affection for me as Bhagavān in my svarūpa or as the chief entity Brahman because I am the greatest, and you continuously meditated upon me. The two moods are seen as equal just to glorify Brahman. They would go to Vaikuṇṭha along with Kaśyapa and Aditi who had similar qualification. Śrīdhara Svāmī comments as follows. “If you were pleased with them, why should they take another birth?” This verse answers that they will not take birth in the future. Or it can be explained that the two should not be considered sādhakas and thus there should not be any worry about not attaining the Lord. In the Padma Purāṇa, Kārtika-māhātmya, it says ete hi yādavāḥ sarve mad gaṇā eva bhāvini: O Pārvatī, all the Yadus are my eternal relatives. Padma Purāṇa, Uttara-khaṇḍa says: yathā saumitra-bharatau yathā saṅkarsaṇādayaḥ tathā tenaiva jāyante nija-lokād yadrcchayā punas tenaiva gacchanti tat padaṁ śāśvataṁ param na karma bandhanaṁ janma vaiṣnavānām ca vidyate Like Rāma’s brothers or Balarāma, the Yādavas appear with the Lord from the Lord’s planet by his will and again go to his eternal abode with him. They are not bound by karma and do not take birth. Such statements are also found in books concerning Kṛṣṇa’s worship, celebration of his birth and his mantra. Their appearance now in their original forms and in their expansions in previous births is only a pastime to preach the worship of the Lord with intense prema by showing their prema, which was intense as that of the Lord. In being born as Pṛśni or Aditi, their attainment of the Lord is not a matter of special sādhana. Rather Devakī attained the Lord as previously by her very nature. That is expressed in the verse. You meditated upon me with a special parental love (putra) and with expectation that I would specially appear (bhāvena), or with ordinary love and with expectations of an ordinary appearance (brahma-bhāvena). The word vā indicates an alternative. The comparison is made in the following verses. pitarau nānvavindetāṁ kṛṣṇodārārbhakehitam Although Kṛṣṇa was so pleased with Vasudeva and Devakī that he descended as their son, they could not enjoy Kṛṣṇa’s magnanimous childhood pastimes. SB 10.8.47 pitarāv upalabdhārthau viditvā puruṣottamaḥ mā bhūd iti nijāṁ māyā tatāna jana-mohinīm Understanding that his parents were becoming aware of his powers as God, he thought that this should not be allowed to happen. Thus he expanded his Yogamāyā, which bewilders his devotees. SB 10.45.1 aho bhāgyam aho bhāgyaṁ nanda-gopa-vrajaukasām yan-mitraṁ paramānandaṁ pūrṇaṁ brahma sanātanam How greatly fortunate are Nanda Mahārāja, the cowherd men and all the other inhabitants of Vrajabhūmi! There is no limit to their good fortune, because the Absolute Truth, the source of transcendental bliss, the eternal Supreme Brahman, has become their friend. SB 10.14.32 itthaṁ satāṁ brahma-sukhānubhūtyā dāsyaṁ gatānāṁ para-daivatena māyāśritānāṁ nara-dārakeṇa sākaṁ vijahruḥ kṛta-puṇya-puṣjāḥ In this way, all the cowherd boys used to play with Kṛṣṇa, who is the source of the Brahman effulgence for jṣānīs desiring to merge into that effulgence, who is the Supreme Lord for devotees who have accepted eternal servitorship, and who for ordinary persons is but another ordinary child. The cowherd boys, having accumulated the results of pious activities for many lives, were able to associate in this way with the Lord. How can one explain their great fortune? SB 10.12.11 Seeing Kṛṣṇa as their son comes first as the main method, and thinking of him as great is a secondary method. Or they meditated only once on the Lord as great (taking the words as vā and sakṛt rather than vā and asakṛt). The word vā can indicate that it may have been possible that they meditated once on Brahman. Later you will go from the pastimes on earth to my abode with the aprakaṭa pastimes. You do not have to depend on sādhana. Doing sādhana would interfere with what is to be accomplished by you as my assistants. The reason is given. You have eternally perfect affection (kṛta-snehau). You two have prema filled with affection for me as a son. It is your nature in the manner of ātmā pahata-pāpmā: the soul is without sin in the liberated state. (Chandogya Upaniṣad 8.1.5) Or, you meditated on me as your son with affection and maybe once meditated on Brahman.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    You think of me as your son, who is Brahman. They are expressed as equivalents, to point out the greatness of the object of affection. You think of me constantly. This indicates their bhāva. Or the word vā (instead of ca) indicates a comparison. You think of me constantly as a son, just as others think of Brahman. The word vā can also indicate the inferiority of Brahman. Being affectionate you two will attain my most attractive (parām) place of attainment (gatim), Vaikuṇṭha. Or you will attain the goal from me (mat). This indicates they will attain it easily, by his mercy. Or you think of me as a son constantly, since it is full of affectionate rasa, and you thought of me of Brahman only once (vā sakṛt), since it is without rasa. Why? It is because, by your affection for me, it is impossible for you to have any obstacles in attaining me. He praises them to pacify them and glorify them, since they suffered in previous births. Though Aditi and Kaśyapa will attain the highest goal after being qualified, they attained it as your expansions. Now you will attain the goal, without another birth. Or Vasudeva and Devakī are eternal associates in Vaikuṇṭha whereas Aditi and Kaśyapa are expansions. tvam eva pūrva-sarge ’bhūḥ pṛśniḥ svāyambhuve sati tadāyaṁ sutapā nāma prajāpatir akalmaṣaḥ The Supreme Lord replied: My dear mother, best of the chaste, in your previous birth, in the Svāyambhuva millennium, you were known as Pṛśni, and Vasudeva, who was the most pious Prajāpati, was named Sutapā. SB 10.3.32 You two attain my abode now. Kaśyapa and Aditi, after being qualified, will attain it. This is understood according to Bhāgavatāmṛta. Or you will attain me as the goal (mad-gatim), by thinking of me as your son.

    Personal Guidance
    Hold Kṛṣṇa close as your own — as son, friend, beloved — while never forgetting He is the Supreme Personality of Godhead; that doubled remembrance carries you home.
    Practical Applications
    • Choose one intimate relationship in your life today and silently offer that affection to Kṛṣṇa, addressing Him by a personal name while bowing inwardly to His supremacy.
    • Refuse, when you read Bhagavad-gītā or hear Kṛṣṇa's name today, to reduce Him to a symbol, archetype, or 'inner self' — speak of Him as a Person to a fellow student or family member.
    • Set a fixed moment morning and night to think of Kṛṣṇa with kṛta-sneha — cultivated affection — and seal it with the conviction, 'You are my Lord, and I am Yours.'
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I treating Kṛṣṇa as merely a sweet, near presence (like a son or friend) while quietly forgetting He is the Supreme Personality of Godhead — and where am I doing the reverse, holding Him at a distance as 'the Absolute' to avoid the intimacy of personal love?
    • If physical separation from Kṛṣṇa did not break Vasudeva and Devakī's connection because they kept Him constantly in mind with sneha, what is the actual quality of my own remembrance of Him across an ordinary day — and what would have to change for that remembrance to be unbroken?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Pick one person you actually live with — a parent, sibling, roommate — and for one week practice seeing them in two layers at once: the everyday person who annoys or comforts you, AND an eternal soul. Notice which layer you drop first when you are tired or scrolling.
    • Audit your feed today: which accounts treat Kṛṣṇa, the Gītā, or 'spirituality' as aesthetic content or self-improvement fuel — divine spark, vibes, energy — rather than as Kṛṣṇa the Person? Mute or unfollow three. Replace with one source that keeps Kṛṣṇa personal.
    • Before your next exam or interview, take ninety seconds to think of Kṛṣṇa with affection — not as a lucky charm, not as 'the universe,' but as a person you are reporting to. Write down afterwards whether the quality of your effort changed.
    householder
    • Tonight at dinner, name Kṛṣṇa out loud once in front of your children — not as a lesson, just as the One whose prasāda you are receiving. Vasudeva and Devakī were told to think of Him as son; you are training your children to think of Him as Lord inside ordinary family life.
    • Take one financial decision pending this week — a purchase, an investment, a gift, a donation — and run it past two filters in writing: does it serve my family's bodily comfort only, or does it also serve their connection to Kṛṣṇa? Decide accordingly, even if the answer costs you.
    • Identify the relative or colleague you most often think of with resentment or anxiety. For seven days, every time their face arises in your mind, deliberately offer that thought to Kṛṣṇa before continuing. Watch what changes — in them, and more honestly, in you.
    senior
    • Vasudeva and Devakī endured eleven years of physical separation from Kṛṣṇa and were taught to stay in touch through constant loving remembrance. Treat this stage of life as your eleven years: choose one fixed daily time when you sit and think of Kṛṣṇa as a person you love, not as a concept you affirm.
    • Make a written list of three attachments — possessions, roles, grievances, or even spiritual reputations — that you are still gripping as 'mine.' Beside each, write the date by which you intend to hand it over. Loosening now is how the dhīra prepares; waiting for the body to force it is how the bewildered are caught.
    • Mentor one younger person this month — child, grandchild, junior colleague, neighbor — not by giving advice about life, but by telling them one specific thing about Kṛṣṇa that you have come to trust through your own years. Personal, not generic. That is your legacy, and it is also your sādhana.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Sentimentalizing the vātsalya mood — relishing the idea of Kṛṣṇa as a charming child while dropping the 'brahma-bhāvena' half of the verse, so the relationship becomes affectionate fantasy rather than worship of the Supreme Person.
    • Swinging to the opposite error — meditating on Kṛṣṇa only as the all-pervading Absolute and treating personal, loving remembrance (kṛta-snehau) as a lower or optional sentiment, when the verse explicitly fuses both as the path to mad-gatiṁ parām.
    • Assuming this instruction is reserved for exalted devotees like Vasudeva and Devakī and therefore not applicable to one's own sādhana, when Prabhupāda explicitly says it is 'especially intended for persons eager to return home, back to Godhead' — i.e., for me, today.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Vasudeva and Devakī are told to hold two truths at once: Kṛṣṇa is our son, and Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Personality of Godhead. In your own life — with a parent, child, spouse, or guru — where do you find it hardest to hold the personal relationship and the spiritual reality together without one collapsing the other? Push past the polite answer in your pair.
    • The purport says modern interpreters 'twist' Bhagavad-gītā for sense gratification. Bring an actual example you have heard (in a book, podcast, class, or your own past reading) of Kṛṣṇa being treated as fictitious or symbolic. Disagree with each other if you must — does the Kṛṣṇa-conscious objection to that reading feel honest to you, or does it feel like gate-keeping?
    • Kṛṣṇa was physically separated from Vasudeva and Devakī for eleven years, yet the verse says constant loving thought of Him as son AND as Bhagavān keeps them in touch. Where in your life are you tolerating physical separation (from a teacher, deity, family, saṅga) by substituting mere memory or sentiment, and where is real cintayantau kṛta-snehau actually happening? Be specific with your partner — no abstractions.
    Role Play

    Two students pair up. Student A plays a college roommate who has just returned from a 'philosophy of religion' seminar and announces: 'My professor proved the Kurukṣetra war never happened — Kṛṣṇa is a literary device, the chariot is the body, the war is inner conflict. It is all symbolic, and frankly more sophisticated that way.' Student B plays a Gauḍīya practitioner who has been reading SB 10.3.45 and its purport that morning. Student B must respond without becoming defensive or scholastic — drawing on the personalist conviction of the verse (Kṛṣṇa as actual son of Vasudeva and Devakī, actual Supreme Personality of Godhead) and the purport's warning about twisting the Gītā for sense gratification. After five minutes, switch roles. Then debrief together: where did the conversation slip into impersonalism? Where did it become preachy? What would 'yāre dekha, tāre kaha kṛṣṇa-upadeśa' actually sound like in a dorm room?

    Objections & Responses
    • Telling Vasudeva and Devakī to 'always know I am the Supreme Personality of Godhead' undermines the parental love. If they have to keep reminding themselves He is God, the affection becomes performative — a doctrine pasted onto a relationship. Surely pure parental love would be enough?
      In Gauḍīya understanding it is exactly the reverse. Vatsalya-rasa, parental love for Kṛṣṇa, is not diminished by knowing He is Bhagavān — it is protected by it. Without that knowledge, the love slides into ordinary sentiment, the kind that ends with the body. Vasudeva and Devakī are not being asked to oscillate coldly between 'son' and 'God'; they are being given the dual vision that keeps their snehā eternal rather than mortal. Caitanya Mahāprabhu's tradition guards both poles: full personal intimacy and full theological clarity. Drop either, and the relationship deflates — into impersonalism on one side, or sentimentalism on the other.
    • This verse and its purport seem narrow and exclusivist — Prabhupāda calls scholars 'fools and rascals,' insists on one reading of the Gītā, dismisses symbolic interpretations. Is that not the same fundamentalism we criticize elsewhere?
      Notice what is actually being defended. The purport is not dismissing inquiry; it is refusing a specific move — the move that empties Kṛṣṇa of personhood so the interpreter can keep his own sense gratification intact. A Gauḍīya teacher would say: read every commentator you like, study every angle, but do not pretend that calling Kṛṣṇa 'symbolic' is neutral scholarship. It is a theological claim, and it happens to be the one that lets the reader off the hook of surrender. The strong language in the purport is not tribal scorn; it is the alarm of someone who has watched students lose Kṛṣṇa to clever readings. Test the claim by its fruit: does the symbolic reading produce people who can love Kṛṣṇa as son and as Bhagavān, separated for eleven years and still in unbroken touch? If not, the question answers itself.
    Analogy

    A mother who knows her son is a great scholar still calls him to lunch, scolds him for forgetting his sweater, frets when he sleeps too late. The knowledge does not collapse the relationship; the relationship metabolizes the knowledge. Kṛṣṇa instructs Devakī and Vasudeva to hold both — putra-bhāva and brahma-bhāva — at once. The two together produce the highest perfection.

    Stories
    Yaśodā's vātsalya knowing-yet-not-knowing

    In SB 10.7–9, Yaśodā repeatedly encounters Kṛṣṇa's divinity — sees the universe in His mouth, fails to bind Him with the rope — and each time her mind reverts to vātsalya, the divinity-knowledge softened by yoga-māyā back into mother-love.

    Kṛṣṇa here in verse 45 instructs Devakī to keep BOTH lenses — putra and brahma — without one erasing the other. Devakī-Vasudeva are aiśvarya-jñāna-yukta-bhakti; Yaśodā-Nanda are pure mādhurya without aiśvarya. Bhāgavatam validates both, but assigns each to its proper couple.

    Important Words
    • tūṣṇīm — silent
      Adverb — silently, quietly. The pause after instruction. In Vaiṣṇava narrative, Bhagavān's silences are themselves significant — the space in which He transitions between modes of self-revelation. Tūṣṇīm here is the seam between aiśvarya-darśana and vātsalya-līlā.
    • hariḥ — Hari, the remover (of sins, hearts)
      Hari — from √hṛ (to take away). One of Bhagavān's principal names. He takes away inauspiciousness, takes away the hearts of those who see Him. In Caitanya tradition Hari-nāma is the yuga-dharma. Subtle: this is the moment Hari WITHDRAWS His own aiśvarya — turning the verb back on Himself.
    • ātma-māyayā — by His own internal energy
      Ātmā (own) + māyā. The same yoga-māyā / svarūpa-śakti that arranges all līlā. The transformation from aiśvarya-form to infant is not material; it is svarūpa-śakti's work. Distinguish from the bahiraṅga-māyā that deludes the jīva.
    • prākṛtaḥ-śiśuḥ — an ordinary-seeming child
      Prākṛta (natural, ordinary, of prakṛti) + śiśu (infant). He appears prākṛta — but Prabhupāda emphasizes that He is ALWAYS aprākṛta in essence. The 'prākṛta-ness' is concession to līlā-frame, not change in svarūpa. Crucial against Māyāvāda misreading: His ordinary form is not less than His extraordinary form; both are full Bhagavān.
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: After thus instructing His father and mother, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Kṛṣṇa, remained silent. In their presence, by His internal energy, He then transformed Himself into a small human child. [In other words, He transformed Himself into His original form: kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam.]
    Purport

    As stated in Bhagavad-gītā (4.6) , sambhavāmy ātma-māyayā: whatever is done by the Supreme Personality of Godhead is done by His spiritual energy; nothing is forced upon Him by the material energy. This is the difference between the Lord and an ordinary living being. The Vedas say: parāsya śaktir vividhaiva śrūyate svābhāvikī jñāna-bala-kriyā ca ( Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8) It is natural for the Lord to be untinged by material qualities, and because everything is perfectly present in His spiritual energy, as soon as He desires something, it is immediately done. The Lord is not a prākṛta-śiśu, a child of this world, but by His personal energy He appeared like one. Ordinary people may have difficulty accepting the supreme controller, God, as a human being because they forget that He can do everything by spiritual energy ( ātma-māyayā ). Nonbelievers say, “How can the supreme controller descend as an ordinary being?” This sort of thinking is materialistic. Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī says that unless we accept the energy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead as inconceivable, beyond the conception of our words and mind, we cannot understand the Supreme Lord. Those who doubt that the Supreme Personality of Godhead can come as a human being and turn Himself into a human child are fools who think that Kṛṣṇa’s body is material, that He is born and that He therefore also dies. In Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, Third Canto, Fourth Chapter, verses 28 and 29, there is a description of Kṛṣṇa’s leaving His body. Mahārāja Parīkṣit inquired from Śukadeva Gosvāmī, “When all the members of the Yadu dynasty met their end, Kṛṣṇa also put an end to Himself, and the only member of the family who remained alive was Uddhava. How was this possible?” Śukadeva Gosvāmī answered that Kṛṣṇa, by His own energy, destroyed the entire family and then thought of making His own body disappear. In this connection, Śukadeva Gosvāmī described how the Lord gave up His body. But this was not the destruction of Kṛṣṇa’s body; rather, it was the disappearance of the Supreme Lord by His personal energy. Actually, the Lord does not give up His body, which is eternal, but as He can change His body from the form of Viṣṇu to that of an ordinary human child, He can change His body to any form He likes. This does not mean that He gives up His body. By spiritual energy, the Lord can appear in a body made of wood or stone. He can change His body into anything because everything is His energy ( parāsya śaktir vividhaiva śrūyate ). As clearly said in Bhagavad-gītā (7.4) , bhinnā prakṛtir aṣṭadhā: the material elements are separated energies of the Supreme Lord. If He transforms Himself into the arcā-mūrti, the worshipable Deity, which we see as stone or wood, He is still Kṛṣṇa. Therefore the śāstra warns, arcye viṣṇau śilā-dhīr guruṣu nara-matiḥ. One who thinks that the worshipable Deity in the temple is made of wood or stone, one who sees a Vaiṣṇava guru as an ordinary human being, or one who materially conceives of a Vaiṣṇava as belonging to a particular caste is nārakī, a resident of hell. The Supreme Personality of Godhead can appear before us in many forms, as He likes, but we must know the true facts: janma karma ca me divyam evaṁ yo vetti tattvataḥ ( Bg. 4.9 ). By following the instructions of sādhu, guru and śāstra — the saintly persons, the spiritual master and the authoritative scriptures — one can understand Kṛṣṇa, and then one makes his life successful by returning home, back to Godhead.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: After thus instructing His father and mother, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Kṛṣṇa, remained silent. In their presence, by His internal energy, He then transformed Himself into a small human child. [In other words, He transformed Himself into His original form: kṛṣṇas tu bhagavān svayam [SB 1.3.28].
    Commentary

    According to the Maha Samhita, atma mayaya means "by ones own free will." Babhuva prakrtah sisuh here means that he became, not a material baby, but his eternally perfect form as a baby. Prakrta means prakrti, svarupa and svabhava. In referring to great souls on earth, they are called prakrti siddha. Thus the word here means svabhava or svarupa. It cannot mean material in this context because there are statements like the following which contradict this. Na cantar na bahir yasya... in this statement it is clear that He who mother Yasoda bound up was like a material (prakrta mata) child, but actually he wasn’t prakrta, he was aprakrta, spiritual. Therefore the Lord showed his original spiritual form as a human-like baby.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Then what happened? After saying this (iti), preparing to withdraw (hari—to take away) and hide his four armed form, the Lord became silent. While his parents watched, without others being given this opportunity, Bhagavān, endowed with six qualities, by his own śakti of knowledge (ātmā-māyayā), his śakti of excellent intelligence, he became a normal child. According to Trikāṇḍa-śeṣa, māyā means illusion or intelligence. Nirghaṇṭu says māyā means knowledge. Or it can mean desire according to Mahā-saṁhitā. ātmā-māyā tad icchā syat guṇa-māyā jaḍātmikā: māyā means desire or matter made of guṇas, without consciousness. According to Viśva-koṣa, māyā means deceit or mercy. Thus by my desire or by my mercy I manifested the state of a baby. The word prākrṭaḥ means “as if material” by taking a secondary interpretation. Or prākrṭaḥ can mean natural, not something newly created. Prakrti can mean svarūpa or svabhāva. The usage is found in a sentence like prakṛti-siddham idaṁ hi mahātma: the great soul has a perfected nature. Thus the Lord manifested the form of a baby who was svabhāva-siddha, perfect by his very nature. In the statement babandha prākrtaṁ yatha: Yaśodā bound Kṛṣṇa as if he were an ordinary child (SB 10.9.14) Kṛṣṇa is shown to be non-material by comparing him to a material child. Kṛṣṇa, revealing his desired pastimes, is always the abode of all śaktis. By those śaktis he shows pastimes desired by his devotees. To accomplish this, they should all be qualified. Thus they are all svabhāva-siddha. Garga will say bahūni santi nāmāni rūpāṇi ca sutasya te: for this son of yours there are many forms and names. (SB 10.8.15)

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    By his special śakti made of eternity, knowledge and bliss equal to himself (ātma-māyayā) or by his mercy, he became a baby--someone having a baby nature (prākṛtaḥ) or having an attractive form with two arms, newly born (śiśuḥ). He was attractive to the mind (hariḥ) and most beautiful (bhagavān). His weapons disappeared and he had an umbilical cord. Otherwise the people of Gokula would be astonished and Nanda would not have given charity to counteract the impurity. He became a baby quickly, while his parents looked on. Or he showed the most astonishing power of his māyā, and thus the parents stared. Or by seeing that event with their vision, they saw everything with affection. With their other vision they had seen the four armed form. Arjuna and Nārada see the four armed form. That is seen in the Gītā when Kṛṣṇa reveals the universal form. Or the two watched, anticipating the baby form. Some persons say that Kṛṣṇa was first born with two arms. To make his parents understand about his birth he then displayed four arms. This form is thus called astonishing (adbhūtam). Later he again returned to his natural form as a baby as when he was born.

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa is never a prākṛta-śiśu — He chooses His form by ātma-māyā; honor Him as svayaṁ bhagavān, not a material child.
    Practical Applications
    • Today, when you bow before the arcā-mūrti, refuse the thought 'this is stone or wood' — address Kṛṣṇa directly, by name, as the same Person who became the child of Vasudeva and Devakī.
    • Notice one moment when you reduce Kṛṣṇa, guru, or a Vaiṣṇava to their material covering, and immediately correct the vision by recalling janma karma ca me divyam.
    • Spend five minutes meditating on ātma-māyayā — that whatever Kṛṣṇa does flows from His own spiritual energy — and offer one task today with that same posture of inner, not forced, action.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life do I quietly insist that Kṛṣṇa must conform to my human categories — and what would it cost my pride to admit His ātma-māyā is beyond my mind's reach?
    • When I bow before the arcā-mūrti or hear of Kṛṣṇa as a small child in Vasudeva's arms, what part of me secretly thinks 'this is only stone' or 'only a baby' — and how does that doubt show up in how I treat guru and Vaiṣṇavas?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice how often you judge a classmate or professor by their 'packaging' — the brand they wear, the accent they speak in, the Instagram they post. That is exactly the materialist error the purport names: śilā-dhīr in social form. Today, pick one person you have written off by appearance and have a real conversation with them.
    • Before exams or interviews, you will be tempted to think 'I am the doer; my prep determines the result.' SB 10.3.46 shows even Kṛṣṇa's appearance as a child is by ātma-māyā, not material cause. Offer your study session at the start: 'Kṛṣṇa, the energy to do this is Yours.' Then study harder than before — not less.
    • On social media you constantly perform a 'self' that is not quite you. The Lord can take any form by His own energy and remain Himself; you take one form and lose yourself. This week, post nothing for three days, and write down what you wanted to perform and why. Bring that to your next class discussion.
    householder
    • Your children watch how you treat the Deity at home and how you treat the pūjārī, the guru, and visiting Vaiṣṇavas. They are learning the arcye viṣṇau śilā-dhīr lesson silently from you. This week, do one act of Deity service or guru-sevā where your child is present and can ask questions afterward.
    • In family financial decisions, you are constantly tempted to reduce people to their material category — this in-law's caste, that colleague's salary bracket, this neighbor's community. Catch yourself once this week mid-calculation, and consciously re-see that person as an eternal soul whom Kṛṣṇa is also reaching toward. Then make the decision again.
    • When your spouse or aging parent's body changes — illness, weight, memory, energy — you feel the pull to identify them with that body. Remember Kṛṣṇa changing form by ātma-māyā while remaining Himself: the soul of your loved one is unchanged. Sit with them today for fifteen minutes with no agenda, looking past the body.
    senior
    • You are watching your own body change in ways you cannot reverse. The Lord changes form at will and is never diminished; you change form unwillingly and feel diminished. The difference is ownership, not change itself. Spend time daily with the verse janma karma ca me divyam — let the contrast of His divya birth with your forced one sharpen your vairāgya rather than your self-pity.
    • Mentor a younger practitioner this season specifically on this point: Kṛṣṇa is a person, not an impersonal Absolute, and the arcā-vigraha is Him, not a symbol of Him. You have decades of hearing this; the youth around you are surrounded by impersonalist drift. Your testimony, not your argument, is what will land.
    • As you loosen attachments to property, position, and even family role, do not loosen attachment to sādhu, guru, and śāstra — those three are precisely how the Lord is staying close to you in this stage. Renew one of them this month: re-read a Prabhupāda purport you marked years ago, write a letter to your guru, or visit a Vaiṣṇava you have not seen in too long.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating Kṛṣṇa's appearance as a 'prākṛta-śiśu' as though He underwent a real material transformation — collapsing ātma-māyā (His spiritual energy) into mahā-māyā (the material energy), and thereby reducing Him to one more conditioned being.
    • Demanding that the Lord's pastimes be intellectually 'explainable' before granting them faith — forgetting Jīva Gosvāmī's warning that without accepting acintya-śakti, the Supreme cannot be understood at all.
    • Applying the verse's lesson abstractly ('God can do anything') while still committing the very offense the purport names — seeing the Deity as wood or stone, the guru as an ordinary man, or a Vaiṣṇava through caste-vision — and missing that this is the nārakī mentality the verse is meant to dissolve.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Kṛṣṇa transforms Himself into a 'prākṛta-śiśu' by ātma-māyā, yet Prabhupāda insists His body is never material. In your own words, where is the line between 'appears as' and 'is'? Share with your partner one place in your own life where you confuse the appearance of something spiritual with its substance — and where your partner might disagree with how you drew that line.
    • The purport says one who sees the arcā-mūrti as stone, or the guru as an ordinary man, is nārakī — a resident of hell. That is severe language. Discuss honestly: have you ever caught yourself making one of those three calculations (Deity-as-stone, guru-as-man, Vaiṣṇava-as-caste)? What pulled you back, or what kept you stuck? Push your partner if their answer sounds too clean.
    • Jīva Gosvāmī says we cannot understand the Lord unless we accept His energy as acintya — inconceivable. Modern education trains us to refuse anything inconceivable. Where is the actual point of friction for you: is it intellectual pride, fear of being fooled, or something else? Disagree productively if your partner names a different friction than yours.
    Role Play

    Two students sit in a temple room before the arcā-mūrti. Student A has just brought a college friend, Student B, to darśana for the first time. Walking out, Student B says, 'Look, I respect your tradition, but that's a marble statue. You bow, you offer food, you dress it — it's beautiful theater, but you and I both know it's stone.' The teacher assigns Student A to respond — not by quoting verses at Student B, but by drawing on SB 10.3.46: Kṛṣṇa, by ātma-māyā, became what looked like an ordinary human child in front of Vasudeva and Devakī; the same personal energy makes Him present in arcā-vigraha. Student A must speak as a fellow practitioner, not a debater, and must address the warning 'arcye viṣṇau śilā-dhīr… nārakī saḥ' without sounding like a threat. After three minutes, switch roles. Then debrief: where did the conversation actually shift, and where did it stay stuck?

    Objections & Responses
    • This is just mythology dressing up an obvious contradiction. If Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme controller, why does He need to 'transform' into a child at all? The whole 'ātma-māyā' move sounds like a theological loophole to protect the doctrine from the awkward fact that He looks like an ordinary baby.
      The verse is not patching a contradiction; it is naming the very point a materialist will miss. An ordinary being is forced into a body by karma — Kṛṣṇa enters a form by His own will, sambhavāmy ātma-māyayā. That is the whole difference. Calling it a 'loophole' presumes the default state is materiality and divinity is the exception that needs explaining. The Vedic position is the opposite: spiritual energy is primary, matter is its separated expression (bhinnā prakṛtir aṣṭadhā). What looks like a contradiction to us is only the strain of fitting an acintya reality into our small categories. Jīva Gosvāmī's whole point: drop the demand that everything be conceivable to your mind, and the 'contradiction' dissolves.
    • Even granting the philosophy, the warning that someone who sees the Deity as stone is 'a resident of hell' is exactly the kind of fear-based religion modern people are walking away from. Can't we keep the beautiful parts and lose the threats?
      Hear what the śāstra is actually doing. It is not threatening — it is diagnosing. If you genuinely treat the arcā-mūrti as stone, the guru as an ordinary man, and a Vaiṣṇava as a caste-member, you have already cut yourself off from the only channels through which Kṛṣṇa is reaching toward you in this age. That self-inflicted cut is the 'hell' — not a punishment imposed from outside, but the natural consequence of refusing the medicine. A doctor who says 'if you keep drinking, your liver will fail' is not being fear-based; he is being honest. Soften the language and you also soften the seriousness of what is at stake — your own return home, back to Godhead. The Gauḍīya teacher does not deliver this warning to scare; he delivers it because he loves you enough not to flatter you.
    Analogy

    A king who has shown his royal robes to convince a witness then steps behind a screen and reappears in traveler's clothes — same person, different presentation. Kṛṣṇa, having instructed His parents, falls silent and becomes the ordinary infant. Aiśvarya was displayed for sambandha; mādhurya now begins for līlā.

    Stories
    Kṛṣṇa's transition into Vraja-līlā

    From this verse forward — the descent into ordinary infanthood — the entire rest of Canto 10 unfolds. The Vraja-līlā that begins in chapter 8 (Yaśodā's vātsalya, the butter-thefts, the killing of demons sent by Kaṁsa, the rāsa-līlā) all begins in the silence of this moment.

    The Gauḍīya line treasures verse 46 as the entry-point to mādhurya-leaning līlā. Bhagavān folds away the catuḥ-bhuja credential and chooses dvi-bhuja sweetness. From here it is the cowherd boy's story, and the Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana would unpack every moment that follows.

    Important Words
    • bhagavat-pracoditaḥ — inspired by the Supreme Lord
      Bhagavat (Bhagavān) + pracodita (impelled). Vasudeva does not act on his own initiative — Bhagavān prompts him from within. Sambandha at work: the bhakta's action is the Lord's prompting; the Lord's prompting is the bhakta's action.
    • ajā — the unborn (śakti, also 'goat'/'mother nature')
      Ajā — unborn (feminine of aja). Same root as ajane in 1-5. Yoga-māyā is unborn in svarūpa, like Bhagavān, and her 'birth' to Yaśodā is appearance, not generation. The Sanskrit doubles the term back on Bhagavān's own ajatva.
    • yoga-māyā — Yoga-māyā, the orchestrating energy
      Yoga (union, joining) + māyā. The internal energy that 'joins' the līlā together — keeps the curtain on aiśvarya, arranges meetings, harmonizes events. Distinguish carefully from mahā-māyā (the external deluding energy). Yoga-māyā serves bhakti; mahā-māyā binds the bound.
    • nanda-jāyayā — by Nanda's wife (Yaśodā)
      Nanda + jāyā (wife) + instrumental. Yaśodā is identified by her relation to Nanda — preserving the marital sambandha. Yoga-māyā chose to take her birth specifically from Yaśodā, not from any other queen — establishing her enduring residence in Vraja from the start.
    Thereafter, exactly when Vasudeva, being inspired by the Supreme Personality of Godhead, was about to take the newborn child from the delivery room, Yoga-māyā, the Lord’s spiritual energy, took birth as the daughter of the wife of Mahārāja Nanda.
    Purport

    Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura discusses that Kṛṣṇa appeared simultaneously as the son of Devakī and as the son of Yaśodā, along with the spiritual energy Yoga-māyā. As the son of Devakī, He first appeared as Viṣṇu, and because Vasudeva was not in the position of pure affection for Kṛṣṇa, Vasudeva worshiped his son as Lord Viṣṇu. Yaśodā, however, pleased her son Kṛṣṇa without understanding His Godhood. This is the difference between Kṛṣṇa as the son of Yaśodā and as the son of Devakī. This is explained by Viśvanātha Cakravartī on the authority of Hari-vaṁśa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Thereafter, exactly when Vasudeva, being inspired by the Supreme Personality of Godhead, was about to take the newborn child from the delivery room, Yogamāyā, the Lord's spiritual energy, took birth as the daughter of the wife of Mahārāja Nanda.
    Commentary

    He was instructed by the Lord "If you are afraid, then take me to Gokula and bring the child of Yasoda, my maya, back here. " After being instructed, Vasudeva saw that his chains automatically were loosened. When he developed the desire to depart to Gokula, Maya took her birth through Yasoda. In the Hari Vamsa it says that in the eighth month of incomplete pregnancy Devaki and Yasoda gave birth at the same time to their children. But here in Bhagavatam it is stated that Yasoda gave birth after Devaki. How to correlate the two contradictory statements? Exactly when Devaki gave birth to Krsna, Yasoda also gave birth to Krsna. After that, as described in this verse, Yasoda gave birth to Yogamaya. Yasoda gave birth to two children at different times. This is confirmed in text 10.4.9, for when Yogamaya falls from the hands of Kamsa, she is called the younger sister of Krsna. But when Krsna was born to Yasoda it is not stated that he had four hands. It is understood that he was born from Yasoda with two hands.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Hari-vaṁśa describes the order of the Lord. vasudeva-vacaḥ śrutvā rūpaṁ saṁharat acyutaḥ anujṣāpya pitṛtvena nanda-gopa-gṛhaṁ naya Hearing Vasudeva’s words, the Lord withdrew his form, requesting with affection for his father “Please take me to Nanda’s house.” Samḥarat means “withdraw.” He then requested with affection for his father (pitṛtvena), “Take me to Nanda’s house.” Vasudeva carefully (sam) took (ādāya) the child from the maternity room. He put the child to sleep in a box lined with soft cloth, placed the container on his head, or raising it up carefully with his two hands, placed it on his breast, embracing it with his arms. He was indescribably fortunate (saḥ). The chains on his feet became loose by themselves. Hari-vaṁśa describes the following. Navamyām eva saṁjātāKkṛṣṇa-pakṣasya vai tithiau: Yogamāyā was born on the Navamī tithi of the waning moon (slightly after Kṛṣṇa).

    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa orchestrates the swap with Yoga-māyā Himself — your duty is to act on His prompt with daksya, even when the path looks impossible.
    Practical Applications
    • Identify one task today where you have been waiting for ideal conditions, and act on the inner prompting now with full skill (daksya), trusting Kṛṣṇa arranges what you cannot.
    • Refuse to dramatize your role — like Vasudeva, do the next concrete step (pick up the child, walk out the door) without theatrics or self-congratulation (adambhitva).
    • When an obstacle dissolves unexpectedly today, pause and acknowledge aloud that Yoga-māyā arranged it, not your cleverness.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life is Kṛṣṇa already arranging the 'Yoga-māyā' — the protective covering that lets me act — and where am I instead crediting my own resourcefulness for what was actually His orchestration?
    • Like Vasudeva, who worshiped his son as Viṣṇu rather than embracing Him as Yaśodā did, where does my reverence for Kṛṣṇa's Godhood become a barrier to the simple, intimate affection He actually wants from me?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Before your next exam or audition, do the Vasudeva move: prepare with full dākṣya (your notes, your sleep, your mock tests), then at the doorway hand the outcome over to Kṛṣṇa out loud. Notice the difference between this and the Instagram version of 'manifesting.'
    • Pick one friendship or group chat where you have been performing a version of yourself — that is ahaṅkāra, not adambhitva. Drop the performance for one full week and watch who stays. Yaśodā loved Kṛṣṇa without the title 'Bhagavān'; let your friends love (or leave) the unstyled you.
    • When peer pressure says 'everyone is doing it,' practice discriminative wisdom by asking a sharper question than 'is this right or wrong?' Ask: 'If Yoga-māyā is arranging this moment for my training, what is she actually testing — my courage, my taste, or my willingness to be uncool?'
    householder
    • In the next family financial decision, separate dākṣya (do the spreadsheet, get the second opinion, run the numbers) from ahaṅkāra (assuming the outcome depends on your cleverness). Vasudeva still had to walk through the river; Yoga-māyā still parted it. Both are required.
    • Watch for the Vasudeva-trap with your children: worshiping them as projects to be optimized rather than souls to be loved. One evening this week, sit with your child the way Yaśodā sat with Kṛṣṇa — no agenda, no future, no metric. Notice your discomfort.
    • Audit one place where you are publicly pious and privately calculating — the office Diwali party, the temple donation, the in-laws' visit. Adambhitva does not mean confessing it; it means quietly closing the gap this month so the inner and outer act match.
    senior
    • You have already 'transitioned' through more bodies than the youth around you — student, earner, parent. Today, name one attachment from an earlier āśrama you are still carrying past its season (a title, a grievance, a hobby-as-identity) and begin the loosening. Vasudeva had to set the child down in another house; you too will set things down.
    • Mentor one younger person this month not by giving advice, but by telling them one specific story of a time you mistook Yoga-māyā's arrangement for your own competence. Discriminative wisdom transmits better through honest narrative than through instruction.
    • Each night before sleep, do the Vasudeva rehearsal: imagine being asked, at this very hour, to carry the most precious thing in your life out of the locked room of your body and hand it over. What resists? That resistance is the work remaining.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating the simultaneous appearance of Kṛṣṇa and Yoga-māyā as mere mythological coincidence rather than a precise teaching about how the Lord personally arranges every detail for His devotee — and then concluding 'I just got lucky' when His arrangements unfold in my own life.
    • Using Vasudeva's awe-laden mood as the spiritual ideal while quietly dismissing Yaśodā's parental affection as 'lower' — inverting Viśvanātha Cakravartī's actual point that pure affection without consciousness of Godhood is in fact the higher position.
    • Imitating Vasudeva's daksya — moving the child, executing the plan — without his prior bhagavat-pracoditaḥ, the inner prompting; acting decisively on our own initiative and calling it surrender, when real skill in action means waiting to be moved by Him.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Vasudeva worshiped his newborn as Lord Viṣṇu, while Yaśodā simply loved her son without knowing His Godhood. Which mood is closer to your own bhakti right now — reverence at a distance or intimacy without theology — and which one do you secretly think is 'higher'? Defend your answer to your partner, then let them push back.
    • Yoga-māyā arranges the entire exchange — the chains fall, the guards sleep, the river parts. Where in your own life have you mistaken Yoga-māyā's arrangement for your own resourcefulness (dākṣya)? Share one concrete example, and let the group test whether you are crediting Kṛṣṇa or quietly crediting yourself.
    • Vasudeva acts the moment he is 'inspired by the Supreme Personality of Godhead' — not before, not after. How do you distinguish bhagavat-pracodita (genuine inner direction from Kṛṣṇa) from your own ahaṅkāra dressed up as inspiration? Disagree with your partner if their test sounds too easy.
    Role Play

    Two students play Vasudeva and a sympathetic but skeptical neighbor. Vasudeva has just been told (inwardly) to carry a newborn out of a guarded prison cell, across a flooding river, into another man's house, and swap babies. The neighbor catches him at the door and says, 'You are a sober, lawful man. This is theft, abandonment, and madness. Sit down, wait until morning, and we will talk to Kaṁsa together.' Vasudeva must respond — not by quoting scripture, but by articulating, in his own words, what bhagavat-pracodita feels like from the inside and why obedience to it overrides every prudential and social dharma in this moment. After five minutes, switch roles. Then debrief: when did the 'Vasudeva' sound like a fanatic, and when did he sound like a dhīra acting under Kṛṣṇa's direction? What is the difference?

    Objections & Responses
    • This whole episode reads like a fairy tale — sleeping guards, a baby switched in the night, a goddess born on cue. Treating it as literal history seems intellectually dishonest in 2026.
      Notice what the verse actually emphasizes: not the magic, but the simultaneity. Kṛṣṇa appears in Mathurā and in Vraja in the same instant; Yoga-māyā takes birth in Nanda's house at the exact moment Vasudeva lifts the child. The point is not 'isn't it amazing that the guards fell asleep' — the point is that the Supreme Person and His internal energy are coordinating reality at a level our ordinary causation cannot reach. To call that a fairy tale is to assume in advance that nothing exists outside the material register the senses report. The Gauḍīya line does not ask you to suspend reason; it asks you to admit that reason, unaided, cannot adjudicate what is possible for the source of reason. Sit with the verse for a year and watch which framing — 'charming myth' or 'literal arrangement of Yoga-māyā' — actually changes how you live. The tradition is empirical in that sense.
    • Vasudeva worshiping his own son as Viṣṇu sounds cold and theological, while Yaśodā's plain motherly love sounds warmer and more real. Why would the tradition prize the awe-struck father over the loving mother?
      It does not — and this is exactly Viśvanātha Cakravartī's point. Yaśodā's vātsalya, where she does not even register Kṛṣṇa's Godhood, is in fact higher in the Gauḍīya estimation than Vasudeva's reverent worship. Vasudeva loves Kṛṣṇa as Bhagavān; Yaśodā loves Kṛṣṇa as her son who needs his face wiped. Aiśvarya-jñāna (knowledge of His majesty) keeps a respectful distance; mādhurya and vātsalya let Him be tied to a grinding mortar. The verse is not asking you to choose theology over love — it is showing you two authentic moods and quietly indicating which one Kṛṣṇa Himself prefers to receive. The corrective the verse offers a modern reader is the opposite of what the objection assumes: do not collapse Kṛṣṇa into a generic 'divine spark' to make Him relatable. Honor His Personhood first; then the intimacy of Vraja becomes available, not as sentimentality, but as the real thing.
    Analogy

    Two acts must happen simultaneously for a substitution to work — the prince must leave the palace at the very instant the decoy enters it, or the timing fails. Yoga-māyā's birth as Nanda-Yaśodā's daughter at the exact moment Vasudeva lifts Kṛṣṇa to leave the prison is this choreographed simultaneity. Bhagavān's līlā is not improvised; it is precisely timed by His own internal śakti.

    Stories
    Yoga-māyā throughout the Bhāgavatam

    Yoga-māyā is named as the orchestrator of Bhagavān's līlās — She arranges the rāsa-līlā (10.29.1), conceals Kṛṣṇa's divinity from Yaśodā (10.7-9), arranges the Mahābhārata's outcomes, even hides Kṛṣṇa from Brahmā during brahma-vimohana-līlā. She is the personal śakti who makes līlā possible.

    This verse marks Her own birth as Nanda-Yaśodā's daughter — Subhadrā / Ekānaṁśā, later worshipped at Vindhyācala. The Gauḍīya tradition recognizes Yoga-māyā as Kṛṣṇa's hlādinī-saṁvit-sandhinī-śakti in her līlā-managing form; mādhurya-rasa runs through Her arrangement.
